name: Credential compromise with a delayed, unrelated second stage
description: A state-sponsored actor harvesting credentials and network descriptions to sell on. The follow-on may arrive weeks later from a different actor with different objectives, including ransomware.
logic: Treat a credential compromise as an event with a delayed second stage rather than an intrusion that either progressed or did not. Re-examine affected accounts weeks later.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.source.user.username in (<compromised_accounts>) and _time > compromise_date + 14d
caveat: Changes incident closure criteria rather than detection. A credential compromise with no observed follow-on is not necessarily contained, and closing it as unexploited is the error this prevents.

name: Accessibility feature used to launch a command shell
description: The sticky keys accessibility binary was used to launch a command shell, probably to change a password. The technique needs no malware, survives reboots and is reachable before anyone has logged in.
logic: Two forms, both cheap to cover: the accessibility binary as the parent of a shell at runtime, and the binary being replaced or debugger-hijacked on disk. The second is the persistence and can be checked as configuration state rather than waiting for execution.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.source.process.name in ("sethc.exe", "utilman.exe", "osk.exe", "magnify.exe", "narrator.exe", "displayswitch.exe") and xdm.target.process.name in ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe")
caveat: Reachable from the pre-authentication logon screen, so it grants a shell without any credential. Legitimate execution of these binaries as a parent of a shell is effectively zero.

name: Public claims of compromise that are not true
description: An actor persona claimed responsibility on a messaging channel for numerous attacks on critical infrastructure, and the authoring agencies record that several of those claimed compromises were false. Claims are a means of effect in themselves.
logic: A verification discipline rather than a detection. When named publicly, confirm or refute against your own telemetry before responding, and be prepared to state a position, because a false claim consumes the same response capacity and causes the same reputational effect as a real one.
caveat: Worth preparing for because the asymmetry favours the claimant: fabricating a claim is free, and refuting one requires evidence and retention you either have or do not. Where a hacktivist persona is involved, treat the claim and the compromise as two separate questions.

name: Group names picked to point at the wrong country
description: Reporting agencies stated they are aware of multiple ransomware groups choosing foreign-language names, almost certainly to complicate attribution, and named one group likely based in a country entirely different from the one its name suggests.
logic: An analytical constraint rather than a query. The group's name, the language of its notes and the apparent nationality of its branding are all attacker-chosen and carry no evidential weight. Attribution has to rest on infrastructure, tooling and operating hours.

markers.expr: attribution_basis includes infrastructure_or_tooling rather than group_name_or_note_language

caveat: Matters where geography drives a decision: sanctions screening before payment, insurance conditions, and regulatory notification that turns on the actor's nationality. A name-based inference in any of those is unsafe, and this is the third mechanism in this corpus for deliberately corrupting attribution.

name: The intruder is reading your investigation
description: The actor was observed targeting the mailboxes of key personnel including information technology and incident response staff. The advisory separately warns that organisations with suspected compromise must be conscious of operational security while responding and planning remediation.
logic: Treat the responder population as a monitored group in its own right: access to their mailboxes and files, mailbox rules created on their accounts, and access to the incident documentation itself. This is a detection to run during a response, not before one.
caveat: Changes how a response is conducted rather than what is detected. If eviction is planned in email and documents the actor can read, the actor leaves before eviction and returns by a route the plan did not cover. The practical control is out-of-band coordination during response, which has to be arranged before it is needed. Also note that access to a responder's mailbox is indistinguishable from ordinary access unless the responder population is specifically watched.

name: Detect the stage, not the ransomware family
description: Where ransomware operates as a service with largely unconnected affiliates, techniques vary widely between intrusions using the same family. A detection built on one family's observed techniques fails against the next intrusion using it.
logic: Detect the stages every affiliate must pass through regardless of tooling: initial access via an exposed service, privilege escalation, recovery inhibition, bulk file modification, exfiltration before encryption.
xql_sketch: see pat-shadow-copy-deletion, pat-mass-process-termination, pat-exfiltration-utility-execution; the stages are the query set
caveat: Not a query. It is why this corpus records ransomware behaviour as shared patterns rather than per-family records, and worth stating because per-family indicator lists are what most organisations are handed.

name: Alarm thresholds changed so nothing will be raised
description: Alarm settings altered on control assets, so that a process excursion no longer produces an alarm. ATT&CK notes asset application logs may record the change but that not all assets produce such logs, and recommends consulting asset management for the expected settings.
logic: Compare the alarm configuration held on the asset against the authoritative engineering record. Where the asset logs configuration changes, alert on alarm limit and enable-state changes outside a change window; where it does not, this becomes a periodic reconciliation rather than an event detection.
caveat: Widening a limit is quieter than disabling an alarm and achieves the same result, so compare against the safe operating envelope rather than against the enabled flag alone. ATT&CK is explicit that many assets do not log this at all, which makes the engineering record the only authoritative copy and its accuracy the whole of the control.
derived_from: MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 (c) The MITRE Corporation, ATT&CK Terms of Use

name: What proportion of alerts a human actually opens
description: An incident response engagement found the endpoint tool had generated the alerts that revealed the intrusion, and nobody had been reading them. An unreviewed alert is indistinguishable from no detection.
logic: Measure alerts raised against alerts triaged per alert class, median time to first review, and how many alert classes have never been reviewed at all.
xql_sketch: dataset = <alert_dataset> | comp count() as raised, count(if(triaged = true, 1, null)) as reviewed by alert_class | alter coverage = reviewed / raised | sort asc coverage
caveat: A resourcing measurement rather than a query, and it usually surfaces an uncomfortable number. Every alert-fidelity detection in this corpus assumes somebody reads the output.

name: Targeted for who you supply, not for what you run
description: Five national authorities warned that organisations well beyond the conflict region faced increased activity as a response to economic measures and to materiel support provided to one side. The selection criterion is the organisation's country and its commercial relationships, not any property of its technology.
logic: A targeting model rather than a query, and it changes who has to raise their posture. Establish whether your organisation, your parent, your customers or your suppliers are in a category named by a threat actor as a legitimate target. If so, the threat level moved without anything in the estate changing.
caveat: The uncomfortable implication is that a risk assessment based on asset criticality and vulnerability count cannot see this. Nothing technical changes; the reason to attack you changes. It also means a supplier's alignment can make you a target through a trusted connection you did not consider part of your attack surface.

name: Payload hidden in an alternate data stream
description: Content written to or executed from an NTFS alternate data stream, where it does not appear in a directory listing and does not change the visible file size. A long-standing hiding place that many tools still do not inspect.
logic: A colon appearing inside a file path where it is not the drive separator, in either a file write or a process command line. Also cover the two utilities most often used to read streams back and the index allocation stream name used to hide directories.

markers.note: a second colon after the drive letter is the stream separator

caveat: Some backup, endpoint and security products legitimately create streams, notably the zone identifier stream on downloaded files, which must be excluded or the rule is unusable. Exclude the zone identifier explicitly rather than by wildcard.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: An implant built to defeat interval analysis and sandboxes
description: The backdoor checked for hard-coded address ranges including reserved space to detect analysis environments and stopped executing if found, and used threshold checks to make delays between command attempts unpredictable.
logic: The counter to interval-based beacon detection. Where jitter defeats periodicity, fall back on properties the implant cannot randomise: the destination set over a long window, the ratio of sent to received bytes, sessions with no name lookup and no browser string, and connections from processes with no business making them.
caveat: Recorded specifically as the limit of the periodic check-in pattern elsewhere in this corpus. A detection tuned to a regular interval will not fire here, and a sandbox verdict of benign may only mean the sample recognised the sandbox. Where dynamic analysis returns nothing, that is not evidence the file is safe.

name: Four ways to find something you have no indicator for
description: The same authorities set out the technical approaches an investigation needs: searching known indicators, frequency analysis against normal baselines, pattern analysis to separate automated and routine human activity from noise, and analyst-led anomaly review. Indicator search is only the first of four.
logic: An assurance question about capability rather than a rule. For each of the four, ask whether the team can actually do it with the data held: indicator search needs retention and coverage; frequency analysis needs a baseline across timing, source, destination, port, protocol, file location, hash, size and naming; pattern analysis needs enough history to separate automation from people; anomaly review needs analysts with system administration experience.

markers.expr: baseline_exists_across(timing, source, destination, port, protocol, file_location, hash, size, naming)

caveat: Most programmes can do the first and struggle with the other three, which is why they depend on somebody else publishing an indicator first. Frequency and pattern analysis are what find the activity nobody has written an indicator for yet, and they need retention and baselines rather than feeds.

name: Work the annual most-exploited list against your own exposure
description: An annual joint publication names the vulnerabilities most routinely exploited in the preceding year across many vendors. The closest thing to an evidence-based prioritisation list for a mixed estate.
logic: Join each annual list, not only the current one, against the externally reachable inventory to produce a defensible remediation order. Recurrence of the same flaws year on year is itself a finding.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | join (dataset = <annual_exploited_lists>) as l l.cve = cve_id | comp count() by product_class, l.year
caveat: Publication lags the year it describes, so it is a review instrument rather than early warning. Pair with the continuously updated known-exploited catalogue for current work.

name: Bulk directory or file system enumeration from an unexpected host
description: Listed as a missed detection opportunity in its own right across red team assessments, alongside network file system enumeration.
logic: Query volume on directory and network file system ports per source host against that host's own baseline. Workstations should be near zero.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (389, 636, 3268, 3269, 2049) | comp count() as queries by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 1h) | filter queries > <host_baseline>
caveat: Identity management, inventory and monitoring products query constantly and dominate any volume ranking. Exclude by asset role first.

name: Traffic to and from an anonymising network
description: Agencies described actors using an anonymising overlay network for reconnaissance, intrusion, exfiltration, denial of service, ransomware delivery and to relay command traffic, obscuring the location and ownership of their servers, and recommended organisations assess their own risk then block or closely monitor traffic to and from known nodes.
logic: Two directions with very different meanings. Inbound from exit nodes is background noise on anything internet-facing and is a filtering decision. Outbound from an internal host to an entry or guard node is the high-value one, because almost nothing in a managed estate has a legitimate reason to reach that network, and it indicates either command traffic or a user deliberately evading controls.
caveat: The node lists are published and change constantly, so this needs an automatically updated feed rather than a static list. Blocking inbound wholesale is a risk decision rather than a security one, since the same network carries legitimate use, but outbound from a server or a control-network host has essentially no legitimate case.

name: Protection disabled by editing its configuration rather than stopping it
description: Before encrypting, actors removed virus definitions and disabled the platform's built-in protection through registry settings. The service may still appear to be running while having nothing to detect with.
logic: Writes to the protection product's policy keys, and execution of its own command-line utility with removal or disable arguments. A health check that only asks whether the service is running will report healthy, so the registry state is what has to be checked.
caveat: Worth pairing with an alert on protection coverage or definition age degrading across many hosts, because that is the consequence and it usually surfaces in a management console nobody alerts from. Distinct from the policy-based fleet-wide variant, which is a directory-side detection.

name: Treat an antivirus hit as a lead, not a resolution
description: A large body of external rules alerts on the antivirus product's own detection events rather than on the malware, grouping them by what was found: exploitation framework signatures, password dumper signatures, remote access tool signatures, and named threat-actor tooling.
logic: Forward antivirus detections into the log platform and treat the signature category as the signal. A blocked exploitation framework or credential dumper means someone reached the point of deploying it, which is an intrusion regardless of whether that particular file was stopped. Alert on category and on repeated detections for one host or user, not on volume.

markers.expr: av_signature_category in (exploitation_framework, password_dumper, remote_access_tool, webshell, hacktool)

caveat: The common failure is treating a blocked detection as a closed matter. Several records in this corpus describe actors who retried, disabled protection, or arrived with tooling the product did not recognise, so the block tells you the adversary was present and not that they left. Requires antivirus telemetry to reach the log platform at all, which is often assumed rather than verified.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Appliance memory leaked in a response, containing a live session token
description: A crafted request header caused a remote access appliance to return system memory contents, which included a valid session cookie. The actor then established an authenticated session with no username, no password and no second factor.
logic: Two halves. On the request side, an anomalous or oversized host header on the appliance's own web endpoints. On the response side, a session appearing in the appliance's authentication log with no preceding credential submission, which is the same absence-of-authentication shape as a forged token.

markers.expr: stddev(response_length) by url_path, source_ip exceeds measured_baseline_for_that_endpoint

markers.note: trigger for the first identifier in this class only; retained as an example, not as the detection
two of five known triggers; every subsequent identifier has used a different path, so this ages by design

caveat: Defeats both the password and the second factor at once, so an appliance protected by strong authentication is fully exposed. Patching does not end it: sessions established before the patch stay valid, which makes terminating all active sessions a mandatory second step that is easy to omit.

name: Integrity monitoring on the application, not just the operating system
description: Altering what an application decides means changing its code or configuration. Most file integrity monitoring covers system paths and stops there, which is where the manipulation is not.
logic: File integrity monitoring extended to the business application's own binaries and configuration, suppressed against the deployment process.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.path in (<application_paths>) and xdm.event.operation_sub_type in ("file_write", "file_replace") | filter change_window = false
caveat: Application updates write to the same paths, so deployment suppression is required. Its value is covering the layer where manipulation lives and monitoring usually is not.

name: Archive created in a web-served directory and then requested
description: Collected data was compressed into an archive placed inside a directory the web server publishes, then retrieved with an ordinary request. Exfiltration used the application's own delivery path, so no outbound connection from the host was needed.
logic: Two halves that are weak alone and strong together: an archive file written beneath a web root, and a subsequent successful request for that file. The second half means the data actually left.
xql_sketch: dataset = <file_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)(webapps|htdocs|wwwroot|/images/|js-lib)" and xdm.target.file.extension in ("tar", "gz", "zip", "7z", "rar")
caveat: Catches exfiltration that never appears as an outbound connection from the compromised host, which is why egress monitoring alone misses it. Requires file write telemetry on servers, which is often collected only on endpoints.

name: Archive utility creating an executable child
description: Archive exploitation relies on the tool launching something other than the file the user selected. An archiver exists to extract files, not run them, so the parent-child pairing is close to unambiguous.
logic: Parent process is an archive utility and child is a shell, scripting engine or signed binary commonly used to run remote code.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.source.process.name in ("winrar.exe", "rar.exe", "unrar.exe", "7z.exe", "7zfm.exe") and xdm.target.process.name in ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "wscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe")
caveat: Self-extracting installers legitimately spawn processes from an archiver context. Identifiable by signer; the exception list is short.

name: Timed for when nobody is on shift
description: Agencies observed increasingly impactful attacks on holidays and weekends, assessing that actors view periods when offices are closed as attractive because fewer defenders and support staff are available.
logic: A resourcing question with a measurable answer: what is the median time to first human review of a high-severity alert at 03:00 on a public holiday, compared with a weekday afternoon. If that number is not known, the exposure is not known either.
caveat: The cheapest thing in this corpus to know and one of the least often measured. It also argues for weighting automated containment higher than analyst-dependent response for the highest-severity detections, because the attacker has chosen the moment when analysts are absent.

name: A new device enrolled onto the tenant by the intruder
description: Having bypassed password authentication and then a second factor through repeated push requests, actors registered their own device on the victim's cloud tenant. Where device validation rules are not configured, the registration succeeds and the device is thereafter trusted.
logic: Device registration and join events, evaluated against whether the device meets enrolment policy and whether the account has registered a device before. A registration shortly after repeated failed or rapidly repeated second-factor prompts is the sequence worth alerting on.

markers.expr: count(mfa_prompt) by account, bin(_time, 15m) preceding registration

caveat: Registration converts a stolen session into durable, policy-compliant access, so it is the moment the compromise becomes persistent. Device validation rules are the control and their absence is the finding; the advisory is explicit that registration succeeds when they are not configured.

name: Tooling hosted on somebody else's legitimate domain
description: The actor used web hosting credentials stolen from victims outside its usual target set to host scripts and tools, creating subdomains on those legitimate domains that imitated well-known mail providers. Separately, domain registration hijacking was used to take over legitimate domains as launch points.
logic: Domain age, reputation and category all return reassuring answers because the domain is genuinely old and genuinely legitimate. The discriminators that survive are the subdomain imitating a service the parent domain has no relationship with, and a newly observed subdomain on an established domain.
caveat: This is the case where reputation feeds actively mislead: the parent domain is a real organisation with real history, and its owner is a victim who does not know. Blocking the parent domain harms them and is usually wrong; the subdomain is the unit to act on.

name: Declining to attribute when the evidence is not yours
description: Two agencies acknowledged open-source reporting attributing a campaign to a named state group, then stated they were still investigating and had not attributed it to any actor at that time, and would update as information became available.
logic: A reporting discipline rather than a detection. Separate what your own telemetry supports from what you are repeating, and record which is which, because downstream decisions about disclosure, insurance and regulatory notification may turn on the actor's identity.
caveat: Worth holding as a standard given how many records in this corpus involve deliberate attribution corruption: a state actor branding itself criminal, a wiper branding itself ransomware, a group named to point at the wrong country, and shared infrastructure serving several actors at once. Repeating an attribution confidently is easy and frequently wrong.

name: The audit policy itself edited so later actions are not recorded
description: Changing the host audit policy or disabling event channels, so that subsequent activity is never written to a log at all. Distinct from clearing logs after the fact, because nothing is generated to clear.
logic: The audit policy utility being run with disable arguments, edits to the channel configuration keys, and the platform's own policy-change event. Central forwarding is what makes any of this survivable, since the whole purpose is to stop local recording.
caveat: More serious than log clearing and less often covered. Clearing leaves a gap you can see; disabling auditing leaves a period that looks genuinely quiet. If the audit policy is not itself monitored centrally, there is no way to distinguish the two afterwards.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Successful login where no second factor was presented
description: A remote access flaw skipped the second factor when the username case was altered, so organisations that had correctly enabled two-factor authentication were bypassed anyway. Every configuration check would have reported the control as working.
logic: Record per successful authentication whether a factor was actually presented, not whether policy requires one. Any success without a presented factor is a misconfiguration or a bypass.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS" and second_factor_presented = false | filter gateway in (<mfa_required_gateways>)
caveat: Many gateways log only that authentication succeeded, not whether a factor was presented. Where that field is absent this cannot be written and the inventory check will report the control as working.

name: Downloads and persistence through the operating system's own transfer service
description: The background intelligent transfer service will fetch a file and run a command on completion, surviving reboots, with the traffic attributed to a platform service rather than to the calling process. Both a download route and a persistence mechanism.
logic: Three surfaces. The command-line utility with a transfer or notify argument. The service's own distinctive user agent in web logs, which reveals the transfer even when the calling process is unknown. And the job database on disk holding queued jobs that survive reboot.

markers.note: BITS-Client operational log: job started, stopped, and error

caveat: The service is used legitimately by platform update mechanisms and by some management agents, so the user agent alone is not actionable. The notify-command argument is the highest-value marker because it is the persistence half and has almost no legitimate use.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Whether the backups are reachable, and whether a restore has been proven
description: Against destructive malware, recovery capability decides the outcome. A backup reachable from the network it protects is a target, not a control.
logic: Two inventory questions: which backup repositories are reachable from the protected networks, and when a restore of system configuration and operational logic was last actually performed rather than a backup job merely succeeding.
xql_sketch: dataset = <backup_inventory> | filter reachable_from_protected_network = true or timestamp_diff(current_time(), last_restore_test, "DAY") > 180
caveat: Not something a detection platform answers. An inventory and exercise question, which is why it gets missed until it matters.

name: Outbound session with no name lookup and no browser string
description: Two absences, each cheap to test, both far more valuable when joined to a host-side signal such as a binary running for the first time.
logic: Outbound sessions to an address with no preceding name lookup from that host, and web requests with an absent or empty browser identification string.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | join type = left (dataset = <dns_dataset>) as d d.answer = xdm.target.ipv4 | filter d.answer = null and xdm.network.http.browser = null
caveat: Monitoring agents and update clients connect to hard-coded addresses with no browser string. Needs a known-good list before it reads as anything.

name: A clean first contact that exists only to earn the second
description: The actor exchanged several harmless interview-themed emails to agree a date and build rapport, sent the malicious document only once the target had agreed, then cancelled the interview. The first message carries nothing to detect.
logic: Defeats first-contact heuristics by design, because the first contact is genuinely benign. The detectable moment is the thread turning: an established external thread that suddenly carries an attachment or a file-sharing link. Score the thread, not the message.

markers.expr: count(prior_clean_messages) in thread with same external sender

markers.note: the payload arrived as a file-sharing link in the body as often as an attachment

caveat: Awareness training built on 'unexpected email from a stranger' does not cover this, because by the time the payload arrives the sender is expected and known. The cancellation afterwards is a useful retrospective marker but arrives too late to act on.

name: Learning about it from someone selling your data
description: The victim organisation was notified that documents containing host and user information, including metadata, had been posted on a dark web brokerage site. The intrusion was discovered from the sale, not from any internal signal.
logic: Two things follow. Monitor brokerage and leak sites for your own identifiers, your host naming conventions and your supplier names, because that channel found this one. And when a listing appears, use its contents to scope: what was listed tells you what was reached, which is often the only starting point available.

markers.expr: external_exposure_monitoring covers own_identifiers, host_naming_conventions and supplier_names

caveat: Worth recording plainly because it is common and uncomfortable: the detection that worked was somebody else's. Host and user information with metadata is also unusually useful to a buyer, since it is the reconnaissance a second actor would otherwise have to perform.

name: Malware watching the browser for a banking session
description: A banking trojan infiltrated browsers, detected access to online banking applications and injected code and keylogging through interface hooking to steal customer login information, enabling fraudulent payment instructions afterwards.
logic: The hooking itself: a process injecting into or loading a module inside the browser that is not a known extension or security product. On the outcome side, the fraud is a business signal rather than a technical one, which makes reconciliation of payment instructions a detection surface in its own right.
caveat: The loss event is a payment, not an outage, so it surfaces in finance rather than in security and often days later. That makes out-of-band verification of payment instructions the control that actually limits the damage, independent of whether the endpoint compromise was ever detected.

name: Browser credential database opened by something other than the browser
description: The credential stores are a small fixed set of file names in predictable locations, independent of how any particular tool copies them.
logic: File access to browser credential databases by any process other than the owning browser or an approved backup product.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.name in ("key4.db", "logins.json", "Login Data", "cookies.sqlite") | filter xdm.source.process.name not in ("firefox.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
caveat: Backup and endpoint management software reads these paths; allow-list by signer. Browser processes must be excluded or this is constant noise.

name: A browser extension as the persistence and collection mechanism
description: The actor used an extension published in the official browser store to steal credentials and maintain access. An extension survives reboot, sits inside the browser's own trust boundary, and reads every page the user visits including after authentication.
logic: Inventory installed extensions against an approved list, and alert on force-installed policy entries nobody set. An extension reads content after decryption and after authentication, so nothing on the network shows what it took.
caveat: Presence in the official store is not a trust boundary; this extension was published there. Session tokens taken this way defeat multi-factor authentication because the factor was already satisfied when the token was minted.

name: Failed authentications followed by a success
description: The success after the failures is the signal. Failures alone are background noise on anything exposed. Spraying inverts the shape, few attempts across many accounts, so count both directions.
logic: Per account and per source, count failures in a window and report where a success follows inside the same window. Separately, count distinct accounts attempted per source.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | comp count(if(xdm.event.outcome = "FAILED", 1, null)) as fails, count(if(xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS", 1, null)) as wins, count_distinct(xdm.source.user.username) as accounts by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 1h) | filter (fails > 10 and wins > 0) or accounts > 20
caveat: Password changes and misconfigured service accounts produce this daily. Requiring the success to come from a source with no history sharpens it a lot.

markers.expr: count(auth_failure) by account, source, bin(_time, 5m) preceding a success

name: Build pipeline changes, signing key use and reproducible output
description: A build server compromise yields source code, signing certificates and the ability to alter what ships. Ordinary server monitoring does not cover any of the three things that matter here.
logic: Watch build definition and pipeline configuration changes outside the review process, signing key use not tied to a build from a reviewed commit, and build output hashes that do not match a rebuild from the same source.
xql_sketch: dataset = <cicd_audit_dataset> | filter event_type in ("pipeline_config_change", "signing_key_use") | filter actor not in (<authorised_pipeline_editors>)
caveat: Very few organisations can answer the reproducible-build question today. Where they cannot, signing key usage records are the practical fallback.

name: Bulk retrieval from an application whose job is moving data
description: Where the objective is theft rather than encryption, the observable is volume rather than damage. Hardest in products that legitimately move large volumes.
logic: Volume of data read out per session and per account against that application's own baseline. Only rate and requesting identity distinguish theft from use.
xql_sketch: dataset = <application_dataset> | comp sum(bytes_downloaded) as volume by xdm.source.user.username, bin(_time, 1h) | join type = left (<account_baseline>) as b b.user = xdm.source.user.username | filter volume > b.p95 * 5
caveat: The baseline must be per account rather than global, or the heaviest legitimate users mask everything.

name: Phishing that genuinely comes from a trusted sender
description: A sophisticated actor used a compromised end-user account at a legitimate email marketing company to impersonate a government organisation and distribute links to malicious destinations, reaching government, intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations.
logic: Sender authentication passes because the mail genuinely originates from the marketing platform, and the platform's reputation is good. So the discriminators are the mismatch between the claimed sending organisation and the platform account sending on its behalf, and the destination of the links rather than the origin of the message.

markers.expr: spf_dkim_dmarc_pass and claimed_sending_organisation not in known_senders_via_that_platform

caveat: Defeats every sender-authentication control simultaneously, because the authentication is correct: the mail really is from the marketing platform, sent by an account that platform legitimately holds. Reputation blocking would take out a widely used commercial service, so the only workable surface is the link destination.

name: Whole file shares leaving, measured in terabytes
description: Actors compressed and exfiltrated very large volumes, in many cases entire network-connected shared drives exceeding a terabyte, using open source tools and file transfer services.
logic: Volume is the signal and it is unmissable if anyone is measuring egress per host. Also cover the staging step, since archiving a share to local disk precedes the transfer and produces a large archive in a place archives do not belong.
caveat: A terabyte leaving a single host is one of the few genuinely obvious signals in this corpus, and it is missed because egress volume per host is often not measured at all. Where the exfiltration is to a file transfer service, the destination is also usually new for that host.

name: Outbound session to a high port nothing legitimate uses
description: Command traffic sent directly to an address on adjacent high-numbered ports carrying encoded data. The port numbers are configuration and will change; the absence of any legitimate business use of high ports is what lasts.
logic: Build an allow-list of permitted outbound destination ports and report everything outside it, weighting up where the destination was reached by address with no preceding name lookup.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port not in (<permitted_egress_ports>) and xdm.target.domain = null | comp count() by xdm.source.host.hostname, xdm.target.ipv4, xdm.target.port
caveat: Specific port numbers from any one campaign will not recur. An egress port allow-list catches the next campaign as well as this one.

name: Command traffic carried over public code hosting or file sharing
description: The destination is a legitimate, widely used service with a valid certificate and good reputation, so the question has to be who in the organisation genuinely uses it and from where.
logic: Connections to public code hosting and file sharing services, weighted heavily where the source is a server or a control-network host rather than a developer workstation.
xql_sketch: dataset = <proxy_dataset> | filter xdm.target.domain in (<public_file_services>) | join (dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter role in ("server", "ot")) as a a.hostname = xdm.source.host.hostname
caveat: Alerting outright produces heavy false positives in most organisations. Narrowing to servers and operator stations makes it defensible.

name: What your exposed cameras can see, and who is watching them
description: Cameras were targeted at scale to observe physical movement of goods, with no network compromise needed. The camera is the intelligence source, which reframes the question from what it gives access to towards what it can see.
logic: Enumerate cameras and recorders reachable from outside, record what each overlooks, and review who authenticates to them. Default credentials remain the dominant route in.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter device_type in ("camera", "nvr") and external_reachable = true | comp count() by site, view_subject, default_credentials_changed
caveat: Cameras are usually owned by facilities or physical security, so they are often absent from the asset inventory and outside any patch process. Establishing ownership is the first obstacle.

name: Certificates and their private keys taken off the host
description: External rules cover certificates exported from the local store, private keys acquired, extraction through the platform certificate utility, and dedicated tooling for abusing certificate services.
logic: Export operations against the certificate store, the platform certificate utility invoked with export arguments, and the named tooling for certificate service abuse. A private key marked exportable being exported is the specific event; certificates without keys are far less useful to an attacker.
caveat: Worth more than its rule count suggests, because a stolen certificate with its private key produces authentication that is cryptographically correct and survives password rotation entirely. That is the same failure mode as the forged-token records in this corpus, and remediation means reissuing the certificate rather than resetting anything.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: All fixes in a chain, not the highest-scoring subset
description: Two exploit chains against one appliance family each combined an administrative bypass with a code execution or injection flaw. The bypass often scores lower than what it enables, so severity-ranked patching can leave a chain open.
logic: Treat a chained advisory as requiring every named fix. For detection, look for requests reaching administrative endpoints with no preceding authentication event for that session.
xql_sketch: dataset = <appliance_dataset> | filter xdm.network.http.url in (<admin_endpoints>) | join type = left (dataset = <auth_dataset>) as a a.session = session_id | filter a.session = null
caveat: A real failure mode of scoring-based prioritisation: the low-scoring bypass is the component that makes the high-scoring flaw reachable.

name: Failed cloud authentication across accounts or from one source
description: External rules cover high numbers of failed authentications for a single user, from a single address, and multiple users failing to authenticate from one source, alongside password policy changes and second-factor disablement.
logic: Count in both directions, since spraying inverts the shape of brute force: many failures for one account, and few failures each across many accounts from one source. Pair with the configuration events that make either easier, namely password policy weakening and second-factor disablement.
caveat: The cloud form of a pattern this corpus already holds for on-premises directories, and it is worth stating separately because the telemetry, the thresholds and the owning team are usually all different. Federated tenants may not log the failure at the provider at all if it happened at the identity provider, so confirm where failures are recorded before setting a bound.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: Cloud credentials fetched through the provider's own interface
description: External rules cover retrieval of instance passwords, database password resets, and console credential access, all performed through documented provider interfaces by a principal that already holds some access.
logic: Credential-retrieval operations in the provider audit trail, evaluated on whether the calling principal has performed that operation before and whether it is one of the small set that legitimately should. Nothing is exploited; the interface is used as designed, so only the identity and the novelty distinguish it.
caveat: Automation retrieves secrets constantly, so a volume rule is unusable and the first-seen form is the only tractable one. The counterpart of the configuration-file credential record in this corpus: there the keys were read off a web server, here they are requested politely through the interface built for it.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: A cloud network control opened or removed
description: External rules cover network access control lists created with all ports open, access control lists deleted, and cloud firewall rules modified or deleted, alongside the host-level equivalents of permitting file sharing and network discovery.
logic: Network control operations in the provider audit trail where the resulting rule permits a wide port range or an unrestricted source. Deletion matters as much as creation: removing a restrictive control achieves the same exposure and is quieter.
caveat: The infrastructure-as-code condition is what makes this tractable: in a managed estate network controls should change through the pipeline, so a change made directly in the console is the finding regardless of what it permits. Where there is no pipeline, this needs a per-account baseline instead.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: A long-lived credential minted inside the tenant
description: External rules cover access key creation, console login profiles being created or updated for accounts that had none, and external guest accounts being invited. Each converts temporary access into a durable credential the attacker controls.
logic: Creation of access keys, login profiles and guest invitations, reconciled against the change record. The highest-value variant is a login profile created or updated for a principal that has never had console access, because that converts a programmatic identity into an interactive one.
caveat: One principal creating a credential for another is the shape worth alerting on; self-service key rotation is routine and should be excluded by that condition rather than by volume. This is the cloud form of the dormant-account and device-registration persistence recorded elsewhere in this corpus.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: A privileged role or application consent granted in the tenant
description: External rules cover assignment of directory administrator and global administrator roles, applications being assigned roles, privileged delegated or application permissions being granted, full-access-as-application permissions, and administrative consent being bypassed by a service principal.
logic: Role assignment and permission grant operations, keyed on the privilege being granted rather than on who granted it. The set of roles that matter is small and enumerable, and legitimate grants are rare enough to reconcile individually against a change record.

markers.value: (?i)(add member to role|add app role assignment|consent to application|add delegated permission|update application|add owner to (application|service principal))

markers.expr: granted_role in (global_administrator, privileged_role_administrator, application_administrator, cloud_application_administrator) or permission_scope in (full_access_as_app, directory_readwrite_all, mail_readwrite)

caveat: The application-permission half is the one most often unmonitored, and it is how an identity that is not a person acquires directory-wide access. It pairs directly with the service-principal credential record in this corpus: the credential addition provides the access and the permission grant provides the reach.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: Temporary cloud credentials minted or assumed unexpectedly
description: Cloud identity services issue short-lived credentials by role assumption or session token request. Abused, this yields access under a different identity with a fresh audit trail and no password or second factor involved.
logic: Role assumption and session token operations, evaluated on whether the calling principal has done it before, whether the assumed role is one that principal has ever used, and whether the call came from outside the ranges the principal normally calls from.
caveat: Automation legitimately assumes roles constantly, so a volume rule without a per-principal baseline is unusable. The first-seen form is the tractable one. Note that these credentials are short-lived, which limits the window to act but also means the audit record is the only lasting evidence.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Productivity suite audit logging enabled and retained
description: A named mitigation in a defence contractor advisory was simply enabling the unified audit log, which is off or under-retained by default. Without it, mailbox access and forwarding rules leave no durable record.
logic: Confirm the unified audit log is enabled, confirm retention exceeds assumed dwell time, and confirm the logs leave the tenant.
xql_sketch: dataset = <tenant_config> | filter unified_audit_log_enabled = false or audit_retention_days < 365 or exported_off_tenant = false
caveat: Longer retention is frequently a licensing purchase rather than a setting, which is why it goes unaddressed. Worth knowing before an incident, not during one.

name: A component object redirected to attacker code
description: External rules cover modification of default class identifier values, redirection of a component to a different implementation, and abuse of the per-user registry hive taking precedence over the machine one, so a normal application load runs attacker code.
logic: Writes under the per-user classes hive for a class identifier that also exists machine-wide, since the per-user entry wins and machine-wide entries change only at installation. Also watch for the redirection key being created at all, and for a component path pointing into a user-writable directory.
caveat: Persistence that survives reboot, needs no administrative privilege because the per-user hive is writable by the user, and produces no new process or service. Legitimate software does register components per user, so the discriminator is the target path rather than the write itself.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Shell history deleted
description: External rules cover clearing script interpreter history, deleting the run dialog history registry key, and clearing logs on network devices. All are small acts that remove the record of what was typed.
logic: History files being deleted or truncated, the history registry key being removed, and the interpreter's own history-clearing commands. Because the purpose is to remove local evidence, the value depends on the command having already been forwarded centrally, which makes this as much a test of the pipeline as of the host.
caveat: Small and easily missed, but it fires at the covering-tracks stage and rarely has a benign explanation on a server. Pairs with the audit policy and event log records here: this removes what was typed, those remove what happened.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: State actors using the same public tools as everyone else
description: Named state-nexus operations were observed relying on widely available frameworks and utilities rather than bespoke capability, alongside publicly known vulnerabilities. Attribution does not imply exotic tooling.
logic: A coverage question with a definite answer: for each named public framework and utility, does anything in the estate detect it. The list is short, stable and published, which makes an honest negative finding possible.

markers.note: default paths of one of the named frameworks

caveat: The strategic point cuts both ways. Commodity tooling means baseline detections earn their keep against state actors, and it means a detection built around a named actor's tooling will fire on unrelated criminal activity. Attribution should not be inferred from the tool.

name: A container image pushed or a workload scheduled by someone unexpected
description: External rules cover container images uploaded outside business hours or by unknown users, registry scan findings, scheduled workloads created in managed clusters, and process execution inside running containers.
logic: Image pushes evaluated on who and when, since a registry push is a supply-chain event equivalent to a build artefact. Scheduled workloads and in-container process execution are the runtime half, and execution entering a running container from outside is categorically different from the container running its own entrypoint.

markers.expr: actor not in authorised_image_publishers or push_outside_business_hours

caveat: A registry push is a code-delivery event and deserves the same treatment as a build artefact, which most estates do not give it. Execution entering a running container, particularly through namespace entry, is the container equivalent of a shell on a host and has almost no legitimate cause in production.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: A control system service stopped or disabled
description: Services on control assets stopped or disabled to make them unavailable, which ATT&CK covers through command, process, service and file telemetry rather than through the process data itself.
logic: Service stop and disable commands on control-network hosts, and the service state itself changing on assets whose service set is fixed. On a control network the running service set barely changes, which makes a stop a strong signal without needing a threshold.
caveat: Pairs with the message-absence pattern, because a stopped collection service is one cause of expected data ceasing and the two together distinguish it from a network fault. The service inventory on a control host is small and stable enough to enumerate once, which is what makes this alertable without tuning.
derived_from: MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 (c) The MITRE Corporation, ATT&CK Terms of Use

name: Sweep of the safety or control network for controllers
description: Tooling carried an unused capability to enumerate controllers by address. Never used in the observed event but present in the code, so worth catching as a precursor.
logic: Many protocol connection requests to many controller addresses from a single source in a short window.
xql_sketch: dataset = <ics_dataset> | filter tristation_message_type = 1 | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.ipv4) as controllers by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 5m) | filter controllers > 2
caveat: Anticipatory rather than evidenced. Cheap to run given how small a safety network's address space is.

name: The source address is somebody's home router
description: Fifteen national authorities described a shift by China-nexus actors away from individually procured infrastructure towards large-scale networks of compromised devices, mainly consumer routers and connected devices, used to route activity across every phase of an intrusion. A single such network may serve several unrelated actors, and some also carry legitimate customer traffic.
logic: Address-based blocking and reputation both fail: the addresses are consumer connections in plausible geographies, they change constantly, and blocking one may block a legitimate user of the same network. Detection has to rest on the behaviour of the session and the account rather than on where it appears to come from.
caveat: Three consequences. Geographic blocking is useless by design. Attribution from source infrastructure is unsafe, because one network may serve several actors and some carry genuine customer traffic. And an address seen attacking you may belong to an ordinary household or small business that is itself a victim, which matters if you intend to report or publish it.

name: Credential material read out of process memory
description: Reading the credential subsystem process to recover material for replay elsewhere. The step that turns one compromised host into many. Corresponds to "poor credential hygiene", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: A process opens the credential subsystem process with read access rights, where the opening process is not an allow-listed security or backup product identified by signer.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name = "lsass.exe" and xdm.event.operation_sub_type = "process_access" | filter xdm.source.process.executable.signature.signer not in (<allowed_signers>)
caveat: Endpoint security products, backup software and crash handlers open this process legitimately. Allow-list by signer rather than by process name, which is trivially copied.

name: Credentials stolen from an appliance still work once it is patched
description: A file reading flaw let actors take the unencrypted credentials of every user on a remote access appliance. The advisory is explicit that access is retained after the system is patched unless all compromised credentials are changed.
logic: A remediation completeness check rather than a detection. For any appliance vulnerability whose impact includes credential disclosure, the required actions are patch, rotate every credential the appliance held, and invalidate active sessions. Verify the second and third actually happened, because the first is the one that gets recorded as closing the ticket.
caveat: The single most commonly incomplete remediation in this corpus. Patching an appliance feels like resolution and is measured as resolution, while the stolen credentials remain valid indefinitely and their later use looks like ordinary authentication. Where the appliance authenticated against a directory, the rotation scope is the directory, not the appliance.

name: Criminal groups declaring political allegiance
description: Cybercrime groups publicly pledged support for a state and threatened operations in retaliation for perceived offensives against it, or against countries and organisations providing materiel support to the other side. Others conducted disruptive attacks in apparent support of a military offensive.
logic: Changes the expected objective rather than the tradecraft. The same criminal tooling and access may be used for disruption or destruction rather than extortion, which means a ransomware playbook assuming a payment negotiation has no counterparty. Watch for public statements naming target categories as a warning input.
caveat: Blurs the ransomware and destructive-attack response plans, which are usually written separately and owned by different people. A group that extorts on Monday and wipes on Tuesday defeats both plans read in isolation.

name: A host talking to a mining pool
description: External rules match name resolution and connections to public mining pool infrastructure, and the command-line switches miners use to control processor priority, alongside cloud rules for compute resources being created unexpectedly.
logic: Name resolution for known pool domains is the cheapest signal and needs only resolver logs. On the endpoint the miner's own priority and pool arguments are distinctive. In cloud environments the equivalent is compute or container resources appearing outside the normal provisioning path.
caveat: Low severity as an outcome and high value as an indicator, because unauthorised compute use means someone already has execution and chose the least valuable thing to do with it. One record in this corpus describes a state actor mining on a compromised federal network, so the mining is often not the objective.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Encoded command traffic carried in an arbitrary HTTP header
description: Client-to-server implant traffic was hidden inside an arbitrary HTTP header field, with a fixed structural shape: a run of alphanumeric characters followed by a fixed-length encoded block. The advisory publishes the regular expressions and Suricata rules.
logic: Header values matching the published shapes, in any header including cookie. Header inspection is the requirement rather than the pattern, since the traffic is otherwise ordinary web requests to ordinary destinations.
xql_sketch: dataset = <http_dataset> | filter http_header_value ~= "^[0-9A-Za-z]{10}[0-9A-Za-z/\\+]{11}=$" or http_header_value ~= "^[0-9A-Za-z]{22}[0-9A-Za-z/;_=]{11}"
caveat: The advisory itself warns of false positive potential in these signatures and that operators can change them easily. Worth deploying anyway because the cost is low and the alternative is no network visibility of this implant at all; treat a hit as a hunt lead, not a confirmed finding.

name: Lateral movement through a remote object model rather than a service
description: Remote instantiation of a component object on another host, which then creates a process there. It uses no remote service creation and no file copy to an administrative share, so the usual lateral movement markers are absent.
logic: The parent process on the receiving host is the giveaway: a management console, an office application or the service host creating a shell where no interactive session exists. On the network side it is an endpoint mapper connection followed by a high dynamic port to the same host.
caveat: Chosen specifically because it avoids the service creation and administrative share writes that most lateral movement detections key on. If your lateral movement coverage is built on those two, this passes straight through it.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Directory replication requested by a non-controller
description: Replication is how domain controllers synchronise with each other, so the legitimate requesting set is small, fixed and knowable. A request from a workstation is unambiguous.
logic: Directory service access events carrying replication extended rights, from any source that is not a domain controller or an enumerated identity synchronisation product.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter event_id = 4662 and properties ~= "(?i)(1131f6aa|1131f6ad|89e95b76)" | filter xdm.source.host.hostname not in (<domain_controllers>, <sync_products>)
caveat: Needs directory service access auditing enabled, which is off by default and is why this is so often missed. Backup and identity sync products hold replication rights legitimately.

name: Vendor default account names attempted
description: Trivial to look for and still effective, because industrial equipment ships with well-known defaults that often survive commissioning. Corresponds to "default configurations of software and applications", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: Authentication attempts using documented default account names for the equipment deployed, weighted by whether the source address is expected.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.source.user.username in ("admin", "administrator", "root", "operator", "engineer", "service", "guest") | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<known_admin_sources>)
caveat: Some of these are legitimate account names in use. The value is in the combination with an unexpected source, not the name alone.

name: The account of someone who no longer works here
description: An actor authenticated to an internal remote access point using network administrator credentials obtained through the account of a former employee that had not been removed from the directory. The advisory notes this is a technique actors commonly rely on.
logic: Reconcile every enabled directory account against the current employee and contractor roster, and separately look for authentication by accounts with no interactive activity for an extended period. The privileged subset is the priority, since a dormant administrator account is worth more than an active ordinary one.

markers.expr: authentication_success by account with last_activity older_than 90d

caveat: The failure is a process one between human resources and identity administration, not a technical one, which is why it persists in organisations that patch well. It is also entirely preventable and entirely measurable: the reconciliation either exists as a scheduled control or it does not.

name: Whether the plan survives data that is gone rather than encrypted
description: The advisory cites historical deployment of destructive malware against government and critical infrastructure and warns that a state is exploring options for further attacks. Destructive activity removes the possibility of paying for recovery, which most ransomware planning quietly assumes exists.
logic: A preparedness question with a testable answer: can the organisation reach a known-good state without any cooperation from the attacker, within its stated tolerance, with the directory service and the virtualisation platform also assumed lost. Destructive campaigns in this corpus have propagated through exactly those two.
caveat: The distinction matters because it is the one variable a ransom decision cannot influence. Where the objective is disruption rather than money, there is no key to buy, and a plan whose worst case is a negotiation has no floor.

name: Device administration from outside the management network
description: Restricting administrative interfaces to internal space is the standard control. Any access from outside it is either a gap in that control or an intrusion.
logic: Administrative protocol sessions to infrastructure devices sourced from outside the management network ranges.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<infrastructure_devices>) and xdm.target.port in (22, 23, 80, 443, 161) | filter incidr(xdm.source.ipv4, <management_cidr>) = false
caveat: Out-of-band and emergency access paths legitimately come from elsewhere. Enumerate them first or the next outage produces a false positive at the worst time.

markers.note: the rule is the negation: source NOT in management zone

name: Device software rolled back to lock out the engineering tools
description: Actors reset the software version of the controller's logic to an older release, which prevented operators from communicating with the device unless the engineering workstation was downgraded to match. Anti-remediation rather than exploitation.
logic: A reported firmware or program version moving backwards. Version numbers only go up in legitimate operation, which makes a decrease close to a pure signal and trivially cheap to check from inventory polling.

markers.note: compare against the last recorded value; the signal is a decrease

caveat: The effect is to make the owner's own tooling incompatible with their own equipment, so recovery requires downgrading the engineering workstation first. Worth recording in the response plan because it turns a configuration restore into a tooling problem.

name: What a management platform can do to everything it manages
description: Mobile device management platforms provide elevated access to thousands of enrolled devices. Compromise of one server yields package deployment to every device, configuration change, personal data on every user, and location data where enabled.
logic: A scoping and privilege question rather than a detection. Record what each management platform can reach, how many endpoints, whether it can push executable content, whether it holds location or personal data, and who can authorise a deployment. Then alert on deployments touching an unusual proportion of the estate.
caveat: The reason to rank these above their severity score: the platform is the blast radius. A management server holding location data for staff also makes physical tracking an outcome of a network intrusion, which most threat models do not contemplate.

name: Equipment renamed or readdressed so its owner can no longer reach it
description: Actors changed the identity of compromised controllers so operators could not reconnect: first by renaming, where the device name is a required field for establishing a remote connection, and later by changing device IP addresses to disconnect them outright. Both are denial techniques rather than evasion ones, and both are answerable the same way, by reconciling the device's identity in the field against the identity in the inventory.
logic: Device identity fields -- name or address -- changing outside a commissioning window. This is answerable from an inventory reconciliation rather than an event stream, and it is worth doing because the change is what prevents the operator responding.
caveat: Belongs in the response plan as much as in monitoring. If the recovery procedure depends on connecting by device name, and the name is attacker-controlled, the procedure fails at the first step. Hold an out-of-band record of device identity and addressing.

name: Copy of the directory database outside its proper location
description: The file name is fixed by the product, so a copy appearing in a temporary or user directory is staging for exfiltration. A precise file-path check needing no log configuration.
logic: File create or write events for the directory database or its flush map anywhere other than the system directory.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.name in ("ntds.dit", "ntds.jfm") and xdm.target.file.path not ~= "(?i)\\Windows\\NTDS\\"
caveat: Directory restore and migration work legitimately produces copies elsewhere, but those are planned and rare. Reconcile against change records.

name: Permissions changed on a directory object or file
description: External rules cover write-permission access on directory objects, dangerous deny and group permission modifications, replication privilege additions, recursive ownership changes and attribute changes hiding files.
logic: Directory object permission modification events, and the host utilities that change ownership or attributes recursively. On the directory side the specific grants that matter are replication rights and write-permission on privileged groups, because they lead directly to credential extraction or self-elevation.

markers.expr: granted_right in (WriteDacl, WriteOwner, DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All, GenericAll) on privileged_object

caveat: The replication-rights grant is the one to prioritise: it is the precondition for extracting the directory database remotely, and it is a permission change rather than an intrusion, so nothing else about it looks wrong. Requires directory object auditing at a level frequently not enabled.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: Signed executable loading a system library from its own directory
description: The executable is genuine and its signature validates, which is the point. The anomaly is the load path, not the loader.
logic: Library load events where a system library name resolves from a user, temporary or application directory rather than the system location.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "image_load" and loaded_module_name in (<system_library_names>) and loaded_module_path ~= "(?i)\\(Users|AppData|Temp|ProgramData)\\"
caveat: Portable and per-user applications legitimately ship libraries beside their executables. Matching system library names loading from non-system paths narrows it considerably.

name: Path from an exposed segment into internal networks
description: Found independently in multiple red team assessments. A correctly configured perimeter blocks it outright; rule sets are correct when built and erode through years of change requests.
logic: Test rather than read the policy: enumerate what a host in the exposed segment can actually reach internally. Separately alert on observed sessions from that segment toward internal hosts.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.source.zone = "dmz" and xdm.target.zone = "internal" | comp count() by xdm.source.ipv4, xdm.target.ipv4, xdm.target.port
caveat: Requires zones in the asset inventory. Needs periodic re-testing, not a one-off review, because erosion is the mechanism.

name: Your domain pointed elsewhere, with a valid certificate to match
description: Using compromised credentials for an account able to change name records, attackers altered address, mail and name server records to redirect traffic to infrastructure they controlled, and because they could set the record values they were also able to obtain valid encryption certificates for the organisation's domains, so redirected traffic could be decrypted with no warning shown to users.
logic: Three surfaces. Change events on the registrar and hosting accounts, which should be rare and are the moment of compromise. Continuous comparison of your published records against an authoritative reference you hold. And certificate transparency monitoring for your own domains, since a certificate issued to someone else is both evidence and the mechanism.
caveat: The advisory notes this creates a risk that persists beyond the period of redirection, which is the crucial point: the certificate obtained during the hijack remains valid afterwards. Restoring the records does not revoke it, so remediation must include finding and revoking any certificate issued during the window.

name: Retain the resolved address, not only the queried name
description: A name lookup resolving to the same address a callback went to is what links two otherwise separate observations. It also survives the actor changing domain while keeping infrastructure.
logic: Record name-to-address resolution in the name resolution log, then correlate resolved addresses against observed session destinations.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | filter dns_answer in (<indicator_addresses>) | join (dataset = <network_dataset>) as n n.target = dns_answer
caveat: Many resolution logs discard the answer. Retaining it costs little and enables correlation that is otherwise impossible.

name: Command traffic carried over DNS
description: Data and commands encoded into DNS queries and responses to cross a boundary that blocks direct egress. Common where the control network cannot reach the internet but resolution still works.
logic: Per internal host, count queries grouped by parent domain. Flag high query volume to a single parent domain with long or high-entropy leftmost labels, particularly where the answers are never subsequently connected to.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | alter parent = arrayindex(regextract(xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name, "([^.]+\.[^.]+)$"), 0), label_len = len(arrayindex(split(xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name, "."), 0)) | comp count() as queries, avg(label_len) as avg_label by xdm.source.host.hostname, parent | filter queries > 500 and avg_label > 25
caveat: Anti-spam lookups, endpoint reputation services and some content delivery networks are indistinguishable on volume and label length. Exclude those vendors by parent domain first.

name: File fetched from somewhere new, then the host talks somewhere else new
description: Two unremarkable events in sequence describing a stager fetching its next stage. Seen in campaigns a decade apart.
logic: Download from a destination with no history, then execution, then a connection to a second destination that also has no history.
xql_sketch: dataset = <proxy_dataset> | filter xdm.target.domain not in (<seen_domains>) | join (dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process") as p p.hostname = xdm.source.host.hostname | join (dataset = <network_dataset>) as n n.hostname = p.hostname
caveat: Needs file, process and network telemetry on one timeline sharing host identifiers. Where they do not, this cannot be built.

markers.expr: first_seen(destination) by host within 1h following file_create

name: Malware sold as legitimate software, with a price and a licence
description: The developers of two of the most prolific families market them as legitimate remote management and penetration testing tools, available online for low cost. Actors purchase them and use them unchanged, so the binary is commercial software rather than malware.
logic: Reputation and signature approaches struggle because the vendor is a real vendor and the product has legitimate customers. Treat it as unapproved software rather than as malware: maintain an allow-list of the remote management products your organisation licenses, and alert on everything else regardless of how it presents itself.
caveat: Blocking on maliciousness fails here by design, because the vendor can point at legitimate customers and a licence agreement. Only an allow-list of what your organisation actually bought produces a decidable answer, which makes maintaining that inventory the control. Longitudinal reporting supports treating this as a standing condition rather than a campaign: the same category of tooling recurs in every year of an eighteen-quarter response series, with the specific products changing and the technique not changing at all. That is the argument for spending the effort on the licensed-software inventory rather than on keeping a detection list current.

name: Appliance image or filesystem integrity mismatch
description: The vendor integrity checker disagrees with the shipped image, or a file exists on an appliance filesystem that no release put there. Applies wherever a vendor offers an integrity verification tool.
logic: Any non-clean result from a vendor integrity check, or any file on an appliance filesystem absent from the release manifest for the running version.
xql_sketch: dataset = <appliance_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "integrity_check" and xdm.event.outcome != "SUCCESS"
caveat: Lead on false negatives, not false positives. Seven national authorities determined that actors can deceive one vendor's internal and external integrity checkers so that compromise goes undetected, and an authority reproduced it in a lab. A clean result from a vendor tool therefore means unknown, not clean. Benign mismatches after a hotfix also occur, so confirm the running version against the manifest the checker used, but treat a mismatch as the useful signal and a clean result as no signal.

name: Edge appliance reboots outside a change window
description: Perimeter appliance restarts, crashes or reloads with no matching change record, often paired with a configuration or profile write shortly after. Implant loading on network appliances frequently costs a reboot.
logic: Group appliance restart events by device over a rolling window, then join to configuration change events on the same device within an hour. Suppress anything falling inside an approved change window.
xql_sketch: dataset = <appliance_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type in ("system_restart", "configuration_change") | comp count() as events, values(xdm.event.type) as kinds by xdm.source.host.hostname, bin(_time, 1h) | filter array_length(kinds) > 1
caveat: Planned maintenance and automated upgrades produce the same shape. Without a change feed to suppress against, this is hunt-grade at best.

name: Edge device loss correlated with operational data going stale
description: Loss of a communications device on the path to a remote site, paired with that site's process data stopping. Either alone reads as a network fault; together they measure a loss of control and its duration.
logic: Reachability loss on a path gateway joined to staleness of the process values from the site behind it.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.host.hostname in (<site_gateways>) and xdm.event.type = "connectivity_loss" | join (dataset = <process_dataset> | comp max(_time) as last_value by site) as p ...
