caveat: Weather, power and carrier faults cause this far more often than anyone attacking. The detection measures consequence, not cause.

name: Elevation obtained without the consent prompt
description: A large family of techniques that reach administrative privilege on a host without triggering the consent prompt, typically by abusing an auto-elevating platform binary or a hijacked path that an elevated process reads.
logic: Two shapes worth covering. An auto-elevating platform process appearing as the parent of a shell or script engine, which is the signature of most bypass chains. And the policy values that permit unprivileged installer elevation, which is a configuration finding rather than an event.
caveat: The parent list needs maintaining because new auto-elevating binaries are found regularly, which is why this is a pattern rather than a fixed rule. The installer policy value is worth checking once as an estate-wide configuration question: where it is set, any user can install as the highest privilege account.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: A malicious reply inside a real conversation you started
description: Actors stole an existing email chain from an infected host and replied into it using a spoofed identity with a malicious document attached. The recipient sees a genuine conversation they remember, continued by someone they have been corresponding with.
logic: The message body is legitimate because it is the real thread. What does not match is the envelope: a reply arriving for a thread whose original recipients did not include the sender's actual domain, a sending address whose display name matches a known correspondent but whose domain does not, and a reply arriving from outside after the thread had been internal.

markers.expr: reply_references_existing_thread_id and sender_domain not in original_thread_participants

caveat: The most effective phishing shape in this corpus, because every heuristic a user is taught fails: the sender is known, the subject is one they recognise, the thread history is genuine, and they were expecting a reply. It also means one compromised mailbox becomes a trusted delivery channel to everyone that person corresponds with, including other organisations.

name: Finding vulnerable components inside larger products
description: Asset inventories list the product, not the components inside it, so a fixed upstream vulnerability can stay exploitable in the field for as long as the equipment vendor takes to ship a tested release.
logic: Not a runtime detection. Fingerprint service banners and listening ports across the control network to find where a component is embedded, then track it as its own asset.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter service_banner contains "<component>" | comp count() by hostname, port
caveat: Active scanning of control networks can disrupt equipment. Use passive fingerprinting, or scan only during a planned outage with the equipment owner present.

name: A flaw in the runtime that everything is built on
description: An integer overflow in a memory allocation function in the C runtime library of a real-time operating system, part of a wider collection of such flaws affecting multiple real-time operating systems and supporting libraries. All programs with a dependency on that library are affected, across a wide range of products.
logic: The operator usually cannot tell which of their equipment embeds the affected runtime, because it is a component of a component. The answerable form is to ask suppliers directly for each product family, and to record the answer, since this class of flaw recurs and the same question will be asked again.
caveat: Exploitation requires the attacker to control the allocation parameters and what is accessed afterwards, and no active exploitation was known at publication, so the urgency is inventory rather than incident. The lasting problem is that the affected product list is unknowable to the operator without asking every supplier, and embedded devices frequently have no update path at all.

name: Application configuration files read from the internet
description: A botnet targeted environment configuration files that hold credentials for cloud, mail and messaging services, reaching them through exposed dependency directories and framework flaws. One file yields working credentials for services the attacker never had to touch.
logic: Requests for configuration and dependency paths that should never be served, and requests using the methods used to read them. Every hit is actionable because there is no legitimate reason for an external client to request these paths at all.
caveat: A successful response to any of these is a credential disclosure that has already happened, so the response is rotation rather than investigation. Rotate every credential the file held, including cloud access keys and mail service tokens, and check for use of those credentials from outside your estate.

name: End-of-life devices with a reachable management interface
description: Unsupported edge devices were implanted and used as relay infrastructure. Your own end-of-life devices are candidates to become someone else's relay, and no patch exists or is coming.
logic: Inventory devices past vendor support that are externally reachable, and plan replacement.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter vendor_support_status = "end_of_life" and external_reachable = true | comp count() by vendor, model, site
caveat: The one case where the honest answer is replacement rather than mitigation. An unsupported device with a reachable management interface has no fix available.

name: End-of-life versions affected by a current vulnerability
description: An advisory noted the flaw also affects two versions past end of life, which are therefore permanently vulnerable. Reporting them alongside patchable assets hides which ones can actually be fixed.
logic: Separate exposed assets with an available fix from those without. The second group needs upgrade, isolation or replacement, none of which is a maintenance window.
xql_sketch: dataset = <vuln_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | comp count() by product, product_version, vendor_support_status, fix_available | filter fix_available = false
caveat: These usually host an application nobody wants to touch, which is why the version is old. The blocker is the application owner rather than the patching team.

name: The response triggered the wiper
description: After roughly fourteen months of quiet access and a year of periodic mail exfiltration, actors launched a file encryptor carrying a political message. When network defenders identified and began to respond to that activity, the actors deployed disk wiping malware.
logic: A response-planning constraint rather than a detection. Assume the adversary observes the response and may escalate when it starts. Decide in advance the order of containment actions, whether they can be executed near-simultaneously rather than sequentially, and what is preserved and isolated before the first visible action is taken.
caveat: The most consequential response finding in this corpus. It means a partial or gradual containment can be worse than none, because it announces the response without removing the adversary's ability to act. It also pairs with the advisory elsewhere here instructing that mitigations be chosen so as not to tip off the adversary, and with the case where responders' own mailboxes were being read.

name: The attacker completes your password reset for you
description: Following an enforced password reset for all users during an incident, actors logged into inactive accounts and followed the reset instructions themselves, regaining access after eviction. The remediation became the re-entry route.
logic: During and after a mass reset, watch for reset completion on accounts that had no activity before the incident. A dormant account completing a password reset is anomalous in itself, because nobody is there to complete it. The safe procedure is to disable dormant accounts before resetting the rest, not alongside them.
caveat: One of the most valuable findings in this corpus because it attacks the remediation rather than the estate. A mass reset issued to every account including dormant ones hands the attacker a supported, logged, entirely legitimate route back in. Disable first, then reset, and treat any dormant account that completes a reset as confirmation the actor is still present.

name: Extortion with no encryption stage at all
description: A group that originally encrypted after exfiltrating shifted primarily to exfiltration-based extortion, leaving victim systems intact, and later shifted to that model exclusively. There is no encryption event to detect and no outage to notice.
logic: Every detection placed at the encryption stage fires never. The only remaining signals are the stages before it: bulk read of file shares and databases, archiving, and outbound transfer to file hosting or by file transfer protocol. Egress volume by host against its own baseline is the backstop when the tooling is unrecognised.

markers.expr: sum(bytes_out) by host, bin(_time, 24h) against host_baseline

caveat: The strategic consequence is that a ransomware programme measured by encryption prevention scores perfectly against this while the organisation still loses its data and still gets extorted. It also removes the natural discovery moment: with systems left intact, the first indication may be the extortion contact itself, or a leak site listing.

name: Bulk transfer and archiving utilities run with transfer verbs
description: Collection with an archiver and a file transfer client, exfiltration with a synchronisation utility to cloud storage. The synchronisation utility is the strongest single signal.
logic: Execution of archiving or transfer utilities with command lines carrying transfer verbs, weighted heavily where the destination is consumer cloud storage rather than a corporate service.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in ("rclone.exe", "winscp.exe", "filezilla.exe", "winrar.exe") and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)(copy|sync|move|remote:)"
caveat: Backup and migration work uses the same tools with the same verbs. A consumer cloud destination answers the question by itself.

name: The messages that should be arriving have stopped
description: Blocking alarm, reporting or command messages, suppressing alarms, and restarting or shutting down a device all present the same way: expected communications stop. ATT&CK's own guidance for each of these techniques is to monitor for loss of network traffic, because none of them can be observed directly.
logic: Model the expected message cadence per device and per message type, then alert when a source that reports on a known interval stops. The bound is the device's own normal interval, which varies by asset and must be measured rather than assumed. Alarm and reporting channels deserve tighter bounds than routine polling because their silence is indistinguishable from nothing being wrong.

markers.expr: count(message) by source_device, message_type, bin(_time, measured_expected_interval)

caveat: The hardest class of detection to run and the most consequential to miss, because silence is the default appearance of a healthy quiet process. Two consequences. The expected interval has to be measured per device, so this cannot ship with a threshold. And more than one device going silent together separates a suppression from an ordinary link fault, which is why the count matters more than any single absence. ATT&CK ships no analytics at all for blocked command and blocked reporting messages, so there is no external implementation to check this against.
derived_from: MITRE ATT&CK v19.1 (c) The MITRE Corporation, ATT&CK Terms of Use

name: A host asking the internet what its own address is
description: The loader tested connectivity and learned its public address by querying well-known public address-reporting services. Those services are legitimate, which is the point, but a server or control-network host has no reason to consult one.
logic: Requests to the published address-reporting services, scoped to hosts that should never make them. The service list is short, stable and public, which makes this cheap to deploy and hard for the operator to avoid, since the whole point is to use somewhere reputable.
caveat: Developer workstations and some legitimate agents do this, so scope by host role rather than deploying estate-wide. On a server or an operator station the legitimate rate is zero, which makes it a clean signal exactly where it matters most.

name: Name resolution going somewhere other than the internal servers
description: Using external resolvers stops responses being cached and sidesteps whatever inspection sits on the internal ones. Forcing all resolution inward is what makes every other name-based detection trustworthy.
logic: Resolution traffic from internal hosts to any destination outside the organisation's own resolver set.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port = 53 and xdm.target.ipv4 not in (<internal_resolvers>)
caveat: Some applications and devices ship hard-coded public resolvers, so expect legitimate hits initially. Encrypted resolution over web ports will not appear here at all.

name: Host authenticating to an external resource without anyone typing
description: Links or documents that trigger Windows authentication against an outside resource, handing over credential material silently. Used by several tracked groups.
logic: Outbound file-sharing authentication traffic leaving the network. It should never happen.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (445, 139) and incidr(xdm.target.ipv4, <internal_cidr>) = false
caveat: Blocking this at the perimeter removes it entirely and breaks almost nothing. Where it has not been blocked, every hit is worth chasing.

name: Targeted scanning of your own address ranges
description: Low value for alerting, moderate for context: knowing your ranges were swept shortly before an intrusion attempt helps scope an investigation. A narrow deep sweep differs from the constant wide shallow background.
logic: Count distinct destinations and ports per source. Treat sustained targeted scanning of a narrow range as meaningful; treat internet-wide background scanning as noise.
xql_sketch: dataset = <firewall_dataset> | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.ipv4) as hosts, count_distinct(xdm.target.port) as ports by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 1h) | filter hosts < 50 and ports > 20
caveat: Advisories name standard tools that your own testers and discovery services also use. Tool identity alone is not evidence of malice, and a detection built on it will accuse your colleagues.

name: A ransom note displayed over data that is already gone
description: Two campaigns displayed a ransomware message while the targeted data was destroyed and unrecoverable, with the vendor stating explicitly that it could not be recovered even if a ransom were paid. The extortion framing was cover for destruction.
logic: Distinguish destruction from encryption early, because the two demand opposite responses. Encryption leaves file structure and a key that exists somewhere; destruction overwrites boot records and file content with no key anywhere. Boot record writes, overwrites of the same sectors across many hosts, and unrecoverable content in the presence of a ransom note are the discriminators.
caveat: The single most consequential misreading available during an incident. Treating a wiper as ransomware leads to a payment decision over data that no key can restore, and to a recovery plan built on negotiation rather than on rebuilding. Both advisories in this corpus that describe it say the data is not recoverable by paying, in those words.

name: Attacker-built software presented as a popular free tool
description: Malware distributed inside spoofed copies of media player and utility software. The installer is attacker-built rather than a tampered legitimate one, so provenance checks against a real vendor cannot help.
logic: Application installation not present in the approved software inventory, prioritised on hosts with access to sensitive systems.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "install" | filter installed_application not in (<approved_software>)
caveat: No purchase at all on unmanaged or personal devices, which is where free utility software is most often installed.

name: The name in the ransom note is not evidence of who did it
description: State actors portrayed themselves as an unrelated criminal ransomware group, operated under third-party foreign affiliate identities, and used foreign intermediaries to receive payment. The branding was chosen to conceal state involvement.
logic: Not a detection but a constraint on how a ransomware incident is scoped and reported. Treat the claimed identity as an assertion by the attacker. Where the branding says criminal but the targeting, dwell time or collection behaviour says intelligence, the branding is the least reliable input available.
caveat: Has direct legal and financial consequences rather than only analytical ones. Payment to a sanctioned state actor operating under criminal branding carries sanctions exposure that a payment decision made on the note's claimed identity would not have accounted for, and the authoring agencies discourage payment partly on that basis.

name: Infrastructure that moves faster than a blocklist
description: Rapidly changing name resolution records used to obscure the location of malicious servers and to build resilient, highly available command and control. Six national authorities describe most networks as having a gap in detecting and blocking it.
logic: Properties of the resolution rather than the name: a very short record lifetime, an unusually large set of distinct addresses for one name over a short window, and those addresses spread across many unrelated networks. The double-flux variant rotates the name servers as well, so also watch for a domain's authoritative servers changing repeatedly.
caveat: Requires retaining the resolved answers and not only the queried names, which is a collection decision many organisations have made the wrong way without realising it. Content delivery networks and large cloud services produce the same shape legitimately and have to be excluded first, which is the main reason this detection is skipped.

name: Default file association changed so ordinary documents launch something else
description: The actor changed the default application for a file type, which both persists and sidesteps application allow-listing, because the user opens a document and the allow-listed handler is not what runs.
logic: File association keys are written at software installation and almost never otherwise, so the change rate outside a deployment window is close to zero. Alert on the write rather than waiting for the execution.
caveat: Cited by the advisory as a way to launch malware outside some application allow-listing solutions, which makes it a control-bypass as much as a persistence mechanism.

name: File whose real format does not match its extension
description: Something named as an image that is actually an executable. Determined from the file header, so it survives whatever the attacker chose to call it.
logic: Compare the format determined from the file header against the declared extension, at the mail gateway, the proxy or on the endpoint.
xql_sketch: dataset = <file_dataset> | alter declared = xdm.target.file.extension | filter file_magic_type != null and file_magic_type != declared
caveat: Needs a gateway or endpoint that inspects headers. Some legitimate software ships payloads with mismatched extensions, so expect a small standing exception list.

name: Forged or abused authentication tickets
description: A correctly forged ticket is cryptographically valid, so this detects carelessness rather than the technique. Once a domain controller falls, authentication logs cannot be trusted.
logic: Service ticket requests with no preceding authentication ticket request for that account, ticket lifetimes exceeding domain policy, and impersonation events where the service has no business acting for that user.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter event_id in (4768, 4769, 4770) | filter ticket_lifetime > <domain_max_lifetime>
caveat: Detects mistakes, not the technique. After controller compromise the remedy is rebuilding trust, not better detection.

name: Valid authentication tokens the identity provider never issued
description: Having reached directory administrator privilege, the actor compromised the token signing certificate and minted its own valid tokens, presenting them to every service that trusts the identity provider. The tokens are cryptographically correct, so nothing rejects them, and no authentication event exists at the provider.
logic: The advisory supplies four concrete token anomalies, all of which need identity provider logs correlated against service access logs. Validity durations far longer than the norm, typically 24 hours against a normal hour. Durations expressed as exact whole seconds. Issue time identical to first use time, which a human never produces. A token in use with no corresponding sign-in for that account within the preceding hour. Add a fifth from the same section: tokens whose multi-factor claims are missing or unusual where multi-factor is enforced.
xql_sketch: dataset = <cloud_audit_dataset> | filter token_validity_seconds > 3600 or token_issued_time = token_first_use_time | filter mfa_claim = null and mfa_enforced = true
caveat: The most consequential detection in this corpus, because it is authentication without an authentication event and it applies to every federated service at once, including hosted mail, file storage and business intelligence. Requires correlating identity provider logs with cloud access logs, which are frequently owned by different teams and retained for different periods. Remediation means rotating the signing certificate, which is disruptive enough that it gets deferred.

name: The address does not tell you where they are
description: An agency set out how tunnelling and spoofing let actors obscure their location, stating that it is not possible to identify the true physical location of malicious activity from the geolocation of an address alone, and that these techniques are used specifically to mislead incident responders.
logic: A constraint on analysis rather than a query. Record source geography as an observation, never as a conclusion, and do not let it drive scoping, disclosure or escalation decisions. Spoofing applies mainly to connectionless activity such as denial of service and amplification, while tunnelling applies to interactive activity, so the two limit different investigations.
caveat: The agency states the purpose of these techniques is to mislead responders, which makes source geography an adversary-controlled input. Together with the shared covert networks and anonymising overlay records here, that leaves very little that source address can support, and the accuracy of geolocation data itself varies widely by provider before any deception is considered.

name: Endpoint protection disabled centrally through policy
description: Having reached a domain controller with a legitimate administrator account, actors deactivated antivirus by modifying Group Policy Objects. One change disarms every machine the policy applies to, and each endpoint records only having complied.
logic: Group Policy object modification events, joined to whether the change was made from a management workstation by an account that administers policy. The detection belongs on the directory, not the endpoint, because the endpoint has nothing anomalous to report.
xql_sketch: dataset = <directory_dataset> | filter xdm.event.id in (5136, 5137, 5141) or xdm.event.operation ~= "(?i)group.?policy" | filter xdm.source.user.username not in (<policy_administrators>)
caveat: Distinct from a local control being switched off, and worse: the scope is the policy's scope. Fleet-wide loss of protection reported as a coverage statistic rather than a security event is the common failure, so pair this with an alert on protection coverage falling across many hosts at once.

name: Someone phoning your staff pretending to be your own IT team
description: Affiliates used open source research on the target, then posed as company information technology or help desk staff and used phone calls or text messages to obtain credentials from employees. The approach arrives on a channel no mail gateway inspects.
logic: Nothing on the approach channel is observable, so detection has to sit on what the credential is then used for: a successful authentication shortly after a reported or suspected call, a second-factor approval from a device or location the account has not used, and enrolment of a new factor. Also make reporting an approach easy, because a staff report is the only signal generated at the time.

markers.expr: mfa_factor_enrolled or mfa_approved from unrecognised_device within 1h of authentication

caveat: The direction of the call is what defeats training built around not trusting inbound email: the attacker is impersonating the very team staff are told to cooperate with. Callback verification through a number the staff member looks up independently is the control, and it has to be a documented process rather than advice.

name: Hidden encrypted file in a system directory
description: The implant's configuration and component store was a fully encrypted file in a Windows system directory, with hidden, system and archive attributes and a predictable double-GUID name. The advisory supplies a Yara entropy rule and both find and PowerShell one-liners.
logic: Entropy at or above 7.0 combined with hidden and system attributes, scoped to system directories where the legitimate population is known and stable. The advisory also notes the separate encrypted store has a file size that is an even multiple of 220, which is a cheap additional filter.
xql_sketch: dataset = <file_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)\\\\windows\\\\(registration|system32\\\\com)\\\\" | filter file_entropy >= 7.0 and file_attribute_hidden = true
caveat: The advisory is explicit that names and paths are easily changed by the operator, so treat the specific paths as a starting point and the entropy plus attributes as the durable part. Because the files are fully encrypted, content signatures do not work at all.

name: Name lookups for domains with no recognisable words
description: A weak signal for combining with others, not for alerting alone.
logic: Score character entropy and dictionary-word content per domain label, and rank rather than threshold.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | alter label = arrayindex(split(xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name, "."), 0) | comp count() by label, xdm.source.host.hostname | sort desc entropy_score
caveat: Short, only slightly odd domains score low and will be missed. Content delivery and telemetry services generate genuinely random-looking names constantly. Combine, do not alert.

name: A large encrypted blob stored in the registry
description: An espionage implant kept its decryption key material and component paths in an encrypted registry value. The advisory gives a location-independent way to find it: search the registry for any value at least 0x1000 bytes with entropy of at least 7.9.
logic: Size and entropy, not path. The registry is a configuration store, so a multi-kilobyte high-entropy value is anomalous wherever it sits. This survives the implant moving its key, which the advisory says is easy for the operator to do.
xql_sketch: dataset = <registry_dataset> | filter xdm.target.registry.value_size > 4096 | filter registry_value_entropy > 7.9
caveat: One of the few detections in this corpus that is genuinely resilient to the operator relocating the artefact, because it keys on a property the data cannot shed. Legitimate large registry values exist, notably certificate and licensing blobs, so enumerate those once and allow-list them.

name: Many endpoints stop reporting to the historian at once
description: Built inside the historian rather than from security telemetry, so it keeps working where endpoints carry no agent. Separates a disruptive event in progress from one machine failing.
logic: Per data source, compare the age of the most recent value against its expected update interval, then count how many went stale in the same short window.
xql_sketch: dataset = <historian_dataset> | comp max(_time) as last_seen by source_tag | alter stale = timestamp_diff(current_time(), last_seen, "MINUTE") | filter stale > expected_interval | comp count() as sources_lost by bin(last_seen, 5m) | filter sources_lost > 5
caveat: A network fault between the historian and a plant area gives the identical shape. The value is knowing early, not knowing the cause.

markers.expr: count_distinct(silent_endpoint) by bin(_time, 5m) where last_update older_than 5m

name: Old campaigns: keep the behaviour, discard the indicators
description: An advisory published nearly a decade after the campaign it describes states plainly that the techniques remain relevant for defenders while the indicators are provided for historical awareness only.
logic: A curation rule for any intelligence programme. Indicators decay on a timescale of weeks to months; the behaviours they accompanied persist for years. Where a source is old, extract the behaviour into a detection and record the indicators as context, never as an active matching set.
caveat: Worth stating because the opposite is common: old indicator sets accumulate in matching rules where they contribute nothing but cost, while the behavioural lesson that would still fire is never written down. This corpus is organised around the behaviour for that reason.

name: Operator and engineering hosts talking outside working hours
description: Configuration work in a control environment is scheduled and infrequent, so time of day carries real information here in a way it does not on the business network.
logic: Sessions, logons or file writes between operator interfaces and engineering workstations outside the known engineering working pattern.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.source.host.hostname in (<hmi_and_ews>) and xdm.target.host.hostname in (<hmi_and_ews>) | alter hour = extract_time(_time, "HOUR") | filter hour not in (<engineering_hours>)
caveat: Shift work and unplanned outages break the time assumption. Works best where engineering access is genuinely by exception.

name: A burst of built-in discovery commands from one place
description: Discovery is the most heavily ruled activity across the external corpora, spread over user, group, account, file, service, registry and system enumeration. Individually each command is ordinary administration; the signal is several of them from one process or account inside a short window.
logic: Count distinct discovery utilities executed by one parent process or account in a short window rather than alerting on any single one. Anchor on parentage as well: a web server process or a scripting engine running these is categorically different from an administrator at a console.
caveat: Consolidated deliberately: the external corpora carry over a hundred rules across nine discovery techniques and they all reduce to the same shape. One pattern with a count threshold covers them and produces far less noise than nine separate alerts. Administrative tooling and inventory agents produce the same burst, so the parent process is what makes it tractable.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Firewall rules added or removed on the host
description: External rules cover rules being deleted from the host firewall exception list, all rules being removed at once, and new rules being added to permit an attacker's own traffic, mostly through the platform's network shell utility.
logic: The command-line forms of the network shell utility and the platform's own firewall policy change events. Rule deletion and wholesale reset are the higher-value cases; rule addition matters because it is how an inbound listener or a tunnel is made reachable.
caveat: Distinct from disabling protection wholesale, which is covered separately: a single added rule is quieter and achieves the specific access the actor needs. Software deployment and management agents change these rules legitimately, so the parent process is the discriminator.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Management console used to reset host passwords, then encryption over SSH
description: Actors used privileged accounts to reach the virtualisation management server, reset the passwords of the hypervisor hosts, then connected to those hosts over secure shell and encrypted the virtual machine files directly.
logic: Three stages, each observable and each preceding the damage. A password reset for a hypervisor host account issued from the management server. A secure shell session to a hypervisor host, which in most estates should be disabled entirely. Then file modification under the virtual machine storage path.
caveat: Secure shell on a hypervisor host is disabled by default in most builds and enabling it is itself the signal. Because encryption happens at the host, no guest agent sees any of it, and every guest is lost at once. Backups held as virtual machine files on the same storage are lost with them. The window joining the three stages has to be measured against your own maintenance behaviour rather than assumed; ATT&CK marks a time window as a locally tunable element for these techniques.

name: Directory group the hypervisor implicitly trusts
description: Where a hypervisor grants administrative rights to a directory group by name, creating or renaming a group to that name yields full host control.
logic: Directory group creation and rename events matching the names hypervisors trust, plus an audit of which groups actually hold that mapping.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type in ("group_create", "group_modify") and group_name in (<hypervisor_trusted_groups>)
caveat: Removing the implicit group trust is cleaner than detecting its abuse. Where the mapping must stay, the group name is a short stable watch list.

name: Encryption performed at the hypervisor rather than in the guests
description: Encrypting at the hypervisor removes every guest simultaneously and guest-level endpoint detection never runs. All observables are on the host, so hypervisor logging must be collected centrally or there is no detection at all.
logic: Shell or secure shell access enabled on a hypervisor host, unexpected commands run there, mass guest power-off, and datastore file modification at a rate no administrator produces.
xql_sketch: dataset = <hypervisor_dataset> | filter event_type in ("shell_enabled", "vm_power_off", "datastore_write") | comp count() as ops by host, event_type, bin(_time, 10m) | filter ops > <normal_rate>
caveat: Maintenance powers guests off in batches legitimately. The harder problem is that many estates forward no hypervisor logs at all, making this undetectable rather than noisy.

name: Commands run in the hypervisor's own shell
description: External rules cover account creation, administrative permission assignment, network configuration discovery, virtual machine termination and storage enumeration performed through the hypervisor's local command-line interface.
logic: The hypervisor shell is disabled by default on most builds, so its use at all is the first signal. Beyond that, the command verbs matter: account creation, permission assignment and virtual machine power operations are the ones that precede damage, while configuration and storage enumeration precede those.

markers.value: (?i)(system account (add|set)|system permission set|vm process kill|network firewall set|system settings advanced set|storage filesystem list)

caveat: Directly supports the two hypervisor ransomware records in this corpus, where the encryption ran on the host after the shell was reached. Because the guests see none of it, this telemetry has to be forwarded off the host or there is no evidence at all. Legitimate use exists during maintenance and should be time-bounded rather than allow-listed.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Hunt against a defined technique list, not for anything unusual
description: A joint hunt searched host, network, industrial control system and cloud telemetry for specific named techniques and their artefacts. A negative finding against a defined list means something; a negative finding against no list means nothing.
logic: Define the technique list before hunting, record which telemetry domains were actually covered, and report coverage gaps alongside the result so the negative finding has scope.
xql_sketch: this corpus is usable as the technique list; every pattern names its required evidence_type
caveat: A negative result is only as strong as the telemetry it ran against. A clean hunt over partial telemetry is not a clean environment.

name: Windows protocols spoken directly rather than through built-in clients
description: An open-source toolkit implements the protocols itself, so the protocol traffic appears without the local process activity that normally accompanies it. Used by multiple state groups at a defence organisation.
logic: Remote service creation, remote command execution and directory replication where no corresponding administrative tool ran locally. Complementary cheap check: an interpreter runtime present on a host with no development or automation role.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (445, 135) | join type = left (dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in ("psexec.exe", "wmic.exe", "sc.exe")) as local local.hostname = xdm.target.host.hostname | filter local.hostname = null
caveat: Widely used by legitimate testers and for administrative automation, so exclude by host and account. The protocol-without-local-process shape is durable; the interpreter check fails against compiled builds.

name: Approached by someone you actually know
description: Actors researched targets through social media and professional networking platforms to identify their real social and professional contacts, then created mail accounts and fake profiles impersonating those specific people, or respected experts in the target's field, using event and conference invitations as lures.
logic: The impersonated identity is a real person the target genuinely knows, so name recognition is worthless as a check. What remains is the channel and the domain: a known contact's display name arriving from a consumer webmail address, or from a domain resembling a legitimate organisation but newly registered.
caveat: The research is done on platforms the target controls and the employer does not, and the impersonated person is real, which defeats both technical reputation checks and the instinct to verify by recognising a name. Verification has to be by contacting the person through a channel already known to be theirs.

name: Separate having the backdoor from having been targeted
description: The advisory states plainly that not all organisations that received the backdoor were targeted with follow-on actions, and that observing the initial beacon domain does not by itself mean the backdoor was used. Further name resolutions associated with that domain do indicate follow-on activity.
logic: Two-stage triage. Stage one is the initial check-in, which indicates the software was present and reached out. Stage two is any subsequent resolution or session beyond that first beacon, which indicates the operator selected you. Retained resolver logs are what separate the stages, including the answers and not only the queries.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | filter xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name ~= "<beacon_domain>" | join (<subsequent_resolutions>) | filter resolution_count > 1
caveat: Stops a mass-delivery event being triaged as a mass-compromise event, which is the difference between a proportionate response and an unaffordable one. It depends entirely on resolver log retention reaching back to before the update was installed; without it, both stages are indistinguishable and every affected host must be assumed actioned.

name: Implant checking in on a regular interval
description: An implant that sleeps, wakes, collects queued commands and sleeps again produces repeated similar-sized sessions between one pair of hosts at a near-constant gap. Tool-independent: the shape comes from the sleep-and-poll design, not from any one framework.
logic: For each source and destination pair, take the gaps between successive sessions over a long window. A low standard deviation across many sessions, especially with similar byte counts, is the signal. Run it over days, since patient operators use long sleeps.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 != null | comp count() as sessions, stddev(xdm.event.duration) as gap_dev, avg(xdm.source.sent_bytes) as avg_bytes by xdm.source.host.hostname, xdm.target.ipv4 | filter sessions > 20 and gap_dev < 5
caveat: Update checks, monitoring agents and telemetry clients beacon identically. An allow list of known-good pairs is a prerequisite, not a refinement. Jitter settings degrade this further.

name: Published indicator lists contain hashes of legitimate tools
description: An advisory publishing indicators noted directly that some file hashes in its own machine-readable set identify legitimate tools, including a common remote access client and core operating system binaries, because the actor used those tools rather than because the files are malicious.
logic: A quality control on ingestion rather than a detection. Before loading an indicator set for blocking or alerting, separate hashes of attacker-built artefacts from hashes of legitimate tools the actor used. The second group belongs in hunting with context, never in blocking, or the estate breaks and the analysts stop trusting the feed.
caveat: Unusually candid of the publishing agency and worth carrying as a standing caution, because the same problem is present in many feeds without the warning. Blocking a core operating system binary by hash is an outage, and alerting on one produces enough noise that the whole feed gets ignored.

name: A command run by something other than a shell
description: Platform utilities that will execute a command as a side effect of their normal function, used so that the parent of the resulting process is not a shell and the chain does not resemble command execution.
logic: The utilities that accept a command argument, and the diagnostic and compatibility helpers that spawn children. The value is that these break parent-child chains a detection would otherwise follow, so covering the utility list restores the chain.
caveat: Several of these run legitimately, notably the console host and the shell process. The pattern is worth holding because a detection strategy built on 'shell spawned by document application' has a blind spot exactly the size of this utility list.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Every route into and out of the networks, including the quiet ones
description: Remote access gets listed anyway. The routes that get missed are business intelligence connections, licensing servers and vendor telemetry that reach out because a product requires it, and those are rarely on anyone's diagram.
logic: Identify and categorise every ingress and egress route for both business and control networks by type, then record which are monitored.
xql_sketch: dataset = <route_inventory> | comp count() by route_type, zone, monitored | filter monitored = false
caveat: An inventory task with no query behind it. The value is what it surfaces: the licensing and reporting links nobody remembers approving.

name: The installer used to run something else
description: External rules cover the platform installer being used to fetch and run a package from the web, and to call a library's unregister function, both of which execute attacker-chosen code under a signed platform binary.
logic: The installer taking a remote location as its package argument, or being pointed at a library with the unregister switch. Both are documented behaviours of a signed platform binary, so signature and publisher checks pass and only the argument form is anomalous.
caveat: Belongs with the other signed-binary proxy execution patterns here, and the same caution applies: the utility runs constantly for legitimate reasons, so the argument form and the parent process are what make it usable rather than the image name.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Test what an ordinary account can reach from inside
description: A two-week assessment found nothing exploitable externally and could not phish in, then compromised the whole domain from inside through multiple separate paths. Perimeter strength and interior strength are unrelated.
logic: From an ordinary workstation with an ordinary user account, establish what can be reached and what privilege can be obtained. Multiple paths existing means fixing one changes nothing.
xql_sketch: not a query; an assessment scope decision, verified by whether internal path testing has ever been performed separately from external
caveat: Cuts against the common preference for external testing, because external findings are easier to explain and cheaper to fix. It is an argument about where assessment budget goes.

name: Whether east-west traffic is observed at all
description: Insufficient internal network monitoring is the single gap that silently disables the largest number of detections in this corpus, because so many depend on seeing host-to-host traffic that perimeter sensors never carry. Corresponds to "insufficient internal network monitoring", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: Per network segment, establish whether internal traffic is observed and where sensors actually sit, then read the detection library against that map before claiming coverage.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | comp count() as flows, count_distinct(xdm.source.ipv4) as sources by segment | filter flows = 0
caveat: The usual finding is a well-instrumented perimeter and a blind interior, which means the detections that matter after initial access are the ones that cannot run.

name: Control equipment reachable from the internet
description: The root cause of the water facility compromises was exposure, not sophistication. The cheapest and highest-value thing an operator in this sector can do, and it is inventory work rather than monitoring.
logic: Enumerate which control assets answer from the internet, and what authentication sits in front of each.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter zone = "ot" and external_reachable = true | comp count() by authentication_present, device_type
caveat: Discover passively where possible; some equipment does not survive being scanned. Smaller utilities often lack the staff to maintain such an inventory, which is why the exposure persists.

name: Which business hosts can reach control assets, and how
description: Where the assessed objective is reaching operational technology from the business network, reachability is the risk. Operational documentation and network diagrams are themselves targets, so access control on that material is part of the same problem.
logic: Enumerate every business-network host that can reach a control asset and the path it uses, then reduce the set. Separately, confirm that operational documentation and network diagrams are readable only by authenticated and authorised users.
xql_sketch: dataset = <reachability_matrix> | filter target_zone = "ot" and source_zone = "enterprise" | comp count_distinct(source_host) as reachers by target_host, path
caveat: An architecture question, not a query. The documentation half is frequently missed because it is not a network control.

name: Service tickets requested in bulk for offline cracking
description: Requesting service tickets for many service accounts in a short window, with weaker encryption negotiated deliberately to make offline cracking feasible.
logic: Aggregate service ticket requests per requesting account, weighting requests that negotiated weaker encryption types.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter event_id = 4769 and ticket_encryption_type in ("0x17", "0x18") | comp count_distinct(service_name) as services by xdm.source.user.username, bin(_time, 1h) | filter services > 10
caveat: Extremely high volume in any domain; needs aggregation per requesting account, not per event. Long random service account passwords make the cracking step fail even when harvesting succeeds.

name: Domain access from a ticket nobody issued
description: Affiliates generated Kerberos tickets for domain access after gaining a foothold. A forged ticket produces authenticated access to services with no corresponding authentication at the domain controller.
logic: Service access with no preceding ticket request for that account, tickets whose lifetime exceeds domain policy, and tickets using encryption types the domain no longer issues. The same absence-of-authentication shape as a forged identity token, one layer down.
caveat: Requires the directory's own authentication logging at a level frequently not enabled. Where the account signing key has been taken, the only remedy is rotating it twice, which is disruptive enough that it is often deferred and leaves the forgery capability intact.

name: When the operating system's own answers cannot be trusted
description: The implant used a kernel module to remove its components from any listing the operating system returns, and to mediate all access to its encrypted store. Anything that asks the compromised operating system what is on it receives an answer the implant controls.
logic: Not a query. Compare what the live operating system reports against an independent view: an offline image, a raw disk read, or memory acquisition. Divergence between the two is the detection, and no agent running under the compromised kernel can produce it.
caveat: Invalidates the assumption underneath every host-based detection in this corpus. Worth knowing which of your controls run under the kernel they are inspecting, because against this class of implant a clean scan result carries no information. The advisory notes per-implant unique keying also defeats signatures used by tools independent of the operating system.

name: Join the known-exploited catalogue to your exposed inventory
description: Where an actor works by breadth across dozens of published vulnerabilities rather than depth in a few, no per-vulnerability detection strategy scales. The catalogue join covers every actor working that way and updates itself.
logic: Intersect the published catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild with the externally reachable asset inventory, and treat the result as the remediation queue.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | join (dataset = <kev_catalogue>) as k k.product = product and k.version_range matches version
caveat: A vulnerability management process, not a detection. The catalogue is a maintained structured file, so this can be automated rather than assembled from advisories by hand.

name: Access reaching the disaster recovery or backup network
description: Actors moved by remote desktop from a compromised production server into the organisation's disaster recovery network. The environment relied on to rebuild was reachable from the environment that had been compromised.
logic: Sessions from production address space into recovery, backup or standby address space. The legitimate set is small, scheduled and usually one-directional, which makes anything outside it worth alerting on.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter incidr(xdm.target.ipv4, <dr_network_cidr>) = true and incidr(xdm.source.ipv4, <production_cidr>) = true | filter xdm.target.port in (3389, 22, 445)
caveat: Worth more than its alert volume suggests, because recovery capability is what determines whether a ransomware event is an outage or a crisis. Recovery networks are frequently omitted from monitoring precisely because they are considered out of band.

name: Watch extortion leak sites for your own and your suppliers' names
description: How many organisations first learn of a compromise. Pairs with requiring vendors and partners to disclose breaches contractually.
logic: Monitor extortion leak sites for the organisation's own name and those of key suppliers and partners.
xql_sketch: not applicable; belongs to supplier risk management rather than a detection platform
caveat: Not a technical detection and not something a monitoring platform does. It only tells you after the fact.

name: An old way in plus a new way up
description: Actors combined multiple legacy remote access and network vulnerabilities with a recent critical privilege escalation flaw in the directory authentication protocol, compromising every identity service in the domain in a single intrusion.
logic: Assess exposure by path rather than by individual severity. An old perimeter flaw rated moderate and a current escalation flaw rated critical are separately unremarkable and together are total compromise, so the question is whether any unpatched perimeter product can reach any unpatched escalation flaw.
caveat: Severity-ranked patching handles each element on its own merits and can leave the chain open indefinitely, because the perimeter flaw never rises high enough to be scheduled. The escalation flaw here compromises all directory identity services at once, which means the chain's outcome is the entire domain regardless of where it started.

name: Hosts that cannot carry an endpoint agent, as a named population
description: A red team persisted several months undetected on legacy hosts with no endpoint agent. Treat the population as a standing design constraint, not a gap to close later.
logic: Reconcile endpoint agent inventory against asset inventory. Distinguish cannot-install from not-yet-installed, and prioritise network sensor placement around the former.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter endpoint_agent_installed = false | comp count() by os_version, zone, agent_supported
caveat: In industrial environments this population is large and permanent because vendor support conditions forbid agents. Several months of undetected persistence is the demonstrated consequence.

name: The older job scheduler, which newer tooling ignores
description: External rules cover the legacy interactive job scheduler and its network protocol equivalent, mechanisms that predate the current task scheduler and are not always visible to tooling built around it.
logic: Execution of the legacy scheduling utility, and job files appearing in its directory. Because it is deprecated, any use is anomalous in a modern estate, which makes this a rare case where the mechanism itself is the signal.
caveat: Deprecated for years, which is exactly why it is worth covering: tooling and reviews built around the current scheduler may not enumerate these jobs at all. Legitimate use in a modern estate is close to zero, so this needs no threshold.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Sort exposed assets by age of oldest unpatched flaw
description: Vulnerability programmes rank by severity and recency, and both biases hide this. A 2009 flaw on an internet-facing application server was exploited successfully by a ransomware operation in 2025.
logic: Sort the externally reachable inventory by the age of its oldest unpatched vulnerability rather than by severity. That surfaces a different and usually more alarming list.
xql_sketch: dataset = <vuln_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | comp min(cve_year) as oldest by hostname, product | sort asc oldest
caveat: Assets carrying decade-old unpatched flaws are usually unsupported, forgotten or owned by nobody currently employed. Remediation is decommissioning or isolating, which needs an owner found first.

name: A malicious build signed with the vendor's own certificate
description: A backdoored library was inserted into the vendor's software lifecycle and signed with the legitimate vendor code signing certificate, then distributed as a normal update. Every signature check passed because the signature was genuine.
logic: Signature validity carries no information here, so detection has to move to behaviour: what the updated software does that the previous version did not. Specifically, name lookups and outbound sessions to destinations the product has no documented reason to reach, and version-to-behaviour comparison across the estate.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.source.process.name in (<management_platform_binaries>) | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.host.hostname) by xdm.source.process.name, software_version
caveat: Defeats code signing, allow-listing by publisher, and reputation, all at once. The residual control is egress restriction for management platforms and behavioural comparison between versions. Note also that the affected versions here were specific builds, so an inventory that records only the product and not the build cannot answer the exposure question.

name: The platform's library loader running attacker-chosen code
description: A signed platform utility whose purpose is to load and execute a function from a library, used to run attacker code with a trusted parent and a trusted image name. The most heavily represented single evasion in the external rule corpora.
logic: The loader utilities themselves, with attention to the argument forms that indicate abuse: a library outside the system directories, an exported function being named, a control panel item, or the documented shell execution helper used to launch an arbitrary command.

markers.note: these signed utilities spawning anything is the signal, not their own execution

caveat: These utilities run constantly for legitimate reasons, so the image name alone is unusable. The argument forms above and the library location are what make it tractable. This technique attracted more external rules than any other single evasion, which is a reasonable proxy for how often it is seen.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: A permitted command used to become root
description: External rules cover a long list of ordinary Linux utilities being used to escalate privilege through their own documented features, alongside changes to the privilege configuration file itself and to alternative elevation tools.
logic: Two halves. Elevation of a utility whose normal use does not require it, particularly package managers, text processors and interpreters, which is the pattern behind the published lists of such binaries. And modification of the privilege configuration, especially entries removing the password requirement, which is the persistence half.
caveat: The utility list is long and grows, so treat the elevation of any interpreter or package manager as the durable form rather than maintaining names. A no-password entry appearing in the privilege configuration is the single highest-value marker here, because it is persistence and it is almost never legitimate outside automation that should be documented.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: Startup shortcut whose target sits in a user directory
description: Shortcut creation in a start menu folder is worth flagging; where it points is the discriminator. Installed software does not launch from application data or temporary directories.
logic: Shortcut files created under a start menu path whose resolved target lies in a user application data, temporary or shared user directory.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.extension = "lnk" and xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)\\Start Menu\\" | filter lnk_target_path ~= "(?i)\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\Public)\\"
caveat: Reading the shortcut target needs telemetry that parses shortcut contents. Without it this degrades to alerting on all start menu shortcut creation.

name: A local account created on a host that should not have one
description: Creation of a local account, commonly with a plausible service or support name, to provide access that survives a directory password reset and does not appear in directory account reviews.
logic: The account creation event on the host, and the command-line forms across platforms. On a domain-joined estate or a control network the legitimate rate is very low, which makes this alertable without tuning in most environments.
caveat: Survives the remediation most organisations perform, which is a directory-wide password reset, and stays invisible to directory-based account reviews. Worth pairing with a periodic inventory of local accounts across the estate rather than relying on the creation event alone.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: The local account and secret stores copied off a host
description: The registry hives holding local account hashes and cached secrets copied or exported, which yields credentials usable elsewhere without ever touching the process that holds them in memory.
logic: Hive export by the registry utility, copies of the hive files themselves out of the configuration directory, and the database utility being used to read a locked hive or directory file. Also cover the well-known dumper tool artefacts, which remain in use.
caveat: Distinct from reading credentials out of process memory, which most credential-theft detections cover. This route avoids that process entirely, so a rule set built only around memory access misses it. Backup software touches these files legitimately and must be enumerated first.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Control asset stops sending its logs
description: Someone with local access to equipment can alter or delete its logs on the device, so evidence survives only where it has already been copied off. Works because it does not depend on the device's own honesty.
logic: Compare the set of assets currently sending logs against the asset inventory, and report silence or sequence gaps at the receiver.
xql_sketch: dataset = <log_receipt_dataset> | comp max(_time) as last_log by xdm.source.host.hostname | alter silent_minutes = timestamp_diff(current_time(), last_log, "MINUTE") | filter silent_minutes > 60
caveat: Cannot distinguish tampering from an equipment or network fault, and faults are far more common. It establishes the gap, which is what an investigation needs.

name: Logs edited back to their prior contents rather than deleted
description: An actor modified logs to their original state and deleted specific files covering only the period of activity. Restoration is quieter than deletion because the usual check, whether the log exists and is growing, still passes.
logic: Compare the forwarded copy against what remains on the host. Divergence for a bounded window is the signal, and it only exists if the logs were shipped somewhere the actor could not reach. Also look for write access to log paths by anything that is not the logging process.
xql_sketch: dataset = <file_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)(localhost_access|/var/log/|logs/)" and xdm.source.process.name not in ("rsyslogd", "syslog-ng", "java", "httpd", "nginx")
caveat: Undetectable on the host alone by design, which makes this a pattern that must be answered by architecture rather than by a rule. If logs are only local, a gap of exactly the intrusion window will look like a quiet period.

name: Whether the logs your detections assume are actually collected
description: The most common obstacle to incident response in reported investigations was missing logs, not missing detections. Several records in this corpus rest on log sources that are off by default.
logic: Per asset class, record whether each log source the detection library depends on is collected, and whether retention exceeds the dwell time the threat model assumes.
xql_sketch: dataset = <log_source_inventory> | filter collected = false or retention_days < assumed_dwell_days | comp count() by asset_class, log_source
caveat: Retention is a cost decision, so this belongs in front of whoever owns that budget. The figure to argue with is assumed dwell time: where an actor holds access for years, ninety days of logs answers nothing. There is now a base rate to argue with rather than an assertion. Across eighteen consecutive quarters of one responder's engagements, insufficient logging appeared as a named weakness in eighteen to forty-two percent of cases, in every year of the series, and in the earliest reports it was worse than a proportion: the initial access vector could not be determined at all in the majority of engagements because the records did not exist. The most recent quarter puts it at forty-two percent and the second most common weakness overall. If the budget conversation needs a number, that is the number, and the honest framing is that this is the control which decides whether any other finding can be reached.

name: The top families are old, known, and therefore answerable
description: Eleven families accounted for the most observed activity in a year, most in use for over five years and two for more than a decade. The authoring agencies note directly that using known strains gives defenders the opportunity to prepare.
logic: A coverage audit with a bounded, published list and a definite answer per entry: for each named family, does anything in the estate detect delivery, execution or command traffic. A negative answer against a fixed list is a finding; a negative answer against no list means nothing.

markers.note: the shared delivery surface across the named families is a mail attachment

caveat: The strategic value is that the list is short and stable rather than that these indicators are current. A decade-old family still topping the annual table is evidence that detection coverage, not adversary novelty, is the binding constraint.

name: Credential capture through a near-miss domain or bad certificate
description: Interception surfaces at the corporate end as certificate mismatches and domains close to the real one. The intercepting device is usually somewhere the employer cannot see.
logic: Requested names close to but not matching corporate domains, and sessions whose presented certificate subject does not match the expected portal.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | alter dist = levenshtein(xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name, "<corporate_domain>") | filter dist > 0 and dist < 3
caveat: Very little of this is observable from the corporate side. Single-use multi-factor authentication is what actually blunts it, by making the captured pair worthless.

name: Computer account created or renamed to impersonate a controller
description: A pair of directory flaws let a low-privileged account create or rename a computer account so its name collides with a domain controller's, then request tickets as that controller.
logic: Computer account creation by a non-administrative account, and any computer account whose name matches or closely resembles a domain controller.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter event_id in (4741, 4742) | filter new_account_name in (<domain_controller_names>) or xdm.source.user.username not in (<admin_accounts>)
caveat: The default machine account quota letting ordinary users create computer accounts is the root cause. Setting it to zero removes the technique in one attribute change, so detection is the fallback rather than the fix.

name: Malicious content in a message property rather than body or attachment
description: Where crafted content sits in an item property, gateway scanning of bodies and attachments never sees it. Retrospective mailbox sweeping matters more than live detection, because messages may predate knowledge of the flaw.
logic: Sweep mailbox item properties, not message bodies, for properties referencing remote paths. Run it retrospectively across the estate rather than only forward.
xql_sketch: not expressible as a traffic query; requires a mailbox-level property sweep, for which vendors sometimes publish a script
caveat: A different operation from gateway inspection, and most organisations lack tooling for it beyond the vendor's own script.

name: Your mail or messaging service sending someone else's traffic
description: Stolen credentials for transactional mail and messaging platforms were used to send through the victim's own reputable infrastructure, which inherits the sender reputation and the authenticated domain.
logic: Volume and pattern anomalies in the sending platform's own audit trail rather than on your network: send rate against baseline, recipient domains never previously used, and access to the sending interface from an address the application does not run from.

markers.expr: send_volume by api_key, bin(_time, 1h) against baseline_multiple

caveat: The harm lands mostly on third parties and on your domain reputation rather than on your systems, which is why it is often noticed by a blocklist operator before it is noticed internally. Detection lives in the provider's console, so somebody has to own watching it.

name: Bulk mailbox access, export or outward forwarding rules
description: Where the objective is covert acquisition of email, the activity is at the mailbox rather than at the login. Low-volume administrative events in a healthy tenant, worth alerting on individually.
logic: Bulk message access, mailbox export or sync operations, and creation of forwarding or inbox rules that copy mail outward.
xql_sketch: dataset = <cloud_audit_dataset> | filter operation in ("MailItemsAccessed", "New-InboxRule", "MailboxExport") | comp count() by xdm.source.user.username, operation
caveat: Depends on tenant audit logging being enabled and retained. Bulk mailbox access logging in particular is frequently a higher licensing tier.

name: Developer, distributor and end user are three different parties
description: In the criminal malware industry developers build, distributors broker, and end users operate. Access to already-compromised systems is bought and sold, and the same access has been sold more than once to different actors for different purposes.
logic: Explains why one malware family maps to many unrelated objectives, and why the family name predicts almost nothing about what will happen next. Scope an incident on the access that was obtained rather than on the reported behaviour of the family, and expect follow-on activity from parties unconnected to the first.
caveat: Directly undermines detection strategies organised by malware family, and eviction plans that assume one adversary. A host compromised by a loader may be sold on after remediation appears complete if the credentials it held were never rotated.

name: Managed file transfer products and what they retain
description: Internet-facing by design, holding the data being transferred, and frequently owned by a business function rather than IT. That combination is why the class was exploited at scale twice by one actor through two different vendors' products.
logic: Which such products you run, whether they are in the patch cycle, and what data is retained on them rather than merely passing through. Retained data is what gets taken.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter product_class = "server.file_transfer" | comp count() by product, external_reachable, patch_status, retention_days
caveat: Retention is usually configured for convenience and never revisited, so impact far exceeds transfer volume. Reducing retention limits damage from the next flaw in this class, which is more durable than patching any one of them.

name: Endpoint management platform pushing something unauthorised
description: Compromising a management platform makes it do what it is designed to do on the attacker's behalf, and every endpoint obeys. Endpoint agents will not flag it, because the platform is trusted by design.
logic: Deployment or script execution tasks created by an account outside the authorised set, or targeting an unusually broad set of endpoints, or at an unusual hour. The platform's own audit log is the primary source.
xql_sketch: dataset = <rmm_audit_dataset> | filter deployment_task_created_by not in (<authorised_deployers>) or deployment_target_count > <normal_max>
caveat: Legitimate mass deployment looks identical in shape. Only authorisation and timing separate them, so a change process is required.

name: Whether the process can run without the control system
description: At one water facility the treatment system was run manually until the compromised control computer was restored. Manual operation is the difference between a control system incident and a service failure.
logic: A preparedness question with a definite answer: for each critical process, can it be operated manually, for how long, by how many trained people, and when was that last rehearsed. The answer determines whether loss of the control system is an inconvenience or an outage.
caveat: One of the few genuinely mitigating factors available in operational technology, and it degrades quietly as staff who remember manual operation retire and as processes are re-engineered to assume automation. Worth testing rather than documenting.

name: File created in the root of a drive
description: One wiper refused to complete unless a specifically named file existed in the system drive root, an execution guard the operator had to satisfy. Almost nothing legitimate writes to a drive root.
logic: File creation directly in a drive root rather than in a subdirectory. Treat the location as the signal; the name is sample-specific.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type = "file_create" and xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)^[A-Z]:\\\\[^\\\\]+$"
caveat: Some installers and older software drop files in the drive root. The specific name from any one sample will not recur.

name: Many unrelated services force-stopped together
description: Ransomware carrying a hard-coded kill list stops named services before encrypting, to release file locks and to remove monitoring. Breadth across unrelated product families in one window is the signal; any single termination is ordinary.
logic: Count distinct terminated service names per host per short window, weighting up where the terminated services span unrelated vendors.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type = "process_terminate" | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.process.name) as killed, values(xdm.target.process.name) as names by xdm.target.host.hostname, bin(_time, 5m) | filter killed > 5
caveat: Patching and upgrade windows stop services legitimately, but usually within one product family. Suppress against maintenance windows.

name: Something writing to the boot record
description: Multiple destructive families corrupted the master boot record so the host fails to boot, in one case after displaying a ransom message. Boot record modification is close to a pure signal, since almost nothing legitimate writes there outside imaging and partitioning.
logic: Raw writes to the physical drive device, to sector zero or to the partition table, by any process that is not a known imaging or partitioning tool during a known maintenance window. Legitimate frequency on a running estate is effectively zero.

markers.note: the value is the exclusion set; invert as an allow-list of imaging tools rather than a literal match

caveat: Fires very late in the sequence, at the moment of damage rather than before it, so its value is scoping and speed of containment rather than prevention. If it fires on more than one host, assume a coordinated destructive stage and act on the estate rather than the host.

name: Second factor skipped by changing the case of the username
description: A flaw in a remote access appliance let an actor log in without being prompted for the second factor simply by altering the capitalisation of the username. The authentication succeeds and looks entirely ordinary.
logic: Two things to look for in the appliance's own authentication log. A successful session where no second factor was recorded, and a username whose capitalisation differs from the canonical directory form for that account. The second is a cheap and unusual marker because legitimate clients submit whatever the directory holds.
caveat: A useful reminder that a second factor is only as good as the code path that enforces it. The case-mismatch marker generalises beyond this one flaw and costs nothing to look for, because a normalised comparison is what most authentication pipelines already do.

name: A second factor satisfied with a forged token rather than bypassed
description: The actor used a previously stolen secret key to generate a cookie that satisfied the multi-factor system protecting web mail. The second factor was not evaded or phished; it was computed, so the login looks fully compliant.
logic: A successful multi-factor authentication with no corresponding challenge event at the multi-factor service, or a session presenting a valid factor cookie where no enrolment or prompt was recorded. Requires the multi-factor product's own logs, separately from the application's.
caveat: The reason multi-factor is not a terminal control against this actor class: the secret that underwrites it is a credential like any other. Where the secret is stolen, every account it protects is open and every login appears policy-compliant. Rotation of the shared secret is the remediation, and it is rarely part of an incident checklist.

markers.expr: exists(mfa_challenge_event) at mfa_provider for this session

name: Multi-factor enrolment moved to a new device
description: The decisive step in service desk social engineering, because it converts a one-time deception into durable access that looks legitimate afterwards. A small, low-volume event class in most organisations.
logic: Alert on every enrolment change, device registration and authenticator reset, especially where a password reset for the same account occurred in the same window, and especially outside working hours.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_audit_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type in ("mfa_device_register", "mfa_device_delete", "password_reset") | comp values(xdm.event.operation_sub_type) as ops by xdm.source.user.username, bin(_time, 1h) | filter array_length(ops) > 1
