caveat: Genuine device replacement produces the same sequence, which is why the attack works. The real control is verification before the service desk acts, such as a callback to a known number. Detection tells you afterwards. Markers were added on 2026-08-12 from reporting on a voice-pretexting operation; this pattern had carried none, which meant the corpus named the decisive step in service desk social engineering without saying how to see it. Lead with the failure-then-enrolment correlation. The geography marker is the weakest and weakening: that operation authenticated through residential and consumer broadband addresses precisely so country and hosting reputation would not separate it from staff.

name: The second factor's own default settings
description: Actors took advantage of an account left on default second-factor settings to enrol a device of their own and reach the network. The agencies recommend reviewing configuration for fail-open and re-enrolment scenarios, and disabling inactive accounts uniformly across both the directory and the authentication system.
logic: Three configuration questions with definite answers. Does the system permit access when the factor service is unreachable. Can an unenrolled account enrol a device by presenting only a password. And is the disabled account set identical in the directory and in the authentication product. The third is a reconciliation, not a setting, and it is the one that fails silently.
caveat: Strong authentication reported as implemented can still be bypassed by its own defaults, so the control's presence is not the same as its effectiveness. The account-set reconciliation is the subtle one: an account disabled in the directory but still enrollable in the authentication product is an open door that neither system reports as open. The prevalence is now measured rather than assumed. Across three years of quarterly response reporting, authentication weakness never fell below roughly a quarter of engagements and reached sixty-five percent in the most recent quarter, where it was the single most common weakness. The sharpest figure in the series is narrower and more useful: in one quarter, one hundred percent of engagements that involved phishing had multi-factor authentication either bypassed or not fully enabled. Where a programme treats strong authentication as a solved control, that figure is the counter-argument, and it points at configuration and enrolment rather than at whether the control was bought.

name: Message brokers and integration middleware reachable from outside
description: Middleware sits between systems and is frequently forgotten in exposure reviews, which look at applications and appliances. Almost none should be externally reachable.
logic: Enumerate broker, queue and management ports and establish which are reachable from outside.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter listening_port in (61616, 61617, 8161, 5672, 9092) and external_reachable = true
caveat: Brokers are usually owned by an application or integration team rather than infrastructure, which is how they escape exposure reviews. Ownership is the first question.

name: Do not scope an incident around the first actor found
description: Two distinct nation-state actors were present at one organisation through two unrelated vulnerabilities. A victim exposed enough to be compromised once is exposed enough to be compromised twice.
logic: Scope by exposure surface rather than by the actor identified. Enumerate every externally reachable service, not only the one known to have been exploited.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | comp count() by service, patch_status
caveat: An investigative discipline, not a query. Recorded because the instinct is to scope around the first actor, which here would have missed a second intrusion entirely.

name: Install chain that includes genuine components mid-sequence
description: Delivery chains deliberately include legitimate non-malicious components at intermediate stages, which defeats any assessment treating a signed legitimate file as evidence the chain is safe.
logic: Follow process ancestry across the whole sequence rather than judging any single file, and treat the chain as the unit of assessment.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process" | comp values(xdm.target.process.name) as chain, count() as depth by xdm.source.process.pid, xdm.target.host.hostname | filter depth > 3
caveat: Requires process ancestry preserved across several stages, which many endpoint products truncate. A legitimate component appearing mid-chain is the specific trap to avoid.

name: The platform's own encryption used to hold the platform hostage
description: State actors were observed using the operating system's built-in full-disk encryption alongside public ransomware families. Nothing malicious is deployed, no signature exists to match, and the tool is signed by the platform vendor. The same idea appears one layer up in a database: the engine's own encryption function applied to table contents, with the originals dropped, needs no binary on the host and leaves nothing for file-based detection to see. There the evidence is the query log rather than process telemetry, so the markers differ even though the scenario does not.
logic: Encryption being enabled or a recovery key being changed on hosts where the organisation did not do it, and where the estate's own encryption management has no record. The absence of a management record is the discriminator, since the command itself is legitimate administration.
caveat: Signature-based and reputation-based controls cannot see this at all, because the binary is a signed platform component doing exactly what it is for. A recovery key that was never escrowed is the difference between an outage and an unrecoverable one, which makes escrow coverage a control worth auditing separately.

name: Domain controller machine account password changed unexpectedly
description: The protocol flaw works by resetting a controller's own machine account password through a burst of authentication attempts. A controller machine account password change is rare and consequential regardless of mechanism.
logic: A burst of authentication attempts against a controller from one source within seconds, and any machine account password change for a domain controller.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter event_id in (4742, 5805) and target_account in (<domain_controller_accounts>)
caveat: Patched long ago and enforcement is now default, so this is chiefly about unpatched or legacy controllers. Retained because those exist and because the machine account change is worth alerting on either way.

name: Access obtained by one actor and sold on to others
description: The actor was observed selling access to compromised infrastructure on a forum, operating as a contractor while also serving its own financial interest. Access gained once may be used by several unrelated parties afterwards.
logic: Changes what a finding means rather than producing an alert. After confirming intrusion by a broker, expect later access attempts with different tradecraft against the same entry point, and scope credential rotation to everything the original access could reach rather than to what the first actor was seen using.
caveat: Undermines eviction as a concept: the objective was resale, so removing one actor does not remove the value of what was taken. Ransomware frequently follows brokered access, which is why the intermediate stage matters even when no damage was seen.

name: A router watching industrial protocol traffic
description: The predecessor framework's modules enabled traffic manipulation, destruction of the infected device, likely exploitation of downstream devices, and monitoring of an industrial control protocol, which the agencies assessed as an ongoing requirement for the actor.
logic: A compromised edge device sitting on the path between business and control networks can observe industrial protocol traffic without touching any control asset. The device's own configuration and firmware integrity is the only evidence, and it cannot be trusted from the device itself, so compare against an externally held copy and watch for the device originating rather than forwarding sessions.
caveat: Reframes a consumer-grade router as an operational technology exposure rather than a networking one. The destructive module in the same framework matters too, since a device that can be bricked on command is an availability risk at the boundary as well as a monitoring position.

name: The device edits what it tells the administrator
description: Actors installed automation policies on compromised routers that strip lines containing chosen strings from the output of legitimate commands, and block other commands outright, including the file operations a responder would use to preserve evidence.
logic: Cannot be answered by asking the device, which is the point. Compare the device's own configuration output against a copy held elsewhere, look for automation or event policies nobody created, and reconcile what the device reports against what adjacent devices observe of its traffic.
caveat: The most complete evasion in this corpus. It defeats the responder rather than the detection: a command whose output has been filtered looks like a clean device, and file commands are blocked so the policy itself cannot be copied off for analysis. Export configuration continuously to somewhere the device cannot reach, because that copy is the only trustworthy one.

name: Configuration or routing change on infrastructure
description: Traffic redirection requires a configuration change, so the change record is the choke point even when the intrusion itself leaves nothing else visible.
logic: Configuration writes, routing changes, tunnel creation or access list edits, reconciled against change records and against the accounts authorised to make them.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_device_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "configuration_change" | filter xdm.source.user.username not in (<authorised_admins>) or xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<management_network>)
caveat: Busy networks generate steady legitimate change. Needs device configuration under version control or a change feed to reconcile against.

name: Container or application hosting running on a network device
description: Running a container on a router puts attacker code inside a device with no endpoint agent, where the device's own configuration listing may not reveal it. The hardest evasion in this corpus to detect externally.
logic: Indirect signals only: application hosting or container features enabled where nobody enabled them, unexplained memory or storage consumption, and sessions sourced from the device's own address rather than forwarded through it. A router originating traffic is categorically different from a router forwarding it.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_device_dataset> | filter device_feature in ("app-hosting", "iox", "guestshell") or xdm.source.ipv4 in (<device_management_addresses>)
caveat: Some organisations legitimately use device application hosting for monitoring agents; enumerate once. A compromised device cannot be trusted to report its own state, so suspicion warrants out-of-band examination rather than interrogation.

name: A new trust added so authentication happens where you cannot see it
description: The actor added new federation trusts to existing on-premises identity infrastructure. Where this is done, authentication can occur outside the organisation's known infrastructure and may not be visible to the legitimate owner at all.
logic: Federation trust and domain configuration changes, alerted on as a set of near-zero expected frequency rather than reviewed. The number of legitimate changes per year is countable on one hand in most organisations, which makes any change worth a call.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_audit_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation ~= "(?i)(add|set).*(federat|domain|trust)" | comp count() by xdm.source.user.username, xdm.event.operation
caveat: The worst persistence outcome in this corpus: the attacker no longer needs to authenticate anywhere you can observe. Nothing downstream detects it, because downstream services correctly trust the identity provider. Detection exists only at the moment of the configuration change, which makes retention of identity audit logs the enabling control.

name: Test and staging instances of an appliance family
description: A critical infrastructure organisation was entered through a non-production instance of an appliance. Non-production instances are routinely internet-reachable for convenience, excluded from the patch cycle because they are not production, and outside the monitoring scope for the same reason.
logic: Enumerate every instance of a given appliance or application family, not just production, and check exposure, patch level and monitoring scope for each.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter environment in ("test", "staging", "development") and external_reachable = true | comp count() by product, patch_status, in_monitoring_scope
caveat: Non-production instances are usually owned by a project rather than operations, which is why they escape both patching and monitoring. Finding them means asking teams, not querying an inventory.

name: Directory database extracted from a volume shadow copy
description: The database engine under Active Directory logs application events whenever the directory database is moved, created, mounted or detached. Those entries persist on the endpoint far longer than security events, which makes them the right place to look when dwell time is measured in months.
logic: Four ESENT application log event IDs describe the whole extraction: a database location change pointing at a shadow copy path, creation of a new database in a temporary directory, the mounting of a copy from the shadow copy, and its detachment on completion. Match on event ID plus the presence of the database file name, not on exact wording.
xql_sketch: dataset = <windows_event_dataset> | filter event_id in (216, 325, 326, 327, 637) and event_detail ~= "(?i)ntds\.dit" | filter event_detail ~= "(?i)(VolumeShadowCopy|GLOBALROOT|\$SNAP_)"
caveat: Backup software shadow-copies domain controllers legitimately and produces the same event family. Allow-list it by schedule and account. Event detail wording varies between environments.

name: One session walking through other people's records
description: Access control flaws where an application uses an identifier to reach an object without checking that the requester is entitled to it. Frequently exploited in breach incidents because they are common, hard to prevent outside development, and abusable at scale.
logic: The abuse shape is volume and breadth rather than anything malformed: one authenticated session requesting many distinct object identifiers, often sequentially, all returning success. Nothing in any single request is anomalous, which is why this has to be counted per session rather than matched per request.
caveat: Every request is authenticated and every response is a legitimate success, so no error rate rises and no signature fires. The permanent fix is on the development side, replacing direct identifiers with unguessable ones, which is why the advisory is addressed to vendors and developers first and defenders second.

name: Persistence loaded by the office application itself
description: External rules cover add-ins written to the application startup directories, macro projects created in the global template, security zone settings altered, and registry entries loading code when the application opens.
logic: File writes into the application startup and add-in directories, changes to the global template, and registry values that load a library when the application starts. These directories change only when a user deliberately installs an add-in, which is rare in most estates.
caveat: Survives reboot, runs whenever the user opens a document, and is invisible to anything watching only autorun keys and services. The mail client variant is the one most often missed because the macro project is a single file with an unfamiliar extension.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Document application launches a scripting engine
description: An office application, document reader or browser creates a shell or scripting engine child process. These applications have no routine reason to do so, which makes it one of the few high-fidelity endpoint detections available.
logic: Parent process is a document or browser application and the child is a shell, scripting engine or a signed binary commonly used to run remote code.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process" and xdm.source.process.name in ("winword.exe", "excel.exe", "powerpnt.exe", "outlook.exe", "acrord32.exe") and xdm.target.process.name in ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "rundll32.exe", "wmic.exe")
caveat: Document automation and some line-of-business spreadsheets do this legitimately. Baseline for a fortnight and allow-list by document path or signing certificate.

name: No custom capability required
description: An agency observed a state intelligence service using publicly available information sources and readily available exploits and exploit toolkits to reach government networks, and stated that where critical vulnerabilities remain unpatched, actors can operate without developing custom malware or using previously unknown flaws.
logic: A prioritisation argument with a measurable form. Establish the interval between a fix being published for an internet-facing product and its deployment, because that interval is the entire opportunity this tradecraft requires. Where it is short, the actor must spend real capability; where it is long, they need none.
caveat: The useful reframing is that patching is not hygiene competing with real security work, it is the control that forces a state actor to spend capability it would rather save. The agency states directly that a rigorous patching cycle remains the best defence against the most frequently used attacks.

name: The screen is lying to the operator
description: Actors disrupted controllers across several critical infrastructure sectors partly through manipulation of the data shown on operator interface and supervisory control displays, producing operational disruption and financial loss.
logic: Where the display is manipulated, the operator's view and the physical reality diverge, so no single source can be trusted alone. The detection is disagreement between independent measurements of the same quantity: the displayed value against the historian, against the controller's own register, and against any instrument on a separate path.

markers.expr: historian_recorded_value != hmi_displayed_value for same tag and timestamp

caveat: Directly undermines the operator-observation defence that worked at a water facility elsewhere in this corpus, because there the operator could see the true value. If the display is manipulated, the human is being deceived rather than assisted, and only an independent measurement path resolves it.

name: Interactive session on an operator interface nobody in the control room started
description: The strongest confirmation comes from the process side rather than security telemetry: a control action nobody initiated.
logic: Interactive sessions on operator interfaces from outside the known source set or outside shift hours, reconciled with whether anyone in the control room initiated the resulting action.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<hmi_assets>) and xdm.target.port in (3389, 5900, 22) | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<operator_workstations>)
caveat: Out-of-hours callouts are legitimate and unscheduled. Reconciliation is with the control room, not a change ticket, so the detection needs a reachable human in the loop.

name: The person watching the screen noticed first
description: At a water treatment facility an actor used the control system's own software to raise a chemical dosing setpoint to a dangerous level. Plant personnel noticed the change immediately and corrected it before the control software itself detected the manipulation and alarmed.
logic: Two things follow. Operator observation is a real detection capability and should be supported deliberately, with a route to report and escalate a suspicious setpoint that does not depend on the control system agreeing. And setpoint changes outside engineering-safe ranges should alarm on the value at the moment of the write rather than on the downstream process consequence.
caveat: In this case the human was faster than the control system's own alarm, which had not yet fired. That is worth designing for rather than treating as luck: the alarm thresholds were set for process safety, not for detecting manipulation, and the two are not the same requirement.

name: Map defences against the five stages of a control system intrusion
description: Two agencies set out the sequence actors follow against control systems: decide the intended effect and pick a target, collect intelligence about the target system, build techniques and tools to navigate and manipulate it, gain initial access, then execute to create the effect. Well-resourced actors run these concurrently and repeatedly.
logic: An assurance exercise rather than a query. For each of the five stages, state what would be observable in your environment and which control addresses it. The agencies' point is that stages one to three happen largely outside your network, so a defence concentrated on initial access engages the sequence late and only once.
caveat: The advisory states twice that traditional approaches to securing these systems do not adequately address current threats, which is unusually direct. The reason is structural: these assets are built for availability and safety, often run decades-old software with no recent updates, and newer ones add connectivity that enlarges the attack surface. So the answer is prioritised hardening informed by actor behaviour, not a control catalogue.

name: Whether the log platform survives the estate being compromised
description: An intruder with administrative control of the estate can reach an in-band log platform and alter what it holds, and a ransomware event that encrypts it destroys the evidence needed to scope the incident.
logic: Verify the aggregation point is not reachable or administrable with ordinary estate credentials, and that retention exceeds assumed dwell time.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter asset_role = "log_platform" | comp count() by joined_to_estate_directory, reachable_with_estate_credentials, retention_days
caveat: Most log platforms are joined to the same directory they collect from, making them in band by definition. Fixing that is an architecture change; the interim measure is an independent copy of the highest-value sources.

name: Application server making an outbound directory or remote-invocation connection
description: Library exploitation that works by having the vulnerable server fetch and load a remote class. Servers have no routine reason to reach outward on these protocols, which makes it a narrow question.
logic: Outbound sessions from server-role assets on directory or remote-invocation ports to external destinations, excluding the known internal directory back ends.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.source.ipv4 in (<server_assets>) and xdm.target.port in (389, 636, 1099, 1389) | filter incidr(xdm.target.ipv4, <internal_cidr>) = false
caveat: Servers legitimately query internal directory services, so those must be excluded first. The external destination is the signal.

name: Servers and controllers reaching broad cloud provider ranges
description: Attacker infrastructure sits in the same provider ranges as legitimate services, so a broad allow rule to a provider is effectively a broad allow rule to anywhere. A domain controller with general outbound internet access is a finding on its own.
logic: Which hosts can reach provider ranges directly, restricted to server and controller roles where the answer should be a named endpoint list rather than a provider.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | join (dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter role in ("server", "domain_controller")) as a a.ip = xdm.source.ipv4 | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<cloud_provider_ranges>)
caveat: Genuine cloud dependencies make a blanket block impractical. The workable version is per-host-role, not per-destination.

name: Tunnelling client publishing an inbound path outward
description: A tunnelling client connects out to a cloud service then accepts inbound sessions through it, defeating perimeter inbound controls without triggering them.
logic: The client process itself, and separately persistent long-lived outbound sessions to tunnelling providers from hosts with no reason to publish anything.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.domain in (<tunnel_providers>) | comp max(xdm.event.duration) as longest by xdm.source.host.hostname | filter longest > 3600
caveat: Development teams use these legitimately for previewing work. Scope by host role; a server or operator station has no such excuse.

name: Exposure created by who does the work, not by what the work is
description: Agencies identified internet-accessible operational technology assets becoming more prevalent because organisations increased remote operations and monitoring, accommodated a decentralised workforce, and expanded outsourcing of instrumentation and control, asset management and maintenance, and in some cases process operations themselves.
logic: Trace each remote path back to the business decision that created it, because the exposure follows the contract rather than the technology. For every outsourced function, establish what it needs to reach, who holds the credential, whether the access is time-bound, and whether it was ever recorded as an architectural change.
caveat: The paths created by outsourcing are the ones least likely to appear on a network diagram, because they were justified as a commercial arrangement rather than as a network change. Where process operations themselves are outsourced, the provider's compromise is indistinguishable from an operator error.

name: Your own edge devices joining somebody else's network
description: The networks are built mainly from compromised consumer routers and connected devices. One publicly named example infected more than two hundred thousand devices worldwide and was operated by a commercial information security company.
logic: The same inventory question as end-of-life edge equipment, asked from the other direction: which devices at your sites and at home-working locations are consumer grade, unmanaged, unpatched and reachable. Then look for the relay shape, a device both receiving and originating sessions with no local user activity to explain either.

markers.expr: device_class in (soho_router, iot, camera, nvr) and internet_reachable and outside_central_management

caveat: Being recruited is not the same as being targeted, and the organisation may never be the intended victim. It still carries the traffic, appears in someone else's incident reporting, and has an unmanaged compromised device on its network. Devices at home-working locations are the hardest part of this to inventory and the easiest to overlook.

name: Encryption that did not finish, and a way back
description: A campaign against more than 3,800 hypervisor servers encrypted configuration files rather than the virtual machine data itself, potentially rendering machines unusable, and an agency published a recovery script allowing victims to attempt to restore access to their files without paying.
logic: During response, establish precisely what was encrypted before deciding anything. Where only metadata, configuration or index files are affected and the underlying data is intact, reconstruction may be possible without a key, and published recovery tooling may already exist for that family.
caveat: A rare case where the answer is recovery rather than negotiation, and it depends on establishing the scope of the encryption before anything else. Preserve the encrypted state and the affected files untouched while that question is answered, because a well-intentioned rebuild can destroy the material recovery depends on.

name: Files encrypted only in part, leaving size and structure intact
description: A ransomware family let the operator choose what percentage of each file to encrypt, lowering it for large files. Faster to run and quieter, because detections keyed on whole-file rewrites see less than they expect.
logic: Entropy sampled across a file rather than over the whole of it, since a file whose first fraction is high entropy and whose remainder is unchanged looks statistically ordinary in aggregate. Rate of modification across many files by one process remains the stronger and cheaper signal.
caveat: Directly defeats detections built on full-file rewrite volume or on whole-file entropy averages. If a ransomware rule was tuned against families that encrypt completely, this will pass under it. Recovery is also affected: partially encrypted files are still unusable but may not be flagged as corrupt.

name: Directory trusts to partner organisations, and what they carry
description: Trust plus weak credentials plus connectivity let a red team reach a partner's domain controller. A transitive trust carries credential material further than anyone intended.
logic: Enumerate every trust and what it permits, especially transitivity, then monitor authentication crossing each trust in both directions.
xql_sketch: dataset = <directory_inventory> | filter object_type = "trust" | comp count() by partner_domain, trust_direction, trust_transitive
caveat: Trusts are established for projects and never revisited, so enumeration usually surfaces relationships nobody owns. Removal is a commercial conversation.

name: Password manager database or process read by something else
description: A script was used to access password manager data during an intrusion. One file read yields every credential the user held, including for systems the actor has not yet reached.
logic: Access to vault file extensions, or memory read of the password manager process, by any process other than the manager itself. The file is normally opened by exactly one program, which makes the legitimate set unusually easy to define.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.extension in ("kdbx", "kdb", "1pif", "opvault", "psafe3") and xdm.source.process.name not in ("keepass.exe", "keepassxc.exe", "1password.exe")
caveat: Backup software and synchronisation clients touch these files legitimately and must be enumerated first. Higher value than most credential theft detections because the yield extends past the compromised host.

name: Time from vendor patch to working exploit, not from disclosure
description: Actors reverse engineered a released update to build a working exploit within 48 hours, then attacked systems that had not applied it. The patch itself was the exploit development input.
logic: Not a detection but a scheduling constraint. Measure your own interval between a vendor release and your deployment for internet-facing products, and compare it against 48 hours. Where the gap exceeds it, the exposure window is a decision you have already made rather than a risk you are carrying unknowingly.
caveat: Inverts the usual assumption that publishing a fix reduces risk before it increases it. For internet-facing products the release itself starts the clock, so a patch cycle measured in weeks is the finding. A neighbouring interval is now measured rather than assumed, and it is deliberately not the patch-to-exploit window this pattern is about. Across 207 advisories from 27 vendors, the median time from a flaw being reported to the vendor to it becoming public was 122 days, ranging from 0 to 1391. That is the vendor's fix interval, not the window between a release and a working exploit. It bounds the other side of the problem: for that long the flaw was known to someone and actionable by nobody defending against it, and the only control available during it is one that does not depend on a patch existing.

name: Executable whose file name is a long hexadecimal string
description: A ransomware payload was named with the hexadecimal string of its own file hash, defeating name-based rules and guaranteeing a different name per build. The structural check outlasts any name list.
logic: Executable or library file names consisting solely of 32 to 64 hexadecimal characters.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.name ~= "(?i)^[a-f0-9]{32,64}\.(exe|dll)$"
caveat: Build and caching systems produce hash-named artefacts legitimately, particularly on development machines and behind content caches. Scope by host role.

name: Root persistence that survives a factory reset
description: A national authority validated in a lab that a threat actor may be able to gain root-level persistence on a remote access appliance despite factory resets being issued. The standard remediation for a suspect appliance does not necessarily remove the intruder.
logic: A remediation-design question, not a query. Where an appliance is suspected compromised and its persistence may survive reset, the options that actually work are replacement of the unit, or rebuild from vendor-supplied media with the device isolated, followed by rotation of every credential it held. Confirm which of those the runbook specifies.

markers.expr: appliance_remediation_plan specifies replace_or_rebuild_from_media rather than factory_reset

caveat: Removes the cheapest and most commonly chosen remediation from the table. A reset that appears to succeed, followed by the appliance being returned to service, is worse than no action because it converts an open question into a false assurance. Continued monitoring of a reset appliance is the minimum, replacement the safe answer.

name: Controller logic replaced with a program that does nothing
description: Actors erased the original control program on internet-facing controllers and downloaded their own containing no inputs and no outputs. The device continues running while controlling nothing, which is a denial of control achieved without any exploit.
logic: A program download to a controller, joined against whether a change was authorised. The strongest confirming signal is not on the network at all: process values and outputs going static while the device still reports healthy. Compare the running program's input and output counts against the project file.
caveat: A controller running an empty program looks alive to anything that only checks reachability or heartbeat. Detection has to include process telemetry, because the device's own health reporting is unaffected by having nothing to do.

name: Controller reached by something other than its engineering station
description: Controllers have a small, effectively fixed set of legitimate peers. The peer list alone is enough to decide whether an access is expected.
logic: Connections to controller management, file transfer or web services from a source that is not the engineering station that owns that controller.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<controllers>) and xdm.target.port in (80, 443, 21, 22, 23, 502, 44818) | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<engineering_stations>)
caveat: Commissioning, firmware upgrades and vendor support produce legitimate access from unusual sources. Expect a burst during any outage.

name: A port forwarder running where nothing should be forwarding
description: A publicly available packet relay tool was used for command and control obfuscation and exfiltration, forwarding traffic through a compromised host so that connections appear to originate inside the network.
logic: Two surfaces. The named relay and tunnelling binaries by image name, which dates quickly. And the durable shape: a host that both accepts an inbound session and originates an outbound one of similar volume, acting as a relay when its role is not to route.
caveat: The behavioural half matters more than the names, because the tools are trivially renamed and recompiled. A server relaying traffic is categorically different from a server serving it, and that distinction survives any change of tool.

name: Remote access software that never installs
description: Actors used portable executables of legitimate remote management software, which establish local user access without administrative privilege and without a full installation, bypassing common software controls and the risk management assumptions built on them.
logic: Because nothing is installed, inventory-based and installation-based controls see nothing. Detection has to be process execution and network destination: the vendor's binaries running from a user-writable path with no corresponding installation record, and outbound sessions to that vendor's relay infrastructure from hosts where the product is not licensed.
caveat: The specific insight worth keeping is that portable execution defeats software allow-listing and installation monitoring at the same time, and needs no administrative privilege, so the usual assumption that unapproved software requires elevation does not hold. Blocking by reputation also fails because the software is genuine.

name: Enumerate every authentication surface exposed
description: Reconnaissance concentrated on finding exposed login portals. Doing that enumeration first, from the inside, is the cheapest defensive move available, and the forgotten contractor and vendor portals are usually the ones that matter.
logic: List every externally reachable service that accepts credentials, including ones no current team remembers owning.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true and accepts_authentication = true | comp count() by owner, service
caveat: Not a detection. It defines the surface every other detection has to cover.

name: Verify keys and credentials were rotated after an appliance compromise
description: A compromised remote access appliance yields both the credentials that authenticated through it and the key material it holds. Patching closes the door while leaving the attacker holding the keys. The most commonly skipped recovery step.
logic: Confirm that key and certificate generation dates postdate the patch and the suspected compromise window, and that every account which authenticated through the appliance during that window has had its credential changed.
xql_sketch: dataset = <certificate_inventory> | filter device in (<compromised_appliances>) and certificate_not_before < patch_applied_date
caveat: Not a detection. Skipping it means the intrusion resumes through legitimate authentication that no detection will question.

name: Script engine invoked with abbreviated or obfuscated syntax
description: Abbreviated switches are more suspicious than full spellings, because administrators spell them out and tooling abbreviates. Mangled casing and caret separation exploit the interpreter ignoring both, which a person has no reason to do.
logic: Command lines carrying abbreviated profile, execution policy, encoded command or hidden window switches, or an executable name written with mixed case or separator characters.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)-(nop|noprofile|ep|exec[a-z]*|enc|encodedcommand|w hidden)\b" or xdm.target.process.name ~= "(?i)p\^?o\^?w\^?e\^?r\^?s\^?h\^?e\^?l\^?l"
caveat: Deployment and automation scripts use the same switches. Excluding known automation paths and service accounts is what makes it usable.

name: Access held with no apparent objective
description: Agencies assessed a campaign against pipeline operators as specifically intended to hold that infrastructure at risk and to help develop capability to physically damage or disrupt operations, rather than to collect information. Of twenty-three targeted operators, thirteen were confirmed compromised.
logic: Changes what an intrusion with no observed theft means. Where an actor reaches control-adjacent systems, maps the process and holds access without exfiltrating anything of commercial value, the absence of an objective is the finding rather than a reason to downgrade the incident. Look specifically for collection of engineering documentation, network diagrams and process detail.
caveat: The instinct on finding an intrusion with nothing taken is relief. Where the target is critical infrastructure the correct reading is the opposite, and this advisory says so explicitly: the purpose was to hold the infrastructure at risk and to develop capability for later physical effect.

name: Print service loading a driver or spawning a child
description: The print subsystem flaw allows loading a driver from a remote location with system privilege. The service has no ordinary reason to spawn a child process.
logic: The spooler service process writing or loading a library outside its own driver directories, or creating any child process.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.source.process.name = "spoolsv.exe" and (xdm.event.type = "process" or xdm.target.file.extension = "dll")
caveat: Legitimate driver installation touches these paths. The stronger control is disabling the print service where unneeded, which on servers is usually everywhere.

name: Privileged directory account used off its tier
description: A high-privilege domain account authenticating to a host outside the administrative tier, leaving reusable credential material where it can be captured. Corresponds to "improper separation of user and administrator privilege", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: Authentication where the account belongs to a high-privilege directory group and the destination is neither a domain controller nor a designated privileged access workstation.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "authentication" and arrayindex(xdm.source.user.groups, 0) contains "Admins" | filter xdm.target.host.hostname not in (<domain_controllers>, <privileged_workstations>)
caveat: Only meaningful where tiering is actually implemented. In a flat domain this fires endlessly and is really a finding about the design.

markers.note: tier-0 account authenticating to a tier-2 asset

name: Safety-relevant setpoint altered, or set outside its safe range
description: One of the few industrial detections that reads directly on consequence rather than technique. In a water treatment context it is the difference between an operational nuisance and a public health event.
logic: Alert on any change to a curated list of safety and quality relevant setpoints, and escalate where the new value falls outside the documented safe operating range. Pair with who made the change and from where.
xql_sketch: dataset = <process_dataset> | filter setpoint_tag in (<safety_relevant_tags>) | join (dataset = <safe_range_table>) as r r.tag = setpoint_tag | filter setpoint_new_value > r.max or setpoint_new_value < r.min
caveat: Requires process engineers to supply both the tag list and the safe ranges; a security team cannot derive either. Legitimate operational changes happen.

name: Traffic whose protocol does not match its port
description: The absence of an application layer firewall able to detect this was called out explicitly in a red team assessment. Catches tunnelling that a port-based rule set permits by definition.
logic: Sessions on well-known ports where the independently identified application protocol is not the expected one.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (80, 443, 53, 22) and detected_protocol != expected_protocol_for_port
caveat: Requires a sensor identifying protocol independently of port, which is the capability the assessment found missing. Where the firewall is port-based only this cannot be written, and that is the finding.

name: Provider accounts with a second factor, and someone watching the failures
description: Seven national authorities put three actions above all others for managed service providers and their customers: disable accounts no longer in use, enforce strong authentication on provider accounts that reach the customer environment and monitor for unexplained failed authentication, and make contractual ownership of security responsibilities explicit.
logic: Three checks with definite answers. Enumerate provider accounts in your directory and confirm each is in use, carries a second factor, and is scoped to what that provider actually needs. Then confirm somebody receives and acts on failed authentication events for those accounts, since an unexplained failure on a provider account is a stronger signal than on an ordinary one.
caveat: Provider accounts are the hardest population to govern because they are created for someone else's staff, often shared, and frequently exempted from expiry so that support is not interrupted. The advisory's emphasis on unexplained failures matters because these accounts have no user to ask.

name: What your service provider can reach, and would you notice
description: Provider accounts are usually highly privileged, permanently enabled and excluded from the conditional access rules applied to staff, making them the least monitored privileged accounts in most estates.
logic: Baseline provider access by source, hour and target, then alert on deviation. Separately confirm whether a second factor is enforced on provider accounts, which is commonly not the case even where it is enforced for staff.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter account_type = "provider" | comp count() by xdm.source.user.username, xdm.source.ipv4, mfa_used | filter mfa_used = false or xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<provider_declared_ranges>)
caveat: Tightening provider access is a contractual conversation as much as a technical one. The achievable first step is usually monitoring rather than restriction.

name: Written agreement on who owns which control
description: The authorities recommend that provider and customer contracts transparently identify ownership of security roles and responsibilities, and that customers verify the contractual arrangements include measures matching their own requirements.
logic: For each control the customer assumes is in place, name the party responsible, the evidence they provide and how often it is reviewed. Logging, patching, backup verification and incident notification are the ones most often assumed by both parties and performed by neither.
caveat: The only pattern here whose remedy is a contract rather than a configuration, which is why it gets skipped. It surfaces during an incident as a dispute about who was supposed to be looking, at the worst possible moment. Providers require trusted network connectivity and privileged access in both directions, so the gap is not theoretical.

name: A communications provider whose compromise reaches your equipment
description: Agencies warned that successful intrusions into satellite communications networks could create risk in the providers' customer environments, and recommended additional monitoring at the ingress and egress points to that equipment on both sides.
logic: Treat the provider's equipment on your premises as an untrusted boundary rather than as part of your network. Monitor traffic at the ingress and egress points to it, know what should traverse it, and hold an independent record of its configuration, because the provider's compromise arrives as legitimate traffic from trusted equipment.
caveat: Where the link serves remote or offshore operations there is often no alternative path, which turns a provider compromise into a loss of visibility over sites nobody can reach another way. The continuity question is therefore as important as the monitoring one.

name: The intelligence stage costs the attacker nothing
description: Control system devices and designs are publicly available, incorporate known information technology components, and are documented in vendor manuals and standards. The intelligence collection stage of an intrusion can therefore be completed without touching the target.
logic: Turn it around and perform the same collection against yourself: what do public sources, vendor documentation, procurement records, planning applications, conference talks and staff profiles reveal about your equipment, and what does an internet scan index show. Anything found that is not on your inventory is the finding.
caveat: Unusual among these patterns in being entirely performable from outside, at no cost, with an unambiguous result. It also explains why obscurity fails as a control here: the design information the attacker needs is published by the vendor, and increasingly by the operator through procurement and planning records.

name: A toolkit that lets a less skilled operator attack a controller
description: Four agencies described custom modular tooling for scanning, compromising and controlling specific controller families, with a virtual console whose command interface mirrors that of the targeted device. The advisory states directly that the modules enable lower-skilled actors to emulate higher-skilled capabilities.
logic: The tooling speaks the devices' normal management and industrial protocols, so nothing malformed appears on the wire. Detection has to key on who is speaking them: engineering protocol traffic and vendor discovery scans originating from anything other than the designated engineering workstations, and configuration or program operations with no authorising change record.
caveat: The strategic point outlives the specific device list. Purpose-built tooling with a familiar console lowers the skill floor for attacking control systems, which breaks the long-standing assumption that operational technology attacks require rare expertise and therefore rare adversaries. It also means the population capable of executing them grows independently of the population capable of building them.

name: Repeated authentication prompts until one is accepted
description: A burst of denied or expired prompts for one account followed by an approval. No genuine login produces that shape.
logic: Count denied, timed-out and expired prompts per account in a short window, then look for a subsequent approval.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_audit_dataset> | comp count(if(mfa_result in ("denied", "timeout"), 1, null)) as denials, count(if(mfa_result = "approved", 1, null)) as approvals by xdm.source.user.username, bin(_time, 30m) | filter denials > 3 and approvals > 0
caveat: A misconfigured device generates repeated denials legitimately, but not followed by an approval from a different source. The approval after the burst is the discriminator. Number matching and rate limiting remove the technique outright.

name: Where the money goes changes the payment decision
description: The authoring agencies assess that revenue from these ransomware and cryptocurrency operations supports state-level priorities, including cyber operations against the very governments and defence industrial base organisations being targeted.
logic: A governance input, not a query. It belongs in the ransom decision framework alongside recovery capability and data exposure: the possibility that the recipient is a sanctioned state actor whose proceeds fund operations against the payer's own sector.
caveat: Worth deciding before an incident rather than during one, because under pressure the note's claimed identity is the only information available and it is deliberately misleading. Payment also does not guarantee recovery, which the authoring agencies state directly.

name: Security settings skipped because the rollout was urgent
description: An agency observed organisations migrating to cloud collaboration services at speed to support home working, and not fully considering the security configuration of those platforms, with hasty deployment leading to oversights that undermine the platform's own security model.
logic: A configuration review triggered by the deployment rather than by an incident. The highest-value single item named is a second factor on the tenant administrator accounts, since those hold privileges equivalent to a domain administrator on premises. Review every platform deployed under time pressure against its own security baseline, and record when that review last happened.
caveat: The configuration debt is invisible because nothing fails: the platform works exactly as intended while its protections sit unconfigured. It is only discovered during an incident or a deliberate review, which is why the review has to be scheduled rather than triggered.

name: Prioritise patching by which actors adopt disclosures fast
description: Some actors have a track record of taking newly published vulnerabilities into operations within days, ahead of any public proof of concept. Patch priority should reflect that, not severity score alone. Corresponds to "poor patch management", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: Cross-reference externally reachable assets against disclosures affecting them, weighted by whether an actor known to target the sector has previously weaponised disclosures quickly.
xql_sketch: dataset = <vuln_dataset> | filter external_reachable = true | join (dataset = <actor_sector_targeting>) as a a.sector = org_sector | sort desc a.fast_adoption_history
caveat: Prioritisation guidance, not a query. The value is the reasoning about which disclosures are urgent, not any specific identifier.

name: Survey commands called by a binary nobody recognises
description: Any one of the built-in survey commands is ordinary. Being called in sequence by a previously unseen binary is not.
logic: Built-in enumeration commands whose parent process has no prior execution history on that host.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in ("ipconfig.exe", "tasklist.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "net.exe", "whoami.exe") | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.process.name) as commands by xdm.source.process.name, xdm.target.host.hostname, bin(_time, 5m) | filter commands > 2
caveat: Administrative scripting produces the same sequences. Requiring a previously unseen parent keeps the volume down.

name: A supply chain attack through software only your sector uses
description: Actors trojanised an open-source messenger used specifically by staff at small and medium hospitals in one country, distributing it from two lookalike domains. Software with a narrow regional or sector user base sits outside the coverage of global reputation and detection products.
logic: Inventory the software that is specific to your sector or region, then treat its distribution points as named dependencies to monitor: which domains it updates from, whether those are pinned, and whether anything in the estate has fetched it from anywhere else.
caveat: The strategic point outlives these indicators. Niche sector software is often unmanaged, installed by staff, absent from the asset inventory, and unknown to every commercial detection product, which makes it a cheaper route in than the software everyone watches.

name: Startup entry pointing outside the program directories
description: The test is not that a startup entry was created but that it references a user or shared application data location, which legitimate software rarely does.
logic: Run key creation or modification where the value data points outside the Windows and Program Files directories.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter registry_key_path ~= "(?i)\\CurrentVersion\\Run" and registry_value_data ~= "(?i)\\(Users|ProgramData|AppData|Temp)\\"
caveat: Per-user installs and updaters legitimately do this. The exclusion list stays short enough to maintain.

name: Command traffic relayed through residential and small business connections
description: Relays chosen in the victim's own region on consumer connections, so geographic and reputational checks pass and the traffic resembles a member of staff working from home. Country blocking is useless against it by design.
logic: Behavioural rather than reputational. An administrative or remote access session from a residential range the account has never used, and especially several accounts arriving from one unfamiliar residential range.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | join (dataset = <asn_lookup>) as a a.ip = xdm.source.ipv4 | filter a.owner_type in ("residential", "small_business") | comp count_distinct(xdm.source.user.username) as accounts by a.range | filter accounts > 1
caveat: Remote working makes residential sources normal, which is why the technique works. An argument for per-account source baselining, not for a blocklist.

name: Remote access tool installed with the user's cooperation
description: Employees talked into running commercial remote access software. Nothing malicious is involved, which defeats controls framed around blocking malicious software.
logic: Any remote access product outside the approved list appearing on a host, weighted up where the user has no history of installing software.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in (<remote_access_tool_list>) and xdm.target.process.name not in (<approved_tools>)
caveat: Requires a single approved remote access product to exist as a standard. Where several are in use across an estate this cannot be written, and the gap is organisational rather than technical.

name: Remote access paths with no second factor enforced
description: The stated common factor in a two-year ransomware campaign was remote access without multi-factor authentication, not a novel technique. Partial enforcement is the usual finding. Corresponds to "weak or misconfigured multi-factor authentication", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: For every remote access path, confirm a second factor is enforced for every account including service and legacy accounts, not just for interactive users.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "authentication" and xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS" | comp count() by xdm.source.user.username, mfa_used | filter mfa_used = false
caveat: Check per account, not per gateway. A second factor on interactive users but not on service accounts or a legacy authentication path is the common gap.

name: Everything encrypted from one machine, without touching the rest
description: A variant used embedded stolen credentials with directory and file sharing protocols to discover every host, enumerate their shares, and then encrypt all discovered share contents remotely from the originally compromised host, including the administrative and domain policy shares.
logic: No malware runs on the encrypted hosts, so endpoint telemetry on them shows nothing but ordinary inbound file operations. The signal is entirely on the source: one host enumerating shares across the estate and then writing to a very large number of files across many hosts over file sharing in a short window.

markers.expr: count_distinct(target_host) by source_host with share_enumeration, bin(_time, 10m)

caveat: Defeats the usual assumption that ransomware is detected on the machines it encrypts. If detection depends on an agent seeing an encryption process locally, this passes entirely, and the domain policy shares being in scope means the directory's own content is encrypted along with everything else.

name: Service or scheduled task created by a remote or scripted parent
description: Built-in service control, task scheduling and registry utilities driven by a scripting engine or a remote execution service rather than by an interactive administrator. The utilities are ordinary; the parentage is not.
logic: Child process is a service, task or registry utility and the parent is a scripting engine, remote management host or remote execution service.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process" and xdm.target.process.name in ("sc.exe", "schtasks.exe", "reg.exe", "at.exe") and xdm.source.process.name in ("powershell.exe", "wmic.exe", "wsmprovhost.exe", "psexesvc.exe", "cmd.exe")
caveat: Software deployment, patching and configuration management do this constantly and at far greater volume than any intruder. Know the maintenance windows and the service accounts first.

name: Which product classes appear on the exploited list every year
description: Reading several annual lists together shows remote access appliances, file transfer products, collaboration platforms and directory services recurring. That is a procurement and architecture signal, not only a patching one.
logic: Count how many separate annual lists each product class appears on. Where a class recurs every year, ask whether it needs to be internet-facing at all rather than only whether it is patched.
xql_sketch: dataset = <annual_exploited_lists> | comp count_distinct(year) as years_appeared by product_class | sort desc years_appeared
caveat: An analytic exercise whose conclusions belong to whoever owns architecture decisions rather than to security operations.

name: Run more than once, so one key is not enough
description: Actors were observed executing their ransomware multiple times within a single victim network, producing different identifiers and file extensions for each run, with the result that the victim required several unique decryption keys rather than one.
logic: During response, count the distinct ransom identifiers and file extensions present across the estate rather than assuming one event. More than one means more than one key is required, which changes both the recovery plan and any payment calculation.
caveat: Directly affects the payment question, since paying once may decrypt only part of the estate. It also means a recovery declared complete after restoring one identifier's files can leave whole systems still encrypted under another.

name: The emergency plan that never considered this
description: At a gas compression facility hit by commodity ransomware, the victim's emergency response plan did not specifically consider cyberattacks, and the operator chose a deliberate controlled shutdown lasting about two days even though control of the process was never lost.
logic: A preparedness question with a decision attached. Establish in advance, for each degraded state, whether operations continue: loss of view with control retained, loss of view and control, and loss of the business network only. Without that, the safe default under pressure is to shut down, and the outage becomes a decision rather than a consequence.
caveat: The most consequential detail here is that the shutdown was a choice, not a technical necessity: the controllers were untouched and control was never lost. Deciding that question in advance, with engineering and safety input, is what separates a two-day outage from a monitored degraded run.

name: Collect the evidence before you touch anything
description: Five national authorities set the order explicitly: first collect and remove artefacts, logs and data for analysis; then apply mitigations chosen so as not to tip off the adversary that their presence has been discovered; then consider third-party response support to ensure eradication and avoid follow-up compromise after closure.
logic: A sequencing control rather than a query. The common failure is remediating first, which destroys the evidence needed to scope and warns the adversary to change or accelerate. Establish before an incident who authorises containment, what must be preserved first, and how the response is coordinated so the adversary cannot read it.
caveat: Pairs directly with the record here where the adversary targeted the mailboxes of incident response staff. Both point the same way: the response has to assume it is being observed, and that has to be arranged before it is needed rather than decided under pressure.

name: A host that should have no internet path successfully reaching out
description: Proxy use from hosts intended to be restricted from internet access appeared in the published missed-opportunity list.
logic: Any successful outbound session, including via a proxy, from the population declared as having no internet access.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.source.ipv4 in (<isolated_hosts>) and xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS"
caveat: Depends on someone maintaining the list of isolated hosts. That list's absence is a more common finding than its violation.

name: Sweep retained data whenever a new indicator arrives
description: A federal network compromise was found by re-examining retained network data with a newly obtained indicator, not by an alert firing at the time.
logic: Maintain a process for sweeping historical data against newly published indicators, and retention long enough for that sweep to reach the likely start of an intrusion.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<new_indicator_list>) | comp min(_time) as first_contact by xdm.source.host.hostname
caveat: Depends entirely on retention. Ninety days of flow data cannot answer a question about an intrusion that began earlier, which is the constraint most estates hit.

name: Malicious changes inside a shared controller code module
description: Agencies published guidance on detecting malicious changes in reusable code modules used within controller programs, alongside disruption caused by malicious project file interactions across several controller manufacturers.
logic: A reusable module is included in many programs, so one alteration propagates wherever it is used and a review of the top-level program will not show it. Compare the running program including its subroutines and modules against the authoritative project file held offline, rather than comparing only version numbers or timestamps.
caveat: The propagation property is what makes this different from a single program change: one tampered module can affect every controller that includes it, and the change is invisible from the top-level logic. It also means the authoritative project file has to exist offline and be trusted, which on older estates frequently is not the case.

name: Judge a hunt by the findings, not by whether an adversary was there
description: A hunt that found no actor still produced remediation work by auditing the environment against a real technique list. Judging hunt value by whether something was found pushes hunting toward chasing noise.
logic: Record risks identified independently of whether any actor was present, and treat those as the deliverable.
xql_sketch: not applicable; an evaluation criterion for hunting programmes
caveat: An argument about how to evaluate hunting rather than a detection.

name: Unsigned firmware plus a modified bootloader to survive reboot
description: Actors modified running firmware in memory to permit installation of unsigned modified firmware carrying a secure shell backdoor, and in some cases a modified bootloader so the firmware survives reboot and continues evading the device's own security features.
logic: The backdoor gives unlogged interaction, so the device's authentication log will not show the sessions. What remains is transfer of firmware images to the device by file transfer or secure shell, reboots outside a change window, and secure shell sessions to the device observed by adjacent equipment but absent from the device's own log.
caveat: The mismatch between what adjacent equipment sees and what the device reports is the only reliable signal, because the backdoor is designed to leave no local trace. Note that unsigned firmware installing at all means the device's image verification was bypassed, so verification success afterwards proves nothing.

name: Encoded command executed from the Run dialog
description: A fake human verification prompt told users to open the Run dialog and paste clipboard contents the page had already filled with an encoded scripting command. The user executes the payload themselves; no exploit is involved.
logic: Two complementary checks: a scripting engine invoked with a long encoded payload and the shell as its parent, and the per-user Run dialog history key containing entries that look like script commands rather than program names.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.source.process.name = "explorer.exe" and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)-(enc|encodedcommand|e)\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{40,}"
caveat: Administrators occasionally paste commands into the Run dialog, so a small per-account exception list may be needed. The technique defeats awareness training framed around attachments and links, because the user is doing neither.

name: Host reconfigured to boot into Safe Mode
description: A ransomware variant rebooted into Safe Mode before encrypting, because endpoint protection does not run there. The reconfiguration happens before the damage, which makes it one of very few ransomware detections that fires pre-encryption.
logic: Boot configuration tool execution with Safe Mode arguments, and service startup entries being added to the Safe Mode start set so the payload runs while security agents do not.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in ("bcdedit.exe", "bootcfg.exe") and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)safeboot"
caveat: Disproportionately valuable because it fires before damage, and legitimate use is near zero outside recovery work. The hard constraint is that once the reboot happens the agent is gone, so it must be actioned in minutes.

name: Safety controller left in a programmable key position
description: Payload delivery was only possible while the controller key was in program mode. Once installed the implant worked regardless, so this detects the window of opportunity rather than the compromise.
logic: Controller key position reported as anything other than run, cross-referenced with whether engineering work is scheduled.
xql_sketch: dataset = <ics_dataset> | filter controller_keyswitch_position != "RUN" | comp min(_time) as since by xdm.target.host.hostname, controller_keyswitch_position
caveat: Engineers legitimately switch to program mode to work. The finding is a controller left that way when nobody is working on it, so it needs the maintenance schedule to be useful.

name: Logic download to a safety controller with status polling
description: Delivery of a payload to a safety controller involved uploading a program, polling a status value in a wait loop to watch the installation, then overwriting the program with a harmless one. The upload, poll, overwrite sequence is distinctive without decoding the payload.
logic: A program download to a controller followed by repeated status reads from the same source within a short window, then a second download.
xql_sketch: dataset = <ics_dataset> | filter xdm.target.ipv4 in (<safety_controllers>) | comp values(ics_function) as funcs, count() as ops by xdm.source.ipv4, xdm.target.ipv4, bin(_time, 10m) | filter array_length(funcs) > 1
caveat: Needs a sensor that parses the proprietary protocol. Flow records show the session but not the function.

markers.note: safety and control protocol ports; the proprietary safety protocol port varies by platform

markers.expr: program_download to safety_controller followed_by repeated status_read from same source within 10m

name: One source touching many hosts in minutes
description: Reconnaissance and credential replay both show as breadth in a short window. Suggested starting thresholds were three attempts to one device, or one source reaching more than two devices, inside five minutes.
logic: Count distinct destinations per source and attempts per destination in five-minute bins.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.ipv4) as hosts, count() as attempts by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 5m) | filter hosts > 2 or attempts > 3
caveat: Those thresholds are deliberately low and need raising in most estates. Monitoring, backup and inventory systems breach them constantly.

name: Something taking pictures of the screen
description: External rules cover the platform's own problem-recorder utility being run, the operating system screen capture binary on other platforms, and policy keys governing screen content analysis.
logic: The built-in capture and recorder utilities executing at all, particularly with output paths and silent switches. On an operator station or a workstation handling sensitive material the legitimate rate is near zero, which makes this alertable there without tuning.
caveat: Most valuable on operator interfaces and on hosts handling regulated data, where a screenshot is the exfiltration. On general user endpoints the legitimate rate is high enough that this belongs in hunting rather than alerting.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Script execution that never launches the scripting binary
description: The actor ran scripts and fetched executables into memory through the HTML application host rather than through the script interpreter's own executable, which means monitoring keyed on that executable's process name sees nothing.
logic: Watch the proxy binaries rather than the interpreter: the HTML application host and the library loaders, especially with a remote address on the command line. Script block logging captures the script content regardless of which process hosts the engine, which is the durable answer.
caveat: Any control that assumes the interpreter's own executable must run is blind here, which includes a large proportion of shipped script-execution rules. Enabling script block logging is the fix and it is off by default.

name: Automated login to many network devices to capture configuration
description: A campaign used valid stolen credentials with scripts to log into Cisco and Juniper routers over secure shell, run commands, capture the running configuration and send it off network. No authentication failure appears anywhere, because the credentials were valid.
logic: The shape rather than the credential: many devices reached from one source in a short window, short non-interactive sessions, similar command sequences, followed by an outbound transfer. Cover the configuration retrieval command forms for each vendor present.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_device_dataset> | filter device_command ~= "(?i)(show configuration|show running-config)" | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.host.hostname) as devices by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 30m) | filter devices > 3
caveat: Configuration backup systems do exactly this on a schedule and will dominate results; enumerate them by source and account first. Requires devices to forward command accounting centrally, which many do not. Patching does not prevent this, since valid credentials were used.

name: Vulnerability classes an operator cannot fix
description: Three national authorities addressed an access control flaw class to vendors, designers and developers before defenders, because the remedy is a development practice: check authorisation on every request, and replace direct object identifiers in addresses with unguessable random values.
logic: Turn the developer guidance into questions asked before purchase and at assurance review: does the application expose sequential object identifiers in addresses, and does it check authorisation per request for every object holding sensitive data. Both are observable from outside the application without source access.
caveat: The honest position is that detection buys time and does not fix anything here. Where the application is bought rather than built, the leverage is entirely at procurement and contract renewal, which is a different function from the one that runs the monitoring.

name: Security and monitoring products as high-value targets
description: A monitoring or audit product holds broad read access and broad network reach, so exploiting one yields visibility and position that would otherwise take considerable lateral movement.
logic: Check exposure and patch currency of security and monitoring products, and alert where their service process creates child processes or reaches destinations outside its documented set.
xql_sketch: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter asset_role = "security_tooling" | comp count() by product, patch_status, external_reachable
caveat: These products legitimately run scripts and reach widely, which makes behavioural detection on them harder than on ordinary applications. Exposure and patch currency are the more reliable controls.

markers.expr: product_class in (security.edr, security.siem, app.rmm, security.backup) and internet_reachable

name: A process that deletes its own file moments after running
description: The loader removed its own executable using a short sleep followed by a delete, issued through the command shell and through the script interpreter. Nothing legitimate installs itself and then erases the installer from a running process.
logic: The sleep-then-delete command shape, where the deletion target is the parent process image. The delay exists so the parent has exited before the file goes, which is what makes the command line distinctive rather than the deletion itself.
caveat: Some installers clean up temporary files this way, but they do not usually delete the image of the process that is still running. Anchoring on the deletion target matching the parent image removes most of the noise.

name: Bulk reading of internal documentation spaces
description: Collaboration platforms are where network diagrams, runbooks and credentials accumulate, and that material has been named explicitly as a target. Which spaces were read matters more than how many pages.
logic: Page or attachment access volume per account against that account's own baseline, weighted heavily where the spaces hold operational or network documentation.
xql_sketch: dataset = <collab_audit_dataset> | comp count() as pages, count_distinct(space) as spaces by xdm.source.user.username, bin(_time, 1h) | join (dataset = <sensitive_spaces>) as s ... | filter pages > <baseline>
caveat: Research and onboarding produce legitimate bulk reading. Tag the sensitive spaces first or this is undifferentiated noise.

name: Privileged accounts that no second factor can protect
