description: Actors used brute force and password spraying against service accounts, which run applications and services, have no human behind them so cannot easily be protected by a second factor, and are frequently highly privileged depending on what they manage.
logic: Because a second factor is not available, the compensating controls are restriction and observation: conditional access limiting where the account may authenticate from, credential rotation with a known age, privilege scoped to the service's actual need, and alerting on authentication from anywhere the service does not run.
caveat: The population where the standard advice does not apply, which is why it persists. These accounts are also the ones most likely to be over-privileged, because privilege was granted once at deployment to make something work and never revisited.

name: A service named one token away from a real one
description: The implant registered a service assessed as chosen to blend in with a genuine Windows service whose name differs by a few characters, and hid its executable among the many legitimate copies of the same filename in the side-by-side component store.
logic: Compare installed service names and their binary paths against the known-good set for the platform build. Two separate checks: a service name that is close to but not identical to a real one, and a binary whose filename is legitimate but whose path is not one the vendor ships it in.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation = "service_install" | filter service_name not in (<known_good_services>) and edit_distance(service_name, nearest_known_good) <= 3
caveat: Reading a service list by eye will not catch a name three characters off a real one, which is the point of choosing it. This has to be a set comparison against a known-good list, not a human review.

markers.note: forms observed in the analysis reports; the local known-good list is what matters

markers.expr: service_binary_name legitimate but image_path not vendor_shipped_path

name: Service permissions loosened so anyone can change it
description: External rules cover service permissions being altered to hide a service from enumeration or to allow an unprivileged user to modify it, and registry permissions on service keys being weakened.
logic: Service control commands that set a security descriptor, and permission changes on service registry keys. Setting a descriptor that denies enumeration is the distinctive case, because it hides the service from the tools an administrator would use to look.
caveat: The hiding case matters most: a service configured to deny enumeration will not appear in the service list, so an administrator reviewing the host sees nothing. That places it with the other records here where the system's own reporting cannot be trusted.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Credentials attached to an existing application identity
description: The actor added tokens and certificates to existing cloud application service principals, giving persistence and a programmatic route to tenant resources. The advisory notes this generates little evidence or telemetry, and that activity then appears to come from the individual whose access is normal.
logic: Credential addition to an application or service principal, keyed on the operation rather than on subsequent use, because subsequent use is designed to look normal. Alert on any addition and reconcile against the change record; the legitimate rate is low and the operation is administrative.
xql_sketch: dataset = <cloud_audit_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation ~= "(?i)(add|update).*(service ?principal|application).*(credential|certificate|secret|key)"
caveat: Chosen precisely because it produces little telemetry, and because on some licensing tiers the individual access it imitates is not logged at all. That licensing dependency means the same attack is detectable in one tenant and invisible in another with identical configuration, which is worth establishing before relying on this.

name: Authenticated session with no authentication event
description: Replaying a stolen session cookie authenticates as the user without the password or the second factor, so every detection built around login behaviour misses it entirely including MFA enforcement.
logic: Consistency within a session rather than at its start: the same session identifier seen from a different address, network or device fingerprint than it was issued to, and sessions living beyond the configured lifetime.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_audit_dataset> | comp count_distinct(xdm.source.ipv4) as sources, count_distinct(device_fingerprint) as devices by session_id | filter sources > 1 or devices > 1
caveat: Requires the identity platform to log session identifiers and their issuing properties, which not all do at commonly purchased tiers. Token binding and short session lifetimes are the better answer than detection.

name: Recovery points destroyed before encryption
description: Deletion or resizing of volume shadow copies, driven either by the usual utilities or through the Windows management interface. Happens immediately before encryption, so it is one of the last chances to intervene.
logic: Command lines referencing shadow copy or shadow storage together with a delete or resize verb, from any process not on the backup allow list.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)(shadowcopy|shadowstorage|Win32_ShadowCopy).*(delete|resize)" | filter xdm.target.process.executable.signature.signer not in (<backup_signers>)
caveat: Some backup products manage shadow copies legitimately. Allow-list by signer and command line.

name: Files on a share modified so other people run them
description: Actors tainted shared content, modifying files or shortcuts in locations many users open so that the malware spreads through normal working behaviour rather than through any network technique.
logic: Writes to executable or shortcut content on network shares by an account that does not normally author there, and one account modifying many files across a share in a short window. The spread afterwards is users opening files they are supposed to open, so the write is the only detectable moment.
caveat: Propagation happens through legitimate user behaviour, so no lateral movement detection fires and no exploit is involved. Restricting who can write executable content to shares converts this from a detection into a control, which is the better answer.

name: Shared infrastructure across smaller organisations
description: Smaller public bodies commonly share infrastructure, a managed provider or a state-level service, so one intrusion reaches several organisations and one outage affects a region.
logic: Establish which services are shared and with whom, and what happens to operations if the shared provider is encrypted rather than only if you are.
xql_sketch: not applicable; a dependency register rather than a query
caveat: The sharing is usually a cost decision taken without a security assessment, and unwinding it is not an available option. Knowing the dependency is what is achievable.

name: Third-party disk or memory access driver appearing where it has no role
description: A legitimately signed commercial driver granting raw disk access was carried in so a wiper could write beneath the operating system's protections. The driver is not malicious; its presence is the finding.
logic: Carve binary and driver files from monitored traffic and flag any third-party disk, memory or process access driver crossing into a segment where no host has a matching role.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.extension in ("sys", "dll") | join (dataset = <asset_dataset>) as a a.ip = xdm.target.ipv4 | filter a.role not in ("backup", "forensics", "disk_management")
caveat: The driver is legitimately signed, so signature and reputation checks pass it. Detection rests on where it appears. Enumerate legitimately deployed drivers first.

name: Attacker script run through a platform-signed script host
description: Scripts shipped with the operating system will execute arbitrary script content passed to them, so the executing image is a signed platform file and the attacker's code never appears as a file being run.
logic: The named platform scripts being invoked, and the script hosts running a script from a user-writable location. The remote management script and the drive encryption script are the two most reused, because both accept a script path as an argument.
caveat: Some of these scripts are used legitimately by administrators, particularly the licensing and drive encryption ones. Pair with the script path location, which is the discriminator, and enable script block logging so the content is captured whichever host runs it.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Shipped system utility running where it has no business
description: Certificate and database maintenance utilities have narrow legitimate uses, mostly on servers and mostly by administrators. Attackers use them to download and decode payloads without bringing anything in.
logic: Execution of these utilities on workstation-role hosts, or with a parent that makes no sense such as an office application or scripting engine.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in ("certutil.exe", "esentutl.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "mshta.exe") | join (dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter role = "workstation") as a a.hostname = xdm.target.host.hostname
caveat: Management and deployment tooling calls these legitimately. Baseline by host role: a database server and a receptionist's machine need different thresholds.

name: Text message second factor and carrier account takeover
description: Where a second factor is delivered by text, control of the phone number is control of the account, and the carrier sits outside your security boundary entirely.
logic: Inventory which privileged accounts still use text message delivery, since that is the exposure. As a detection, a successful text-factor authentication from a new device or location shortly after failed attempts.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_audit_dataset> | filter mfa_method = "sms" | join (dataset = <privileged_accounts>) as p p.username = xdm.source.user.username
caveat: Nothing on the carrier side is observable to you. The real content is that text delivery should be removed for privileged accounts rather than monitored.

name: Peer to peer relay over SMB named pipes
description: Implants chained to each other over file-sharing named pipes so only one host holds the external channel. Reduces the number of hosts with outbound traffic to one, which is exactly what egress-based detection looks for.
logic: Named pipe creation or connection where both ends are ordinary workstations, neither being a file server or domain controller. Pipe names change per operator, so match on the host roles rather than the name.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "pipe" | join (dataset = <asset_inventory> | filter role not in ("file_server", "domain_controller")) as inv inv.hostname = xdm.target.host.hostname
caveat: Default pipe names get changed as a matter of course, so any name list decays fast. Workstation-to-workstation file-sharing traffic is the durable half.

name: Network management protocol queries from anything but the monitoring system
description: A four-year-old management protocol flaw was used to deploy malware onto routers. Version 2 of the protocol has no meaningful authentication, so the community string is the whole control.
logic: Which sources send management protocol queries to network devices, and whether any device still answers a default or weak community string.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (161, 162) and xdm.target.ipv4 in (<network_devices>) | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<monitoring_systems>)
caveat: Monitoring platforms poll constantly and dominate results; enumerate them first. Changing a community string means touching the monitoring configuration too, which is why old ones survive.

name: Connections to sites imitating services staff log into
description: Aimed at people rather than systems, and covering personal services as well as corporate ones, since a captured personal account is often the route to a corporate one.
logic: Score requested domains for similarity against a maintained list of logon domains genuinely in use, corporate and common personal alike, weighted by registration age.
xql_sketch: dataset = <dns_dataset> | join (dataset = <known_logon_domains>) as k | alter dist = levenshtein(xdm.network.dns.dns_question.name, k.domain) | filter dist > 0 and dist < 4
caveat: A valid certificate proves nothing; imitation sites obtain them freely. Needs the list of services that matter, including personal ones the organisation does not control.

name: Repeated failed secure shell authentication
description: Stale or wrong captured credentials produce this. Worth watching not because the technique is advanced but because orienting on the source and what followed turns a noise source into a lead.
logic: Count failed secure shell attempts per source, then examine what any subsequent success did rather than the failures themselves.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port = 22 | comp count(if(xdm.event.outcome = "FAILED", 1, null)) as fails, count(if(xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS", 1, null)) as wins by xdm.source.ipv4, bin(_time, 1h) | filter fails > 10 and wins > 0
caveat: Internet-facing secure shell sees constant background brute forcing, and user error looks identical. Only the follow-on activity distinguishes it.

name: Startup shortcut or autostart entry created
description: Standard persistence, worth alerting on rather than logging because the correct standard is strict: every startup item should map to known legitimate activity and anything that does not should be treated as malicious.
logic: Shortcut creation in a user startup folder, or creation and modification of autostart registry entries, compared against a per-build inventory of legitimate startup items.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter (xdm.target.file.extension = "lnk" and xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)\\Startup\\") or registry_key_path ~= "(?i)\\CurrentVersion\\Run" | filter xdm.target.file.name not in (<known_startup_items>)
caveat: Only workable where an inventory of legitimate startup items exists per host build. Without that baseline this is a large undifferentiated list.

name: A state-affiliated group running ransomware
description: Eight national authorities assessed a group affiliated with a state military force as exploiting known vulnerabilities for initial access and then using that access for disk encryption and data extortion to support ransom operations.
logic: Changes the interpretation of a ransomware event rather than its detection. Where the operator is state-affiliated, the encryption may be revenue, cover for collection, or an effect in itself, and the payment carries sanctions exposure. So the ransom decision cannot be taken on the assumption of a commercial counterparty.
caveat: The scoping consequence is the practical one: if encryption may be cover for intelligence collection, restoring from backup and closing the incident leaves the collection objective unexamined. Look for exfiltration and persistence with the same seriousness as recovery, which is not how a commercial extortion event is usually handled.

name: State work performed by a commercial contractor
description: A prosecution established that intelligence officers directed employees of a named commercial front company to conduct network exploitation, resulting in theft of trade secrets, intellectual property and high-value information from companies and multiple foreign governments.
logic: An attribution and motivation caution rather than a query. Where operations run through contractors, tradecraft quality varies between operators on the same programme, tooling is shared with unrelated commercial work, and the objective may serve both a state requirement and the contractor's own interest. None of that is inferable from the artefacts.
caveat: The second contractor-run state programme in this corpus, alongside one whose operator also pursued its own profit. In both cases inferring a single coherent objective from the intrusion was unsafe, and in both the commercial motive coexisted with the state one.

name: Programme data flows down the chain, security resourcing does not
description: Targeting explicitly spanned large and small defence contractors and subcontractors, because the information is shared down the chain while the ability to protect it is not.
logic: Which suppliers hold your programme data or have network access, and what their verified posture is rather than what their contract asserts. For a small supplier, whether being small is being treated as a reason for low likelihood.
xql_sketch: dataset = <supplier_register> | filter holds_programme_data = true | comp count() by supplier, security_verified, access_type
caveat: Verification is contractual and commercial, and small suppliers often genuinely cannot afford what a prime would specify. Recording the disparity is achievable; closing it usually is not.

name: The route in is a subsidiary nobody governs
description: Actors targeted international subsidiaries, then pivoted from trusted internal routers to other subsidiaries and to headquarters, abusing the trusted relationship of small branch routers inside the corporate network and using the public-facing ones as proxy infrastructure.
logic: An inventory and architecture question first: which subsidiary and branch networks have a trusted path to headquarters, who administers those devices, and whether they are in the monitoring scope at all. Then watch for branch-to-core sessions that are not the expected application traffic.
caveat: The advisory's own recommendation is that multinationals review all subsidiary connections and verify access. The governance gap is the vulnerability: branch routers at remote offices are frequently administered locally, excluded from central patching, and trusted by the core anyway. Acquisitions are the common origin of this.

name: A platform utility running under a different name
description: Actors copy or rename a signed platform binary so that detections and reviews keyed on the image name do not match, while the file's own metadata still identifies what it really is.
logic: Compare the running image name against the original filename recorded in the binary's own version resource. A mismatch is close to a pure signal, needs no list of names, and survives any renaming the operator chooses. Also watch for copies of system binaries appearing outside the system directories.
caveat: The original-filename comparison is the durable half and requires process telemetry that records binary metadata, which not every product collects. Without it this falls back to path heuristics, which are far weaker. Some legitimate deployment tooling copies system binaries and needs excluding first.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: The ten misconfigurations assessments most often find
description: Aggregated from red team, blue team, hunt and incident response engagements at large organisations, explicitly including ones with mature security postures. Prevalence rather than novelty is the contribution.
logic: Audit for the ten as published: default configurations, improper privilege separation, insufficient internal network monitoring, lack of network segmentation, poor patch management, bypass of system access controls, weak or misconfigured multi-factor authentication, insufficient access control lists on shares and services, poor credential hygiene, unrestricted code execution. Record present or absent per environment.
xql_sketch: not applicable; an audit checklist that ranks a remediation queue rather than a query
caveat: None of it is new and none of it is a query. Every one of the ten already has detections elsewhere in this corpus; what this adds is the order to fix them in. The advisory also assigns several of them to software vendors rather than operators.

name: The botnet was taken down; your host is still infected
description: Following a coordinated international operation that took over a botnet and severed the connection between victim computers and its command servers, the agencies state directly that the disruption does not mitigate other already-installed malware or ransomware on victim computers.
logic: Treat a public takedown as a hunting trigger rather than a resolution. Search retained telemetry for historical contact with the named infrastructure, then examine those hosts for whatever the loader delivered before the disruption, because the loader's removal says nothing about its payloads.
caveat: A takedown is widely reported as good news and is easily read as the end of the matter. It removes the command channel, not the access that was sold, the credentials that were taken or the ransomware that was staged. The published indicator set is most valuable retrospectively, against data from before the operation.

name: The target is a person, and their work is not behind your controls
description: Collection was aimed at named subject-matter experts, think tanks and journalists rather than at organisations, on foreign policy, nuclear and sanctions topics. The advisory recommends those inside the target profile adopt a heightened posture as individuals.
logic: Not a query but a targeting model that changes where controls have to sit. Identify the individuals in your organisation whose subject expertise makes them targets independent of their employer, and treat their personal accounts, personal devices and public profiles as part of the attack surface, because the actor will.

markers.expr: person in (published_experts, executives, policy_staff, journalists, researchers) and personal_account_used_for_work_correspondence

caveat: Almost nothing an organisation controls covers this, because the approach arrives at a personal mail account, a professional network message or a home device. The practical measures are strong authentication on personal accounts and a route for staff to report an approach without it becoming an incident about them.

name: Template expression syntax inside a request parameter
description: A server-side template injection flaw was exploited by placing a template engine expression in a URL parameter, which the application evaluated. The exploit is visible in the request line itself.
logic: Template delimiters and engine class names appearing in query strings or form fields. Attackers must send the expression in clear to have it evaluated, so unlike most exploitation this is directly greppable in web logs even after the fact.
xql_sketch: dataset = <web_dataset> | filter xdm.network.http.url ~= "(?i)(freemarker|velocity|\\$\\{.*(class|Execute|Runtime|getRuntime).*\\}|%24%7B)"
caveat: URL-encoded forms must be covered as well as literal ones, since the observed exploit arrived encoded. Some applications legitimately carry dollar-brace syntax in parameters, so confirm against your own estate before alerting.

name: Remote desktop session manager log reviewed as a sequence
description: Logon, shell start, logoff, disconnect and reconnect are separate events each carrying the source address. The shell start event confirms an interactive session actually began, which a successful logon alone does not.
logic: Review the full session event sequence rather than only successful logons, joining the source network address to that account's own history of source addresses.
xql_sketch: dataset = <windows_event_dataset> | filter event_id in (21, 22, 23, 24, 25) | join type = left (<account_source_baseline>) as b b.username = xdm.source.user.username | filter b.address = null
caveat: This log is not collected by default in many estates, which is the real obstacle. Where remote desktop is routine for administration the volume is high, so the source-address join does the work.

name: Pressure applied through your staff, partners and customers
description: Actors contacted the victim's employees, business partners and clients with harassing emails and phone calls to increase pressure to pay, and supplied screenshots or file directory listings as proof of theft.
logic: Not a technical detection. It is a communications and preparedness question: whether the incident plan anticipates the attacker contacting your customers and partners directly, who is authorised to respond, and how partners are told what is happening before the attacker tells them.
caveat: Belongs beside the out-of-band victim contact recorded elsewhere in this corpus. The escalation here is that the pressure is applied to people who are not your staff and whom you cannot brief in advance unless the plan already says how.

name: Coverage measured by tool category, not by tool name
description: Five national authorities grouped the publicly available tooling seen in incidents worldwide into five functional categories: remote access trojan, web shell, credential stealer, lateral movement framework, and command and control obfuscator. Names change; the five functions do not.
logic: An audit with five questions rather than a rule. For each category, name the detection you would rely on and the telemetry it needs, then test it. A gap in one category is a gap for every tool in that category, present and future, which is a far more durable statement than a per-tool indicator list.
caveat: The advisory is explicit that its five examples are not exhaustive and should not be treated as a checklist for network defence. The categories are the useful part. It also notes that widespread availability of these tools complicates attribution, so presence of any of them says nothing about who is present.

name: Business outcomes diverging where security telemetry looks healthy
description: Attackers altered card transaction authorisation responses inside a legitimate application. Nothing broke, so security telemetry showed a healthy system and the evidence lived in the business data.
logic: Approval rates diverging from their own baseline, approvals that should have been declined, and geographic or temporal clustering no ordinary customer pattern explains.
xql_sketch: dataset = <transaction_dataset> | comp count() as txns, avg(if(outcome = "approved", 1, 0)) as approval_rate by switch_id, bin(_time, 1h) | filter approval_rate > baseline_rate * 1.2
caveat: Requires the fraud and security functions to share data, which in many organisations they do not. Neither can see this alone.

markers.expr: count(withdrawal_or_authorisation) by account, bin(_time, 1h) against historical_baseline

name: A known administrative tool that is not the real thing
description: Loader malware masqueraded as three separate widely trusted system utilities, carrying embedded packed executables. Analysts and allow-lists both recognise the names, which is what the choice of names buys.
logic: Reputable utilities have stable signatures, sizes and publishers. Alert where a file carrying a known tool name has an unexpected hash, is unsigned, is signed by an unexpected publisher, or runs from a path the real distribution does not use. Do not match on name alone.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name ~= "(?i)(logonsessions|psping|^du\\.exe|pspasswd|psexec|procdump)" | filter xdm.target.process.executable.signer = null or xdm.target.process.executable.signature_status != "signed_verified"
caveat: The trusted-name choice defeats analyst review as much as tooling, since the name looks correct in a process list. Signature state, not the name, is the discriminator.

name: A working application built to take what it manages
description: Actors used social engineering across several communication platforms to encourage individuals to download trojanised applications for the asset class they worked with, built for both major desktop operating systems, then used them to reach the host, spread, and steal the private keys needed to move the assets.
logic: The application works as advertised, which is what earns the install, so the discriminator is provenance and behaviour rather than function. Software installed from a source that is not the vendor's own distribution, and an application of that class making connections or reading key material beyond what its function needs.

markers.expr: application_installed and download_source not in vendor_official_distribution

caveat: Where the target is an individual holding valuable assets rather than an organisation, no corporate control is in the path at all: the approach arrives on a personal messaging platform and the install happens on a personal device. The loss is also irreversible once the transaction settles, which removes recovery as an option.

name: A signed developer tool compiling or running code on a production host
description: Platform-signed build and diagnostic utilities can compile and execute arbitrary code, which passes signature checks and publisher allow-lists. On a host that is not a developer workstation none of them has any business running.
logic: Execution of the named build, compiler and tracing utilities outside a developer or build population. The framework directory path is a strong secondary marker because these tools live there and are rarely invoked by anything but a build system.
caveat: Noisy on developer estates and on build servers, useless there without scoping. Scoped to servers and general user endpoints the legitimate rate is close to zero, and the technique defeats code signing and publisher allow-listing entirely, which is why it is worth the scoping effort.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: Enumerate and watch the links you grant regulators and providers
description: An intrusion at a regulator, authority or service provider compresses the attack chain across every organisation it serves. Those links deserve monitoring proportionate to that reach, not to the counterparty's size.
logic: List every privileged connection and direct network link granted to third parties, record what each can reach, and monitor those specific paths.
xql_sketch: dataset = <third_party_link_inventory> | comp count() by counterparty, link_type, reachable_zone, monitored | filter monitored = false
caveat: The counterparty's security is outside your control and usually outside your visibility. Enumerating and monitoring the link is all that is actually available.

name: API routes reachable with no authentication at all
description: An authentication bypass allowed unauthenticated access to specific API paths on a mobile device management platform, yielding personal data, configuration change, package deployment to enrolled devices, and location data.
logic: Successful responses on API routes where the request carried no session or bearer credential. The web tier records both the route and the absence of an authorisation header, which makes this answerable retrospectively as well as prospectively.
caveat: The absence of an authorisation header is the whole signal, so a web log configuration that does not record headers cannot answer this. Confirm what your access logs retain before relying on it.

name: Any remote access product that is not the approved one
description: These tools are signed, legitimate and often already present, so detection cannot rest on the binary being bad. Decide which one is approved; everything else is unauthorised by definition.
logic: Maintain an allow list of approved remote access products and alert on execution or installation of anything outside it.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name in (<remote_access_tool_list>) | filter xdm.target.process.name not in (<approved_tools>)
caveat: Fails immediately where the organisation has no single approved product, which is common after acquisitions. Establishing that standard is an IT decision and a prerequisite. The product names are now enumerable rather than left to the reader. Commercial remote management tooling appears in every year of an eighteen-quarter response series, named across reports as Syncro, ITarian, AnyDesk, SplashTop, Atera, TeamViewer, LogMeIn, ScreenConnect, QuickAssist, TightVNC, Level and MeshAgent. Treat that as a starting list and not a closed one, because the supply of such products is effectively unlimited and the allow-list remains the control. The second marker is the one that survives a mixed estate: a second remote management product where one is already approved is anomalous even when both are legitimate software.

name: Accounts and computers holding unconstrained delegation
description: Compromising a server configured this way yields the credentials of everything that authenticates to it. The configuration is the exposure.
logic: Enumerate accounts and computers with unconstrained delegation and reduce the set. Each is a controller compromise waiting for one server to fall.
xql_sketch: dataset = <directory_inventory> | filter delegation_type = "unconstrained" | comp count() by object_type, object_name
caveat: Legacy applications sometimes require it. Where it cannot be removed, protect those servers at domain-controller tier rather than as ordinary servers.

name: Chosen because you cannot afford to defend yourself
description: Agencies recorded a sector where organisations with limited security capability and constrained resources are the most vulnerable, and anticipated attacks increasing at a predictable point in that sector's calendar when disruption is most costly.
logic: A prioritisation argument rather than a detection. Where capability is constrained, the honest response is to pick a very small number of controls that break the most common chains, rather than a broad programme that will not be completed. The records in this corpus that fire before damage are the candidates.

markers.expr: minimum_viable_control_set defined and covers(second_factor_on_remote_access, offline_backup_tested, known_exploited_vulnerability_patching)

caveat: Worth stating because most guidance implicitly assumes a resourced security function. Where that assumption fails, a long control catalogue produces nothing, and the agencies' own observation is that the constrained organisations are the ones being hit. Predictable calendar peaks are also plannable, which is unusual.

name: Mailbox access by an application nobody uses
description: An agency identified nation-state access to hosted mailboxes by noticing mail item access events carrying a client and application identifier that did not normally access mail in its environment. The actors had forged authentication tokens using an acquired signing key, impersonating both consumer and enterprise users.
logic: Baseline which application identifiers legitimately access mailboxes in your tenant, then alert on any identifier outside that set. The set is small and stable, and this works even against forged tokens because the token is valid but the application using it is not one of yours.
caveat: The most encouraging detection in this corpus: a customer found a nation-state token forgery before the provider did, using logging and a baseline rather than any indicator. It depends on the mail access event being generated and retained, which on some licensing tiers is not the default, and on somebody having established what normal looks like beforehand.

name: Domain account created outside the joiner process
description: New domain accounts created for persistence, in one observed case an administrative account named to resemble IT staff convention. Account creation is infrequent and already governed by a process, so every one can be reconciled.
logic: Reconcile every domain account creation against the joiner feed. Weight up names resembling administrative or IT function, since that choice is deliberate camouflage.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type = "account_create" | join type = left (dataset = <joiner_feed>) as j j.account = new_account_name | filter j.account = null
caveat: Automated provisioning creates accounts at volume in larger estates. Reconcile against the joiner feed; the name pattern is a weighting, not the test.

name: Workstation listening on a port it should not
description: Malware bound a listening port on an infected desktop and relayed onward, turning an ordinary workstation into a hop point. Workstations should be answering almost nothing.
logic: Listening ports on workstation-role assets compared against the known service baseline for that role.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "listen" | join (dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter role = "workstation") as a a.hostname = xdm.source.host.hostname | filter xdm.source.port not in (<expected_workstation_ports>)
caveat: Remote support tools, collaboration software and development tooling bind ports legitimately. Baseline per host role, not per host.

name: Unsigned or unseen executable running on a control-network host
description: Control-network software inventories change rarely, so previously unseen executables are tractable to spot there in a way they are not on the business side. Corresponds to "unrestricted code execution", one of the ten misconfigurations NSA and CISA reported finding most often across red team, blue team and incident response engagements at large organisations, including ones with mature security postures. Treat that as prioritisation weight: this is empirically common, not theoretical.
logic: Execution on a control-network asset where the binary is unsigned or has no prior execution history, especially from a path that is not a normal install or update location.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.zone = "ot" and xdm.target.process.executable.signature.status = "UNSIGNED" | filter xdm.target.process.executable.path ~= "(?i)(users|temp|programdata)"
caveat: Plenty of legitimate industrial vendor software still ships unsigned, so signing often cannot be enforced. Where it cannot, run this as a detection rather than a control.

name: Incident response plan that has never been exercised
description: An untested plan fails at the points nobody anticipated: who may disconnect a system, where the contact list lives when mail is down, whether anyone can restore from backup.
logic: Exercise the plan, specifically under the assumption that normal tooling and communications are unavailable. Record the date of the last exercise and whether it included loss of primary communications.
xql_sketch: not applicable; a governance record rather than a query
caveat: Not technical work and not completable by a security team alone, since it needs the people with decision authority in the room. That is why it goes untested.

name: Software installed outside the approved inventory
description: Where an attacker builds an entirely fictitious vendor, product and website, provenance checks against a real vendor cannot help and a valid code signature is not evidence of legitimacy. The inverse works: an approved software inventory.
logic: Alert on application installation not present in the approved software inventory, prioritised on hosts with access to financial or operational systems.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "install" | filter installed_application not in (<approved_software>)
caveat: Only works where an approved inventory exists, which is the harder half. It has no purchase at all on personal or unmanaged devices used for work, which is how several of these intrusions began.

name: A vendor discovery scan run by something that is not an engineering station
description: One module runs a rapid scan identifying all controllers of a given vendor on the local network using the vendor's own multicast discovery, which is the same mechanism engineering workstations use legitimately.
logic: The protocol is legitimate and the traffic is well formed, so the only discriminator is the source. Enumerate the hosts entitled to run vendor discovery, which on a control network is a very short list, and alert on discovery traffic from anything else.
caveat: Cheap to build and cheap to maintain because the entitled host list on a control network barely changes. It fires at the reconnaissance stage, which on this kind of intrusion is unusually early relative to the damage.

name: The vendor's own integrity checker reports clean on a compromised appliance
description: Threat actors were determined to be able to deceive an appliance vendor's internal and external integrity checking tools, resulting in a failure to detect compromise. A national authority independently reproduced this in a lab and stated the tool is not sufficient to detect compromise.
logic: A clean result from the vendor tool carries no information, so it cannot be the basis for declaring an appliance uncompromised. Fall back to evidence the appliance does not control: outbound sessions from the appliance's own address, authentication patterns for accounts it holds, and traffic observed by devices adjacent to it.
caveat: Inverts a control most appliance response runbooks depend on. Where the vendor tool is the only integrity evidence available, the honest conclusion after a clean result is unknown rather than clean. Treat stored credentials as compromised regardless of what the tool says, which is what the authoring organisations instruct.

name: Verify industrial software before installing it
description: Industrial software distributions get contaminated, sometimes incidentally rather than deliberately. The controls belong before installation, and on control networks they are realistic because installations are infrequent and planned.
logic: Obtain installers only from the vendor's own portal, never from email, confirm the signature where the vendor signs, and hash-check against a known-good copy.
xql_sketch: dataset = <software_inventory> | filter download_source != "vendor_portal" or signature_valid = false or hash_verified = false
caveat: Many industrial vendors still ship unsigned installers, so a missing signature is not a failure on its own. Hash comparison works regardless.

name: A vulnerability older than some of the staff
description: An advisory published in 2026 names a router vulnerability first identified in 2008, alongside a widely exploited management protocol flaw, as continuing to be used by a state security service against critical infrastructure networks worldwide.
logic: Inventory network devices by software age rather than by patch status alone, since a device may be fully patched against its own end-of-support release and still carry a flaw fixed elsewhere years ago. The oldest unremediated identifier on any internet-reachable device is the number worth knowing.
caveat: Network devices are the one asset class where an eighteen-year-old flaw is still a current advisory item, because they are rarely replaced, rarely inventoried by software version, and their management services are frequently enabled by default and never turned off. Disabling the unused management protocol is usually cheaper than upgrading the device.

name: Your compromise changing hands
description: Agencies recorded ransomware groups sharing victim information, including one group transferring its existing victims to another group's infrastructure after announcing a shutdown, and another beginning to sell access to victim networks for follow-on attacks.
logic: Changes what eviction has to achieve. Scope remediation to every credential and access path the original intrusion could have exposed, not to the observed activity of the group that was found, and expect unrelated tradecraft against the same entry point afterwards.

markers.expr: remediation_scope covers all_access_exposed_by_intrusion rather than observed_actor_activity

caveat: Also explains why attribution is unreliable in this ecosystem, which the agencies state directly: complex networks of developers, affiliates and freelancers make it hard to conclusively identify who was behind an incident. A group announcing a shutdown does not mean its victims are safe; it may mean they have been handed on.

name: Your compromised host relaying traffic for attacks on someone else
description: The implant formed a covert peer-to-peer network across more than fifty countries in which many infected hosts served purely as relay nodes, routing disguised operational traffic to and from implants on the operator's actual targets. Being infected did not mean being the target.
logic: A host both receiving and originating sessions of the same unusual shape, with no local user activity to account for either. Traffic transiting a workstation or server that is not a router is the signal, independent of whether anything on that host was accessed.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | comp count() as inbound, count_distinct(xdm.source.ipv4) as peers by xdm.target.host.hostname | filter peers > 3 and host_role != "router"
caveat: Reframes what a finding means. The advisory notes targeting is purposeful and tactical while infrastructure spans all industries, so an organisation of no intelligence interest can still be carrying traffic for an operation against a government. Scoping the incident to your own data loss would miss the actual role the host was playing, and the legal and disclosure position differs too.

name: Operator interface reachable over remote framebuffer protocol
description: The entire attack path for hacktivist activity against operational technology depends on an operator interface being reachable from outside over VNC, frequently with no password. Enumeration closes the path; detection only observes it.
logic: Enumerate control-network assets answering on remote framebuffer ports and from where. For anything that must stay reachable, alert on every session: the legitimate user population for an operator interface is tiny, named and stable.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.target.port in (5900, 5901, 5902, 5800) and xdm.target.zone = "ot" | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<operator_workstations>)
caveat: Often deployed by an integrator years earlier and forgotten. Removing exposure needs the operations team's agreement on out-of-hours support, so it is an operational conversation and not only a firewall change.

name: Remote access appliance probed straight after a disclosure
description: The interval between a remote access vulnerability being published and it being used in operations was observed as days. The exposed appliance's own logs are the first place it shows.
logic: Requests to the paths a published proof of concept touches, from sources with no prior successful authentication against that appliance.
xql_sketch: dataset = <vpn_dataset> | filter xdm.network.http.url in (<poc_paths>) | comp count() as attempts by xdm.source.ipv4 | filter xdm.source.ipv4 not in (<previously_authenticated_sources>)
caveat: Always noisy after a disclosure; researchers and scanning services arrive with everyone else. What succeeded matters, not what was attempted.

name: Remote access credential that was stolen somewhere else entirely
description: Ransomware actors bought initial access from brokers who harvest remote access credentials out of information stealer logs. The credential is valid, was taken from a device that may not be yours, and may have been taken long before it is used.
logic: A successful remote access authentication with no preceding failures, from a source address, autonomous system or device fingerprint that account has not used before. There is no brute force to detect because there was no guessing, and the theft happened outside your estate.
xql_sketch: dataset = <vpn_dataset> | filter xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS" | comp count() by xdm.source.user.username, xdm.source.ipv4 | filter first_seen_for_user = true
caveat: The supply side is an information stealer campaign against personal and unmanaged devices, so no control inside the estate prevents the theft. Multi-factor authentication on remote access is what breaks the chain, which is why its absence is the finding rather than the alert. Where a stealer campaign is reported publicly, treat it as a reason to force rotation rather than as someone else's incident.

name: Remote access session from a network the account has never used
description: Depends on the authentication record rather than device integrity, so it survives the appliance itself being compromised.
logic: Successful remote access where the source network or country falls outside that account's own ninety-day history.
xql_sketch: dataset = <auth_dataset> | filter xdm.event.outcome = "SUCCESS" | join type = left (<account_source_baseline>) as base base.username = xdm.source.user.username | filter base.asn = null
caveat: Travel, home connections and mobile carriers move accounts legitimately. Rank on distance from the account's own history, not a country blocklist.

name: The controls that were missing, ranked by how often
description: Six national authorities listed the weak controls, poor configurations and poor practices that actors routinely exploit for initial access, alongside the five techniques those weaknesses enable. Every item is a configuration state with a definite answer rather than a detection.
logic: Work the list as an audit with a yes or no per item: is a second factor enforced everywhere including administrators, are privileges and access control lists correct, is software current, are vendor defaults still in place, are internet-facing services securely configured, is logging centralised, and are detection tools deployed. The value is that it is short, ordered by observed frequency, and finishable.
caveat: The agencies single out remote desktop as one of the most common ransomware infection vectors and say explicitly not to exempt any user, particularly administrators, from a second factor. The administrator exemption is the specific failure worth checking first, because it is usually granted deliberately for convenience.

name: Audit passwords against breach corpora, not against policy
description: The named causes of a full domain compromise were misconfigurations and weak passwords, neither of which appears in a vulnerability scan.
logic: Check credentials against known-breached corpora rather than against a complexity policy, and audit for the specific misconfigurations on the published top-ten list.
xql_sketch: dataset = <identity_inventory> | filter password_found_in_breach_corpus = true or (account_type = "service" and password_age_days > 365)
caveat: Complexity policies do not prevent weak passwords, they shape them predictably. Checking against breached credentials reflects what an attacker actually tries.

name: The web server stops logging, or gains a module
description: External rules cover request logging and event tracing being disabled on the web server, new modules being registered, and previously installed modules being removed. A native module runs inside the server process on every request.
logic: Configuration commands that disable request logging or tracing, and module registration or removal. The logging half matters because it precedes activity the operator wants unrecorded; the module half is a web shell that never appears as a file in the served directory.
caveat: A native module is the web shell variant that file integrity monitoring on the served directory will never see, because there is no file in the served directory. Combined with logging being disabled first, the requests that follow leave no record at all, which is why the logging change deserves the higher severity of the two.
derived_from: splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)
SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)

name: New or altered file in a served directory
description: Creation or modification of a script file anywhere a web service can serve from. Catches both a newly written page and a shipped page that has had code added to it, though the second case needs a content hash baseline rather than a file listing.
logic: File create or write events under served directories with a servable script extension, compared against a hash baseline of the shipped files.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type in ("file_create", "file_write") and xdm.target.file.path ~= "(inetpub|wwwroot|htdocs|webapps|owa|ecp)" and xdm.target.file.extension in ("aspx", "asmx", "ashx", "php", "jsp", "jspx")
caveat: Product updates rewrite these directories wholesale. Suppress against the patching window or the update buries the signal.

name: Application server creating a shell
description: A web or application server process creating a shell or interpreter child. Either an exploited request or an application that shells out by design, and both are worth knowing about.
logic: Parent process is a web or application server and the child is a shell, interpreter or reconnaissance utility.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process" and xdm.source.process.name in ("w3wp.exe", "java", "java.exe", "httpd", "nginx", "php-fpm") and xdm.target.process.name in ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "sh", "bash", "whoami.exe")
caveat: Some applications shell out for reporting, image conversion or backup. The legitimate set is usually small enough to allow-list by command line.

name: The security, system or application log deleted outright
description: Ransomware actors deleted the system, security and application event logs before encrypting. Clearing a log is itself a logged event, so the artefact survives the act provided the log was forwarded off the host first.
logic: The log-cleared event identifiers, and the utilities that clear logs being run at all. Because the actor's purpose is to remove local evidence, the value of this detection depends entirely on central forwarding already having happened, which makes it as much a test of the logging pipeline as of the host.
caveat: Near-zero legitimate frequency outside deliberate maintenance, which makes it one of the cleanest markers in this corpus. Its weakness is timing: it fires when the actor is already at the stage of covering tracks, usually minutes before encryption.

name: Remote execution through the management service
description: External rules cover the management service being enabled, remote commands invoked through it, and offensive tooling built specifically to use it. Its handler process appearing as a parent is what reveals remote execution on the receiving host.
logic: On the receiving host the handler process appears as the parent of whatever ran, which is the clearest evidence of remote execution. On the network side the service listens on two fixed ports. Enabling the service where it was not enabled before is itself worth an alert.
caveat: Widely used for legitimate administration, so this needs scoping to the hosts and accounts that should never be managed this way rather than deploying estate-wide. Its value is that it is a lateral movement route which leaves no service creation and no file written to an administrative share, so the usual lateral detections miss it.
derived_from: SigmaHQ/sigma (Detection Rule License 1.1)
splunk/security_content (Apache 2.0)

name: A script file appears in a directory the web server serves
description: A web shell dropped into the document root of a web server or appliance. Across the analysis reports the filenames are deliberately unremarkable, chosen to match the naming of the application already installed, which makes the name the one property not worth matching on.
logic: Alert on the creation or modification of a server-side script file beneath a served directory where the writing process is the web server, the application server, or a shell descended from either. The served paths are deployment-specific and have to be enumerated locally; so does the set of paths where the application legitimately writes, which is normally a small upload or cache directory and can be excluded once.
caveat: The name is the wrong marker and that is the whole point of the pattern: of 110 web shell filenames extracted from the reports, the most cited were index.php, discover.aspx, common.php and footer.php, all chosen to be indistinguishable from the application around them. Deployments and plugin installers write scripts into served directories legitimately, so this needs a deployment window or a change record to be alertable rather than a hunt; without one it still narrows well. On appliances the served root is often not documented, and finding it is a prerequisite rather than a detail.
derived_from: CISA malware analysis reports (AR series), US Government work, public domain

name: An appliance's internal handler is requested from outside its own flow
description: Requests to the internal CGI, servlet and handler paths of a network appliance, reached directly rather than as part of the authentication or administrative flow that normally calls them. The Pulse Secure reports supply the clearest example, where the exploited and backdoored components sit under the vendor's own internal path tree.
logic: Model which internal handler paths the appliance calls as part of a normal session and in what order, then alert on a request to one of them that arrives without the preceding step, from an unauthenticated session, or from a source that never completes a login. The path inventory is vendor-specific and enumerable from the appliance itself.

markers.note: Pulse Secure and Ivanti Connect Secure internal tree

markers.expr: handler_path requested without preceding_expected_step in session
request_count by source_ip, handler_path over measured_baseline_window exceeds baseline

caveat: The specific paths named here are one vendor's and will not transfer; what transfers is the method, which is to take the appliance's own handler inventory and treat a direct request to one as anomalous. Health checks, load balancer probes and the vendor's own update client all call internal paths directly and have to be excluded first, which is why this is a sequence against the session rather than a match on the path alone. Eighteen of the reports concern this one product line, so the evidence is deep rather than broad.
derived_from: CISA malware analysis reports (AR series), US Government work, public domain

name: A service registered under a name borrowed from a security product
description: Persistence through a Windows service whose name is chosen to read as a security or platform component at a glance. The reports supply windefenders as a service name, alongside others shaped to sit unremarked in a service listing.
logic: Alert on service creation where the service name is close to, but not, a name on the platform's known-good service list, and separately where the name contains a security vendor token but the image path is not the vendor's installation directory. The known-good list is per platform build and must be taken from the estate rather than assumed.

markers.expr: service_name contains security_vendor_token and image_path not under vendor_install_path

caveat: The edit-distance bound is the tunable part and has to be measured against the estate's own service inventory, because a bound wide enough to catch a plausible near-miss also catches genuine vendor variants that differ by a version suffix. Pluralising an existing name, as windefenders does to windefend, is the cheapest version of this and the one an edit-distance check catches most reliably. The image-path half is the stronger of the two conditions and is worth running alone where the service inventory is not clean enough for the first.
derived_from: CISA malware analysis reports (AR series), US Government work, public domain

name: A device that reports continuously goes quiet, then comes back
description: Logging suppressed at the device rather than entries deleted at the collector, either for the duration of a session or persistently by changing the accounting configuration.
logic: Measure each device's own reporting cadence and volume, then alert when a reachable device falls silent or drops sharply against its own history. The detection has to live at the collector, because the record of the suppression is precisely what the suppression removes.
caveat: Reboots and outages produce the same silence and are far more common, so this needs a reachability signal and a maintenance feed from somewhere other than the device itself, or it becomes an outage alarm. The bound is the device's own cadence and cannot be a constant across a mixed estate. Where suppression is session-scoped rather than persistent, the gap may be minutes and will be missed by any check that runs daily.
derived_from: Mandiant and Cisco Talos public threat research, cited per record

name: A device the operator did not add appears in the management platform
description: Registration of an unknown device to a platform that manages other devices, which grants the registrant whatever the platform holds about its estate.
logic: Alert on every device registration and reconcile against the change record and the asset inventory. The rate is low in a steady estate, the platform logs it natively, and it precedes rather than follows the theft it enables.
caveat: A management platform is worth more than any single device it manages, and this is the event that says something joined it. The legitimate rate spikes during estate expansion, which is the worst time for extra alerts and the obvious time to hide a registration, so reconcile rather than suppress during change windows.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: A listener that never calls out, waiting to be woken
description: An implant with no outbound channel, activated by a crafted packet, which defeats every detection built on beaconing behaviour.
logic: Compare the ports a device actually offers against the set its platform and version should offer, and treat inbound traffic to anything outside that set as the signal. Because there is no outbound channel, egress analysis contributes nothing here and the listening surface is the whole of the evidence.
caveat: The reason to carry this separately from ordinary command-and-control detection is that it breaks the assumption those rules rest on: no interval, no destination, no volume, nothing to profile. Scanning your own estate answers it better than any log query, which makes it the rare detection whose implementation is an active measure rather than a search.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: The device is told to serve its own configuration
description: A built-in file transfer or export service enabled and pointed at the stored configuration, turning configuration theft into a supported feature.
logic: Alert on the command forms that enable configuration export and on the enabled state appearing in a configuration diff, reconciled against the accounts and change records permitted to do it. Cover each vendor's own command wording present in the estate.
caveat: Unlike an interactive harvest this leaves the device serving its configuration continuously until somebody notices, so the window of exposure is open-ended rather than bounded by a session. Backup processes that use the same mechanism will dominate and must be enumerated first; where backup runs over something else entirely this is close to false-positive free.
derived_from: Cisco Talos public threat research, cited per record

name: The implant is not on the appliance, it is in what the appliance is built from
description: An appliance whose running filesystem is unpacked from a compressed image at each boot, modified in the image rather than on the filesystem, so that live inspection returns clean.
logic: Compare the boot image against the vendor's rather than the filesystem against anything, and where that is not possible, look for the boot-time evidence instead: start-up scripts that differ from the vendor baseline, and processes that run once at boot and delete their own binary.
caveat: The technique exists because a running appliance will not let you read the image, and that asymmetry is the whole of its value to an actor. Treat any live inspection of such a platform as evidence of nothing, and note that an upgrade rewrites the image, so integrity work belongs after the upgrade rather than before it. Where the vendor ships an integrity or malware removal tool, that tool is worth more than anything expressible as a query.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: Patching does not remove it, because it is watching for the patch
description: An implant that monitors the file it has replaced and restores its own copy when an update overwrites it, so that the appliance is reinfected by the act of being fixed.
logic: Verify integrity after an update and then again after a delay, because the first check is the one designed to pass. Look for a file whose hash returns to its pre-update value, and for copies of legitimate components under names the vendor does not ship.
caveat: This removes patching from the list of things that remediate, which makes it a planning finding as much as a detection: where it is suspected, the answer is rebuild or replace. It pairs with the credential-rotation pattern for the same reason, since both describe an intrusion that survives the action taken to end it.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: Credentials taken at the server every device trusts
description: Interception of the administration protocol that authenticates operators to network devices, either by capturing and decrypting it on the wire or by replacing the daemon that serves it.
logic: Look at what runs on the authentication server rather than at what it logs, since every authentication involved succeeds. A packet capture process on that host, a daemon binary that does not match its package, and capture configuration carried in process environment variables are the three checks that work.
caveat: Centralised device authentication gives an operator one place to manage credentials and an actor one place to collect them, and the server is typically monitored for availability rather than for what runs on it. Nothing here appears in an authentication log, because every authentication succeeded. Verifying the daemon against its package costs almost nothing and is the highest-value check available.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: A second secure shell service behind the real one
description: Interactive access served by something other than the platform's own daemon, reached over a local socket or via an injected library, so that sessions appear in no authentication log.
logic: Three independent checks, any of which stands alone: a listening local socket owned by something that is not the secure shell daemon, secure shell binaries that do not match their package, and a package manager hold placed on those packages so an update cannot replace them.
caveat: A version lock on a security package, on a server otherwise kept patched, is close to a zero-false-positive signal and is trivially cheap to check across an estate, which makes it the best value marker here by a distance. Enumerate legitimate pins first; that list is worth reviewing on its own merits regardless of what this finds.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: The application gains a route its vendor never wrote
description: Interpreted platform source edited to register an additional route and handler, with authentication decorators omitted, so the backdoor is part of the application rather than a file in a served directory.
logic: Compare the platform's interpreted source against the vendor baseline for that version, and separately watch for successful requests to an API path that were never preceded by an authentication. The second needs no baseline and is the one to build first.
caveat: This defeats a file-integrity check scoped to the web root, because the modified file is part of the product rather than content. Vendors rarely publish per-version hashes of interpreted source, so the baseline usually comes from a freshly imaged unit, which is why the request-side marker matters more than it looks.
derived_from: Mandiant public threat research, cited per record

name: The actor picked the assets you cannot watch
description: Target selection by monitoring coverage rather than by value or version, concentrating on appliances that cannot run an endpoint agent.
logic: Reconcile endpoint agent coverage against the asset inventory, separate cannot-install from not-yet-installed, and treat the first group as the set where only network-derived evidence exists. That list is also a reasonable prediction of where an actor will choose to sit.
caveat: The output is a list of assets where certain detections are impossible, which makes this a scoping exercise before it is anything else. Long dwell on these platforms is usually a consequence of the coverage gap rather than of the implant being clever, and the remedy is sensor placement rather than better rules.
derived_from: Volexity public threat research, cited per record

name: The cloud sign-in came from your own address space, because it did
description: A compromised edge appliance used as a proxy so that access to cloud services originates inside the trusted network, satisfying location-based conditional access rather than bypassing it.
logic: Correlate cloud sign-ins attributed to corporate address space against internal session records for the same account and time, and separately watch for edge appliances originating outbound sessions to the tenancy. Location is not evidence once an appliance inside that location is compromised.
caveat: The control was satisfied rather than bypassed, which is why nothing in the access logs looks wrong. Any policy resting on network location inherits the trustworthiness of every device in that location, including those that cannot be monitored, so the durable fix is a device condition and this correlation is the stopgap.
derived_from: Volexity public threat research, cited per record

name: The endpoint answered with more than it should have
description: Memory disclosed through a web endpoint that returns uninitialised buffer contents when a request omits something its parser assumed present. Detected on the response, because the request trigger differs with every instance.
logic: Baseline the response shape of each authentication and pre-authentication endpoint, then alert on responses that break it: length varying materially between requests from one source, non-printable bytes in fields that should be text or empty, and repeated requests from one source because a single request returns only whatever was on the stack.

markers.expr: stddev(response_length) by url_path, source_ip exceeds measured_baseline_for_that_endpoint
count(request) by source_ip, url_path within measured_short_window

caveat: Written on the response side deliberately. Request-side markers for this class have a short life because each instance is a different parsing path, and a pattern built on one of them silently stops matching when the next identifier appears. The length baseline must be measured per endpoint: a patched and an unpatched appliance can differ by a few hundred bytes. Exploitation resembles failed authentication in an access log, and the leaked content never appears there at all, so response inspection is required rather than access logging.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The same fault, the same product, a new identifier
description: One product yielding repeated instances of a single fault class under separate identifiers, indicating that each fix addressed an instance rather than the cause.
logic: Group identifiers by product and by fault class rather than counting them. Three or more instances of one class in one product, spanning more than a single release cycle, means the next instance should be planned for rather than waited for.
caveat: Deliberately narrower than the repeat-offender pattern, which is about a class recurring across vendors. This one says a single product keeps producing the same fault, which is a stronger claim and a harder conversation. Where it holds, being current on patches evidences very little, because the next identifier in the sequence has not been published yet and the exposure decision is the only control that does not depend on it. Measured against 207 coordinated-disclosure advisories, 7 products meet this pattern's own threshold of three or more identifiers in one fault class, and 4 go further and concentrate in a single named component. The sharpest is Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build, where 11 of 11 advisories name the same component, parsing of SSD files: the fix history there is a series of instances of one fault rather than 11 distinct problems. Where a source names the component as well as the fault class, group on the component, because the fault class alone is broad enough that unrelated flaws share one.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: It stopped answering, then restarted
description: Memory corruption attempted against pre-authentication request handling, detected by the appliance failing to respond and restarting rather than by the payload that caused it.
logic: Correlate a request against the appliance with the absence of any response to it, followed by a service restart, and suppress restarts matched to maintenance. Add oversized values in fields with a known maximum, measured per field rather than assumed.
caveat: This catches attempts and failures, not success: an exploit that works may leave the appliance running normally, so a burst of resets that stops abruptly deserves more attention than the burst did. Written on the effect rather than the trigger deliberately, because the trigger is a different field for each identifier in these recurring classes. Restart records are more trustworthy taken from a monitoring system than from the appliance itself.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The channel opened before the check finished
description: A management interface that becomes usable during a race between the channel opening and the authentication governing it, so that privileged sessions exist with no corresponding login.
logic: Join the appliance's command or administrative session log to its web authentication log and alert where a privileged session exists with no login to account for it. Separately, look for connections to loopback management services from the web tier carrying no session context.
caveat: Each log looks unremarkable alone, which is why this has to be a join: the appliance records a legitimate privileged session and the web tier records nothing, and neither is anomalous by itself. Establish first that the platform logs command sessions separately from web logins, because where it does not this cannot be written at all.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The endpoints that have to work before anything is configured
description: Licensing, activation, setup and unlicensed-state endpoints, which cannot require authentication and therefore constitute the pre-authentication surface of a product regardless of its access control elsewhere.
logic: Enumerate these endpoints per product, then alert on any being reached from outside the management or partner ranges. A licensing endpoint answering an internet client on an already-licensed system has no legitimate explanation.
caveat: These are routinely absent from an application's access control review because they predate authentication, and from threat models that begin at the login page. The enumeration is the work; once done, a request from the internet to one of them on a configured system is close to false-positive free. Confirm periodic licence re-checks in the product first, since some genuinely call outward.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The application logged the attack for you
description: A failed object deserialisation attack raising an exception the application records itself, naming the deserialisation call in the stack.
logic: Search application error logs for exceptions naming deserialisation or object input handling, and correlate each with whether the request that caused it carried authentication. Works retrospectively against logs already held, with no signature to maintain.
caveat: Needs the application's error log, which is a different source from the access log and frequently is not forwarded anywhere. Establish that first, because the check costs nothing where the log exists and is impossible where it does not. A successful attack may raise no exception at all, so in the general case this finds attempts and near misses rather than confirming compromise. ASP.NET ViewState is the documented exception to that: there a successful deserialisation raises an InvalidCastException and a wrong key raises a MAC validation failure, so the exception type separates success from failure rather than marking both as near misses. See pat-viewstate-exception-distinguishes-key-validity, and do not apply the general caveat to a ViewState endpoint.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The platform that watches everything is worth more than anything it watches
description: Security monitoring and management platforms as the objective rather than the observer, giving raw logs, integration credentials, visibility into the defence, and control of what the defender believes.
logic: Assess the platform as the highest-value asset in its own scope. Check whether its console is reachable from outside the management network, whether administrative access to it is authenticated more strongly than the estate it monitors, and whether each integration account is scoped to read rather than to administer.
caveat: The hardest consequence to plan for is not theft but assurance. After a compromise here an absence of alerts means nothing, and every conclusion drawn from the platform during the window has to be re-established elsewhere. That is the argument for holding a copy of the most important logs outside the platform, which the log-tampering patterns reach independently.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The log platform became a credential store by accident
description: Secrets submitted in clear by service accounts and scripts, forwarded verbatim into log aggregation and retained there for as long as the retention policy allows.
logic: Search the aggregation platform's own index for credential-shaped content rather than assuming it is absent: connection strings in application errors, token and key parameters in recorded query strings, password arguments in captured command lines. Treat each hit as both a credential to rotate and a source to fix.
caveat: Rotation alone does not fix it, because the emitting source will send the new credential too.
