The field has to be masked at ingestion or the component changed, and retention decides how far back the exposure runs. Running this the first time usually finds a source that has been leaking for years rather than a single incident.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: Nobody owns it any more, and nothing noticed
description: Infrastructure decommissioned or allowed to lapse while other systems continue to trust and query it, making it acquirable by anyone rather than requiring compromise.
logic: Inventory in both directions. Outward, the external endpoints your estate still contacts that nobody owns any more, visible as resolution and outbound sessions to names absent from your asset register, especially from appliances carrying endpoints hardcoded at build time. Inward, every domain your organisation has registered and released, since anything still pointing at one now points at its next owner.
caveat: Requires no capability at all, only somebody noticing before you do, which is what makes it different from every other supply chain pattern here. Most affected systems are not misconfigured by any standard an audit applies, because nothing was wrong when the configuration was written. A register of every domain ever held, renewed rather than released, is cheaper than any detection this describes.
derived_from: watchTowr Labs public research, cited per record

name: The weakest way in is the one that decides
description: Access paths into one estate protected to different standards, so that credentials refused by the hardened path succeed on a path that was never treated as remote access.
logic: Enumerate every path an account can use to reach the estate and record what each actually enforces rather than what policy claims. Then join failures on the strong paths to successes for the same account on weaker ones, which is the sequence an actor confirming credentials produces.
caveat: Wireless is the path most often left at a password, because it is thought of as physical security rather than as remote access, and the building is treated as the control. The blocked spray against the hardened service is the part that reads as a non-event and is actually the reconnaissance. The joining log is often held by a network team rather than forwarded centrally, so establish that before designing anything.
derived_from: Volexity public threat research, cited per record

name: One machine, two networks, no decision
description: A host with adapters active on two networks at once, collapsing a separation everything else depends on, usually by accident rather than by design.
logic: Inventory hosts reporting more than one active adapter on distinct networks, watch for wireless enumeration and profile commands on hosts with no roaming role, and on the receiving side alert on wireless clients whose name or directory affiliation belongs to another organisation.
caveat: Survives audits that check the design rather than the running state, because nothing in the design says a machine may bridge. The same shape is the classic route across an industrial boundary, which is why this applies to engineering workstations as much as to offices. Client identification beyond an address is required for the affiliation marker, and many wireless controllers do not record it.
derived_from: Volexity public threat research, cited per record

name: It asked over plain HTTP what to install, and installed it
description: Applications retrieving update instructions or installers without encryption or signature verification, so that anyone able to answer the request chooses what runs.
logic: Alert on a plaintext fetch followed shortly by an executable written and run with the fetching process as parent, which is the shape regardless of who answered. Separately inventory which installed applications update over an unencrypted channel at all, a finite list answerable before an incident.
caveat: The inventory half is worth more than the detection half, because the list is short, knowable in advance and largely consists of software nobody approved. Where the answer is poisoned upstream of the organisation nothing internal looks wrong at all, which leaves comparing resolution against an independent path as the only remaining check, and that is a deliberate control rather than a query.
derived_from: Volexity public threat research, cited per record

name: It fetched whatever is at that name today
description: Build and deployment pipelines resolving external artefacts by a mutable name at fetch time rather than by an immutable digest, so that whoever controls the name controls what runs.
logic: Inventory every external artefact reference in build and deployment configuration and record whether each pins a digest or a commit. On the wire, watch for a redirect or a miss immediately followed by a successful fetch of the same name, and for publishers whose account is newer than the reference pointing at them.
caveat: The pinning inventory answers this from source control without touching a log and is worth more than every network marker here. Pinning stops substitution but not compromise of the pinned artefact, so mirroring to an internal registry after scanning is the stronger control. Applies well beyond models: container tags, package ranges and action references have the same property.
derived_from: Unit 42 public research, cited per record

name: The request did not come from a person
description: Connected tool servers issuing model completion requests, reversing the direction the surrounding architecture assumes and breaking the premise that user intent drives every invocation.
logic: Attribute completion requests to a connected server or to a user turn and baseline the ratio per server. Then reconcile executed tool calls against those a user actually saw, and compare model response length against displayed output length, since the host commonly condenses before display.
caveat: Depends entirely on the host logging server-originated requests separately from user turns, which is not universal and is the first thing to establish. Baselines are young, so treat thresholds here as provisional. Reconciling executed against displayed tool calls is the strongest marker and the least threshold-dependent.
derived_from: Unit 42 public research, cited per record

name: Data carrying the grammar of instructions
description: Content from a tool, document, page or message heading into a model context while carrying role markers, turn delimiters, control characters or directives aimed at future behaviour.
logic: Match on structure rather than meaning, scoped to content entering a model context: role and system markers, turn delimiters, zero-width and bidirectional control characters, encoded blocks in prose fields, and text directing future behaviour rather than describing itself.
caveat: Hunt-grade because documentation about prompts contains prompts and technical content discusses these markers constantly. The discriminator is where the content is heading, not what it contains, so scope strictly to content entering a model context. The persistence marker is the one that matters most: an injection reaching stored memory outlives the session it arrived in. This is the same instrument the corpus uses for account fields carrying foreign grammar, applied to a different field.
derived_from: Unit 42 public research, cited per record

name: The signalling says the subscriber is somewhere they are not
description: Inter-operator signalling requesting subscriber location or profile from a network the subscriber has not roamed into, which is the shape of location tracking and home-routing bypass alike.
logic: Do not try to characterise the message; check it against state you already hold. For each inbound signalling request naming a subscriber, ask whether that subscriber is currently registered as roaming into the network the request came from. A request from a network the subscriber has never visited is implausible regardless of how well formed it is, and the plausibility check works the same way for the successor protocol as for the current one.
caveat: This is the check that survives the protocol changing, which matters because the same abuse has now been carried over three generations of signalling. It needs the roaming register joined to the signalling log, which sits with different teams in most operators and is the practical obstacle rather than the logic. Legitimate roaming partners generate volume, so the per-origin baseline has to be measured rather than assumed.
derived_from: MITRE FiGHT (c) The MITRE Corporation, Public Release Case 22-2192

name: A keepalive with cargo
description: Mobile transport tunnelling used as a covert channel, including echo and keepalive messages carrying payload they have no reason to carry.
logic: Two halves that support each other. On the wire, inspect tunnel control messages for payload: an echo request is a fixed, small, predictable thing and anything beyond that shape is the signal. On the host, user plane network functions run a known set of processes and should not be opening raw sockets, so an unexpected process or a raw socket on one is worth an alert by itself.

markers.note: control and user plane tunnel ports

caveat: The host half is the stronger one and the easier to run, because a network function has a small fixed process set and a raw socket on one has no ordinary explanation. The wire half needs inspection of tunnel contents, which many operators do not do at all on internal interfaces because the volume is enormous. Note this is the technique two independent sources in this corpus describe, which is unusual and worth weighting accordingly.
derived_from: MITRE FiGHT (c) The MITRE Corporation, Public Release Case 22-2192

name: A base station that is not yours, seen by your own handsets
description: A false base station or rogue access point standing up in coverage, detected through what genuine subscriber equipment reports about its radio neighbourhood rather than by finding the transmitter.
logic: The handsets are the sensor. Base stations already collect measurement reports naming the neighbouring cells each device can hear and at what power, so parse those for identifiers that are not in the operator's own cell inventory, and for power levels inconsistent with the known layout. A transmitter can hide from a survey but not from every device that measures it.
caveat: Requires the cell inventory to be accurate and current, which in a large estate it frequently is not, and an out-of-date inventory turns every legitimate new cell into an alert. Neighbouring operators and legitimate small cells appear in these reports too and must be enumerated first. The measurement reports exist already, which is what makes this cheap where the inventory is good.
derived_from: MITRE FiGHT (c) The MITRE Corporation, Public Release Case 22-2192

name: A network function nobody ordered
description: Virtualised network functions or containers deployed by something other than the sanctioned orchestrator, in an estate where every legitimate deployment has a record.
logic: Reconcile what is running against what the orchestrator was asked to run. Container and workload creation, enumeration and modification events are recorded natively, and in a network estate every legitimate instantiation traces to a change record, so the discriminator is the absence of that trace rather than anything about the workload.
caveat: Depends entirely on the orchestrator being the only sanctioned route to deploy, which is the stated design in most operators and not always the practice. Where engineers can deploy directly the exceptions have to be enumerated first, and that enumeration is usually the more useful finding.
derived_from: MITRE FiGHT (c) The MITRE Corporation, Public Release Case 22-2192

name: The command and control is a reputable AI provider
description: A legitimate model or assistant API used to carry commands and exfiltrated results, so that the traffic terminates on infrastructure with excellent reputation and a valid certificate.
logic: Reputation, domain age and category all return reassuring answers here because the destination genuinely is a major provider, which is the point of choosing it. What remains is fit: which hosts in the estate have any business calling an inference API, and does this one. Alert where a host with no AI workload and no developer role holds sessions to a model or assistant endpoint, and where the calling process is not one the organisation deploys for that purpose.
caveat: This is the case where reputation feeds actively mislead, and blocking the destination is not available because the organisation very likely uses it legitimately elsewhere. The inventory of which hosts should reach these services is the whole control, and it is worth building before it is needed rather than during an incident. Periodicity helps but assistant APIs are polled legitimately too, so it is a supporting marker rather than a deciding one.
derived_from: MITRE ATLAS (c) The MITRE Corporation; markers derived from documented incidents, not from ATLAS text

name: Somebody else is spending your model quota
description: Stolen cloud AI credentials used to consume inference the account holder is billed for, frequently resold through a proxy, and used to reach capability the thief could not obtain in their own name.
logic: The abuse is visible on the account before it is visible on the network, because the account is what pays. Watch for enumeration of which models are enabled, which is the first thing an actor does with a stolen key and something a legitimate workload has no reason to do repeatedly; for inference calls whose source, region or user agent does not match any deployed workload; and for consumption departing from the shape the account's own workloads produce.
caveat: The billing signal usually arrives before the security one, so the finance owner may know first and is worth telling in advance that this is a security question rather than a budgeting anomaly. Enumeration of enabled models is the earliest and cheapest marker here, and it is the one most likely to be present in an audit log an organisation already collects. Guardrail bypass tooling built on top of this is a separate consequence: the account holder's identity carries the abuse.
derived_from: MITRE ATLAS (c) The MITRE Corporation; markers derived from documented incidents, not from ATLAS text

name: The process is lying about where it came from
description: Token manipulation and parent process spoofing used so that a process presents an ancestry and an identity it did not actually have, defeating detections that key on the parent-child pair.
logic: Rules keyed on a parent-child pair are defeated by an actor choosing the parent, which is cheap and well documented. What resists it is comparing the claim against something the actor does not control: the creating process recorded by the kernel against the parent the process reports, the token owner against the account that authenticated, and the image on disk against the memory the process is actually executing.
caveat: This is the pattern that undermines a large share of any endpoint rule library, because parent-child pairs are the most common thing such rules key on and they are attacker-controlled. Whether it can be written at all depends on the sensor recording the creating process separately from the reported parent; many do not, and establishing that is the first task rather than a detail. Legitimate installers and service managers spoof ancestry too, so the service inventory has to come first.
derived_from: Restricted internal detection library; abstracted, no rule text reproduced

name: The evidence was edited, not deleted
description: Timestamps rewritten and identifying strings stripped from tooling, so that artefacts survive but no longer say what they are or when they arrived.
logic: Deletion is noisy and leaves a gap somebody notices. Editing is quieter and leaves the artefact in place looking ordinary. The checks that work compare one recorded time against another: the filesystem's own metadata timestamps against each other, and the file's claimed creation time against the first time any other system observed it. A file that claims to predate the log line that first mentions it is not old, it is edited.
caveat: The last marker is the one worth the effort and the hardest to build: tooling with its identifying strings removed still behaves the way the tool behaves, so detections resting on names and strings fail while detections resting on sequence survive. That is an argument for how the rest of a library should be written, not only a detection in itself. Backup and deployment tooling rewrites timestamps legitimately and must be enumerated first.
derived_from: Restricted internal detection library; abstracted, no rule text reproduced

name: The traffic looks like something you allow
description: Command and control shaped to resemble a permitted service, whether by fronting through a trusted domain, impersonating a common protocol on its usual port, or splitting transfers to stay under size expectations.
logic: Three separable checks, none of which needs the destination to be known bad. Where the name resolved and the name presented in the encrypted session disagree, the session is fronted. Where the protocol on a port does not behave like the protocol that port implies, it is impersonated. And where transfers from one source cluster just below a round threshold, the size is being chosen rather than occurring.
caveat: Content delivery networks legitimately serve many names from one address and will dominate the fronting check unless enumerated, which is the main cost here. The size-clustering marker is the most durable of the three because it detects the actor's own caution: a threshold chosen to stay under a limit is itself a pattern, and it survives every change of destination.

name: Out of the container and onto the machine
description: A process inside a container reaching the host, through the kernel interfaces that exist for legitimate reasons and are reachable when the container is privileged or over-permissioned.
logic: Watch for the specific kernel and namespace machinery an escape needs, rather than for the escape. Writes to the cgroup release-agent interface, which causes the host to execute a path of the container's choosing. Loading a kernel image from inside a container. Changing root and mounting host filesystems. And a general-purpose relay appearing in an image that has no reason to carry one. Each is rare enough in a container to alert on, and together they cover the routes that do not depend on a specific vulnerability.

markers.note: cgroup interfaces that make the host run a chosen path
an interactive shell as parent inside a container is itself unusual

caveat: The privileged-container marker is the one to inventory first, because it decides whether any of the rest is reachable, and it is a configuration fact rather than an event. Build tooling and node agents legitimately use several of these binaries, so exclude by image and by node role rather than by binary name. An interactive shell inside a running container is worth reviewing on its own merits regardless of what follows it.

name: Changes at the tier above the accounts
description: Manipulation of the organisation that contains the cloud accounts, rather than of the identities inside them: policy attachment and detachment, account removal, organisation creation.
logic: The identity tier is well covered by most detection libraries and the tier above it usually is not, which is what makes it worth watching: a control policy detached at the organisation level silently removes a guardrail from every account beneath it, and no single account records that as a change to itself. These operations are administrative, rare, and performed by a small set of people, so alert on all of them and reconcile against the change record rather than trying to decide which are suspicious.
caveat: Detachment matters more than attachment and is the easier of the two to miss, because removing a restriction produces the same event shape as adding one. Landing-zone automation performs these legitimately during account provisioning, so enumerate the automation principals first; that list is short and stable, which makes this close to false-positive free afterwards.

name: A key pushed into a machine that is already running
description: Interactive access obtained through the cloud provider's own facilities for pushing a key or opening a console into a live instance, which needs no credential on the instance and leaves no failed authentication.
logic: These operations sit in the cloud audit log rather than on the instance, which is why an instance-side detection never sees them, and they succeed on the first attempt because the provider is authorising the push rather than the instance authenticating a user. Alert on the push itself and reconcile against whether that instance is one anybody should be reaching interactively. Pair it with modification of the account's authorised key file on the instance, which is where a pushed key becomes a persistent one.
caveat: The absence of any failed authentication is the point and the reason this is easy to miss: every detection built on brute force or credential stuffing is looking at the wrong layer. Break-glass procedures use exactly this route, which is a good reason to enumerate them rather than to exclude the technique. The authorised-key file marker is what separates a one-off session from persistence.

name: Access to the mailbox without the password
description: Persistent access to another person's mail obtained by granting a delegation, a folder permission or an administrative role, rather than by taking their credential.
logic: No authentication fails and no password changes, because none is needed: the grant is an administrative operation and every subsequent access is legitimate for the principal holding it. Alert on the grant itself, reconciled against whether the two parties have any working relationship, and treat a role assignment that confers mailbox access across the tenancy as a different severity from a single delegation.
caveat: Delegation is a normal business practice and leave cover produces it in bursts, which is why the relationship check matters more than the operation. Verify whether the identity, the client and the address making the change should be making changes in your environment at all, because the grant is frequently made from a session that is itself the intrusion. The role-assignment marker is the one to alert on hardest: a single assignment can confer access to every mailbox and it looks like one administrative event.

name: The account was given a history it never had
description: Directory attributes that confer privilege altered directly, including history injection, delegation flags and service installation, in a domain where each is administrative and rare.
logic: History injection grants the privileges of another principal without joining any group, so group membership review will not find it and the account looks ordinary. Watch the directory events that record attribute change and account modification, alongside service installation, and reconcile each against the small set of people entitled to perform it. Directory replication from a source that is not a domain controller belongs in the same family: it is the same idea applied to the directory itself.
caveat: The reason to carry this separately from group-membership monitoring is that it defeats it: an account with injected history holds privilege that no membership review will show, so the usual quarterly access review reports it as ordinary. Migration tooling uses the same mechanism legitimately and in volume, so a migration in progress must be known about before this is alertable rather than discovered through it.

name: Somebody opened the password file by hand
description: Credential and key material on Unix hosts read or copied using ordinary interactive tools, which is how it happens when a person is at a shell rather than running tooling.
logic: Automated credential theft uses tooling with a recognisable name; a person at a shell uses whatever is installed. Alert on ordinary readers and editors touching the shadow file, the root key directory or the privilege-configuration directory, and on the same paths being copied into shared-memory or temporary directories, which is where they are staged before leaving.
caveat: Configuration management and backup agents read these paths constantly and will dominate unless excluded by account and parent, which is the whole of the tuning work. The staging marker is the one worth building first because it is far rarer than the read: material copied into shared memory is being prepared to leave, and shared memory is chosen precisely because it is not on disk.

name: The website filled the clipboard and asked the user to paste
description: A compromised site overwriting its own content with a fake verification prompt, placing a command on the clipboard, and instructing the visitor to run it themselves, so that the user performs the execution rather than the browser.
logic: Nothing exploits the browser, which is why browser hardening and exploit detection see nothing: the user is asked to do the running. The shape that remains is a scripting engine started from a shell or a run dialog shortly after browser activity, with a long encoded or obfuscated argument, and no parent chain back to the browser process at all. On the serving side, a legitimate site suddenly loading script from a domain it has never referenced and rewriting its own body is the compromise that precedes it.
caveat: The reason this defeats a lot of endpoint tooling is that there is no exploit and no malicious parent process: the chain the detection expects, browser spawning something, never happens, because a person typed it. That also makes the clipboard marker the most direct evidence and the least commonly collected; establish whether the sensor records clipboard writes at all before designing around it. Administrators legitimately paste commands, so pair with the encoded-argument marker rather than alerting on paste-then-run alone.
derived_from: ASD's ACSC alerts and advisories, Australian Government work

name: A read-only grant executing code, because the upgrade request is a GET
description: A service account holding only a read verb on the proxy resource executing commands in any pod on a node, because the WebSocket handshake that opens an exec session is an HTTP GET and the authorisation check never runs again after the connection upgrades.
logic: Command execution is supposed to need a create verb. A WebSocket handshake has to begin as a GET carrying upgrade headers, the node agent maps that GET to the read verb, allows it, upgrades the connection, and hands it to the execution handler without a second check. So the observable is not a privilege the account should not have; it is an ordinary read privilege used against an execution path. Look for connections to the node agent port carrying an upgrade header and an exec path, and separate them by whether they reach the node directly or through the orchestrator API.
caveat: The maintainers have classified this as working as intended, so it is not going to be patched away and a version check will never clear it. Monitoring, logging and observability agents legitimately hold this grant and legitimately talk to that port, which is exactly why it is worth detecting rather than blocking: the traffic that matters looks like the traffic that is supposed to be there. Distinguish on the path and the upgrade header, not on the identity.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: The execution that produced no execution record
description: Reaching a node agent directly rather than through the orchestrator's API, so that the operation is authorised and performed but generates no audit entry naming it, leaving only the authorisation check behind.
logic: Two routes reach the same agent. Through the orchestrator API the operation is recorded by name, including the full exec path. Straight to the node, only the authorisation subquery is recorded, and the execution itself is invisible. That asymmetry is detectable without seeing the execution: an authorisation check for a proxy or execution resource that is never followed by a corresponding execution entry means the request went round the audited path. Network telemetry to the agent port is the other half, and is the only direct evidence the operation happened at all.
caveat: This is a logging-coverage finding before it is a detection. Establish first whether the node agent's own traffic is collected at all: in many estates it is not, and the honest answer is that the unlogged path cannot currently be seen, which is a more useful thing to report than a rule that silently matches nothing. A detection written only against the audited path will look healthy while the other route is in use.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: Enumerate what read-only actually confers
description: Reconciling the identities granted a read verb on a proxy or passthrough resource against those that can reach the underlying agent, on the basis that the grant confers execution rather than reading.
logic: Not an event detection. Two lists and an intersection: the identities holding the read verb on the passthrough resource, and the identities with network reach to the agent port. Everything in both can execute code in any workload on the reachable nodes. The grant is shipped by default in a large number of widely deployed monitoring charts, so the answer is rarely zero and is rarely known before it is asked.
caveat: The finding is usually inherited rather than chosen: the permission arrives in a vendor's deployment template and is never revisited. That makes remediation a conversation with the monitoring stack's owner rather than a configuration change, and it is the reason this belongs on an inventory footing rather than as an alert nobody can action.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: The identity provider was trusted to say who, and answered what
description: An application accepting a federated authentication assertion without checking it was issued for that application or bound to a permitted group, allowing an unauthenticated party to have a privileged local account created for them at first login.
logic: The account is created by the login rather than before it, so there is no provisioning event to correlate against and no administrator in the chain. What remains is the shape of the first successful authentication: a privileged role assigned at creation, the account's first-ever login being the one that created it, and an assertion whose audience or issuer does not match what the application should accept. Where group binding is the control, the observable is an account landing in a privileged group with no membership change recorded on the provider side.
caveat: Federation makes the application's own logs the wrong place to look for the decision: it recorded a successful login, and by its own reasoning that is what happened. The discrepancy only appears by comparing the two sides, so this needs provider-side records as well as application-side ones. Where only one side is collected, say so rather than writing a rule against the half that cannot show the problem.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: Enforcing a second factor the attacker gets to choose
description: A multi-factor requirement satisfied by the account holder enrolling their own factor at first login, so that an attacker who can create or reach an unenrolled account supplies the factor themselves and the requirement is met rather than bypassed.
logic: Nothing fails and nothing is bypassed, which is why failure-based and bypass-based detections see nothing: the policy is enforced and satisfied in the same step. The observable is enrolment adjacency -- a factor registered during the account's first authentication rather than at any later point -- and the enrolment arriving from the same address and client as the login it authorises.
caveat: Genuine first-day joiners produce exactly this sequence, so the count of legitimate matches is a function of hiring rather than of attack, and the rule is unusable without joining it to a source that knows who was expected. In estates with no such source the honest form is a periodic reconciliation rather than an alert. Pairs with the federated-account pattern, where the account being enrolled should not exist at all.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: The old interface nobody secured because nobody uses it
description: A superseded protocol endpoint retained for compatibility and left reachable without authentication, offering functionality the current interface gates properly.
logic: Hardening follows use, and nothing exercises the old endpoint, so it is neither monitored nor reviewed while remaining routable. Requests to superseded paths are close to zero in normal operation, which makes even a single one meaningful and makes a baseline cheap to establish. Look for legacy protocol verbs and paths answered with a success status, particularly where the modern equivalent requires authentication for the same operation.
caveat: Establish the baseline before alerting: some estates genuinely still run an integration against the old interface, and in those the pattern inverts into an inventory question about who. The wider point is that the modern endpoint being properly authenticated says nothing about the old one, so a review that only tested the documented interface will have reported the product secure.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: One database holding the credentials for everything it manages
description: A management platform's own datastore holding the credentials, keys and integration secrets for every system it administers, so that reading it once converts a single compromise into standing access to the managed estate.
logic: The exfiltration is the quiet part and the use of it is the loud part. What follows a read of the platform's credential store is authentication to many managed systems from one origin, using accounts that legitimately exist, within a short window. Detect on the fan-out rather than on the read: one source authenticating to an unusual breadth of destinations with valid credentials, and integration or service accounts appearing at hosts they have never previously reached.
caveat: Every credential used is valid, so nothing fails authentication and volume-of-failure detections stay silent. Rotation after such a compromise means rotating the managed estate rather than the platform, which is the finding worth stating in advance: the blast radius is the contents of that datastore, and it is usually larger than its owners expect. Overlaps deliberately with the device-management force-multiplier pattern, which is about pushing actions out; this one is about what reading it once yields.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public attack research, cited per record

name: The repository told the internet where its credentials were
description: Internet-wide scanning for repository configuration and environment files left served by a web server, extracting the credentials inside them, validating each one, and using the survivors to clone private source.
logic: Nothing is exploited. A deployment copies a repository directory to a web root, the server cheerfully serves the configuration file inside it, and the file names the remote and often carries the token. The observable is on the serving side and is close to unambiguous: requests for repository metadata and environment paths, at volume, from sources with no other relationship to the site. Because the same scan is run against enormous address ranges, one site sees only a handful of requests, so this is worth aggregating across an estate rather than judging per host. What follows a successful hit is the second half: a clone of private source from an address that has never authenticated interactively, and shortly after, first use of a cloud credential from an unfamiliar network.
caveat: A 200 on these paths is the finding and a 404 is not, so alerting on the request alone will bury you in background scanning that found nothing. The reported operation stored its loot in a bucket belonging to an earlier victim, which is worth knowing before assuming the infrastructure is attacker-owned: blocking or attributing it may implicate somebody who is themselves compromised. Secret management does not close this, because the leak is a deployment artefact rather than a secrets-handling failure, and the credential is valid wherever it is read from.
derived_from: Sysdig Threat Research Team public reporting, cited per record

name: Installing the dependency ran the dependency
description: A package manager's install-time hook executing attacker code on the developer or build machine, which then collects registry and cloud credentials and uses them to publish itself into further packages.
logic: The hook is a supported feature, so nothing is exploited and no version is vulnerable. The shape is a package manager process spawning an interpreter during installation rather than after it, and that interpreter then reading credential material and opening network connections, which an install step has no reason to do. The self-replicating variant adds a distinctive second half: the same host authenticating to the package registry to publish, and to the source forge to write, shortly after an install it did not initiate. Treat publish-after-install as the strongest single signal, because a machine that consumes packages and a machine that publishes them are usually not the same machine.
caveat: Install hooks are used legitimately by a great many packages to compile native code, so the hook firing is not the signal and a rule built on it alone is unusable. The credential read and the outbound connection are what separate them. The visibility-change marker is the one worth wiring to a person rather than a queue: a repository going from private to public is rarely accidental, is trivially checkable, and in the reported campaign was how the stolen material was published. Note also that disabling install scripts estate-wide is a real control here and is cheaper than detecting this, which makes the inventory question -- who actually needs them -- worth asking first. That control is ecosystem-specific and does not generalise: it holds for npm, which can be told to ignore scripts, and not for Cargo, whose build scripts have no stable equivalent switch and which runs them at compile time rather than at install. Where the ecosystem offers no such switch, detection is the only remaining option rather than the expensive one.
derived_from: Sysdig Threat Research Team public reporting, cited per record

name: A backdoor that only ever talks to somewhere you trust
description: A self-hosted continuous integration runner registered by an intruder on a machine they already hold, taking work from a repository they control, so that command and control runs entirely over the forge's own protocol to the forge's own address.
logic: Every network-side detection fails here by design: the only destination is the forge, which the estate already permits, already trusts and frequently already allow-lists. There is no unfamiliar domain, no unusual port and no self-signed certificate. So the detection has to be on the host and on the forge's own records rather than on the wire. On the host: a runner agent installed and registered on a machine that is not a build server, persisting as a service or scheduled task, long-polling outbound. On the forge: a runner registered against a repository by an account that does not normally administer runners, and a workflow whose job runs on a self-hosted label when the project's other jobs do not.
caveat: Do not try to detect this on the network. The traffic is genuinely to the forge, over its genuine protocol, and any rule keyed on destination reputation, domain age or novelty will score it clean and be right to. The asset question decides whether any of the host markers are usable at all: an organisation that cannot answer which of its machines are build machines cannot use the not-a-build-server condition, and that inventory is a prerequisite rather than a refinement. Registration is also low-friction by design, which is a product decision rather than a flaw, so this will not be fixed upstream.
derived_from: Sysdig Threat Research Team public reporting, cited per record

name: The build step that read the build's own memory
description: A widely depended-on pipeline action altered upstream to fetch a payload at run time and search the memory of the runner's own worker process for credentials, which are then emitted where the pipeline's output is readable.
logic: The secret is never at rest where a file-based detection would see it. It is in the memory of the process the pipeline runs, and the compromised step opens that process's memory mappings and reads them, which is a straightforwardly detectable act on a host with process telemetry: one process reading another's memory, inside a build, where nothing legitimate does that. The retrieval half is equally distinctive because the payload is not in the action at all: an encoded blob in the step decodes to a fetch of further code from a paste or gist service, so a build host reaching a code-sharing site mid-run is worth alerting on by itself. Then look at where the secrets went, which in the reported case was the build log, readable by anyone who could read the pipeline output.
caveat: Pinning actions to a commit digest rather than a tag prevents this outright and is worth more than every marker here, because the compromise was an upstream change to a name the pipeline resolved at run time. Where pinning is not in place, the memory-read marker is the highest-value one and also the least commonly collected: establish whether the build fleet runs process telemetry at all before designing around it. Scanning build logs for credential-shaped strings is worth doing regardless of this campaign, since it catches accidental disclosure at the same time, but treat a hit as an exposure to rotate rather than as proof of compromise.
derived_from: Sysdig Threat Research Team public reporting, cited per record

name: The trigger that hands secrets to a stranger's branch
description: A pipeline configured with a trigger that runs in the context of the target repository, with access to its secrets, while checking out and executing code proposed by somebody with no write access.
logic: This is a configuration finding first and an event detection second, because the vulnerable state is visible in the repository without waiting for anybody to exploit it. Inventory every workflow whose trigger grants the privileged context, and flag those that also check out the proposed branch or run a build command against it, which is the combination that turns a review request into arbitrary execution with the project's secrets. The event half, where telemetry exists, is a build run whose trigger came from an account with no write access to the repository, followed by that build reading secret material or reaching the network.
caveat: The privileged trigger exists for good reasons and is used correctly by many projects, so its presence is not the finding; the pairing with a checkout of the proposed code is. Note this was found in repositories maintained by security-literate organisations, which is the useful part: it is not a sign of a careless project, and an audit that assumes otherwise will skip the places most worth checking. Where the repository is public, the exposure inventory is also available to anyone else reading it.
derived_from: Sysdig Threat Research Team public reporting, cited per record

name: Whatever was top last quarter probably is not this quarter
description: The leading initial access vector across a large response population alternating between phishing and exploitation of public-facing applications from quarter to quarter, rather than trending in one direction.
logic: Not a detection. A planning constraint, and a reconciliation you can run against your own history. Measured over eighteen consecutive quarters by one responder, the top vector traded places repeatedly: phishing at half of engagements, then a third, then exploitation of public-facing applications at over sixty percent, then back to phishing at over half. Run the same count against your own incidents and compare the shape rather than the level. Where a programme's coverage is concentrated on one vector, the finding is the concentration itself, because the population it was tuned against does not hold still.
caveat: One responder's engagement population is not the world, and the mix reflects who calls them in as much as what attackers do. Use it to argue against over-fitting to one vector, not as a forecast of which vector is next. The third marker matters more than the other two: where your own vector distribution has a large undetermined bucket, the distribution is not evidence of anything yet, and the logging gap is the finding.
derived_from: Cisco Talos Incident Response quarterly trend reporting, cited per record

name: Controller password changed so the operator cannot get back in
description: Changing the credential on a controller is an availability attack, not a stealth one. The actor already has the access; altering the password removes the owner's, and on equipment where the password cannot be reset without vendor procedure or a stored image it converts a short intrusion into a long outage. Sits alongside renaming and readdressing as anti-recovery work.
logic: An authentication or credential-change function issued to a controller from a source that is not its engineering station, or outside a change window; and the confirming signal, the owner's own engineering station failing to authenticate to a controller it authenticated to before. The second half is what separates this from routine credential rotation, and it is observable even where the controller logs nothing itself.
caveat: Legitimate password rotation and commissioning produce the first half on its own, so the credential change alone is not alert-grade; it is the pairing with the owner losing access that is. Belongs in the response plan as well as in monitoring: recovery depends on holding a known-clean controller image off-device, because once the password is unknown the restore path is a vendor procedure rather than a login.

name: A passkey assertion the user never approved
description: Synced passkeys move the private key off the authenticator and into a platform key store, which means an assertion can be produced by anything that can reach that store. The property the relying party is supposed to check -- that a human verified themselves for this assertion -- is carried in a flag the client sets, so a relying party that does not enforce it accepts a signature produced with no user present at all. The weakness is in the acceptance, not in the cryptography.
logic: Authentications that succeeded on a passkey where the user-verification flag was absent or false, and authentications whose signature counter did not advance between uses. Both are fields the relying party already receives and usually discards. Count them per account and per relying party, because the population that never sets the flag is a configuration finding in its own right.
caveat: The signature counter half is currently weak against synced passkeys specifically: the research notes synced implementations report a constant value, so a static counter is normal there rather than suspicious. Use it on hardware authenticators, and rely on the verification flag for synced credentials. Enforcing the flag at the relying party is the actual fix; this detection exists for the estate you do not control the acceptance logic of.

name: The assistant kept a transcript of what they were trying to do
description: AI coding and agent clients write prompt history, persistent instruction files and memory stores to local disk. On a compromised or misused host these are an unusually direct record of intent, because unlike most forensic artefacts they contain the operator explaining the objective in their own words -- including the scope claims used to talk the model past its guardrails, and often the operator's own language. Cuts both ways: the same files identify an insider running unsanctioned offensive tooling and an intruder using the host's installed assistant.
logic: Locate the local state directories of installed AI assistant clients and treat three things as collectible evidence: prompt or session history, configuration files carrying persistent instructions to the model, and memory or context stores. Flag on content rather than on presence -- authorisation assertions, scope definitions naming hosts the organisation does not own, and target lists -- because the clients themselves are ordinary developer tools.
caveat: The publisher states plainly that separating legitimate red-team work from a claimed authorisation is hard, and it is: an in-scope definition in a config file looks the same whether or not the scope is real. Resolve it against the engagement record, not against the file. Reading these files also means reading employee prose, so treat the collection as monitored personal content and handle it under whatever policy governs that.

name: The payload explains itself, and repairs itself faster than a person could
description: Payloads delivered through an execution channel that carry natural-language reasoning: why this target and not that one, which database is largest, what each step is for. Human operators do not annotate disposable one-liners this way; a language model does it reflexively. The second half is the timing -- when a step fails, a specific corrective payload follows in tens of seconds, addressing the actual cause rather than retrying blindly. Both halves are observable in the delivered payload itself, not inferred from behaviour.
logic: Where an application exposes a code-execution or validation endpoint, retain the submitted payload rather than only the fact of execution, and read it. Two signals sit in the text: commentary explaining intent in prose, and a corrective payload issued within roughly a minute of a failure that names the specific cause. Neither is a rule that fires on its own -- this is a triage and attribution aid that tells you what the operator was trying to achieve, in their words, and whether a person or an agent was driving.
caveat: Retaining submitted payloads means retaining whatever a caller sent, which on a public endpoint includes other people's data; scope the retention before enabling it. The rate marker needs a local baseline -- what counts as above human rate depends on the endpoint -- and no bound is supplied here because inventing one would be worse than leaving it open. Self-narration is also trivially suppressible once operators know it is read, so treat its absence as no evidence either way.

name: The files a backup does not bring back
description: Mass encryption or renaming of machine-learning artefacts: model checkpoints and serialised weights, vector indices, embedding stores and columnar training sets. The detection is ordinary ransomware detection; the reason to separate it is the impact assessment. Restoring these from a backup returns a stale model, and the gap between the snapshot and the attack is a retraining run rather than a copy. Where the training data sits on the same host, recovery is blocked until the data is reconstructed first.
logic: Watch directories holding model and dataset formats for a burst of writes that rename to a single new extension, or that rewrite file contents without the file count changing. Treat the artefact type as a severity input rather than as the trigger: the same burst against documents and against model weights are the same detection and very different incidents. An inventory of where model artefacts actually live is the precondition, and most estates do not have one.

markers.note: the artefact types that make this different from document ransomware

caveat: Training pipelines legitimately write checkpoints in bursts, so volume alone is a false positive generator; the rename-to-one-new-extension shape is what separates them. No count or window is given because both have to be measured against how the estate's own training jobs behave. A build that encrypts regions of a file rather than the whole file will not change file size much, so size-delta checks are not a reliable confirmation.

name: A second door into the same service that the audit log does not watch
description: A cloud service reachable through more than one API surface, where one of them does not produce audit records. Console-only, undocumented and legacy endpoints are the usual cases: the documented service logs every call, the parallel one logs none, and the two return the same data. Reconnaissance carried out through the unlogged surface leaves an account looking untouched.
logic: Compare what the provider's audit log claims a principal did against an independent record of the same window -- network egress to the provider's API endpoints, console session activity, or billing and quota movement. A principal whose network layer shows sustained API conversation while the audit log shows a handful of calls or none is using a surface the log does not cover. The inverse framing is the cheaper inventory question: enumerate the API hostnames and service targets your estate actually calls, and check each one appears in the audit log at all.

markers.note: X-Amz-Target for the iamadmin surface; the logged IAM service uses AWSIdentityManagementV20100508
console-backing paths sitting beside the documented one

caveat: The specific endpoint that motivated this pattern was fixed by the provider in October 2022, so hunting for that one string finds nothing. The class is what recurs: every provider carries console-backing and legacy API surfaces, they are not enumerable from documentation, and their audit coverage is a provider decision that can change without notice. Treat an audit log as a claim about the surfaces it covers rather than about the account.

name: Privilege parked where the reviewer cannot see it or undo it
description: Directory platforms offer scoped administrative containers with two properties that are protective by design and useful to an intruder: membership can be hidden from anyone outside the container, and members can be made modifiable only by principals scoped to that container, so tenant-level administrators cannot alter them. Privilege placed inside one is concealed from a permissions review and survives an eviction attempt made from the tenant level.
logic: Alert on the creation of a scoped administrative container, on a container being switched to restricted-management or hidden-membership, and on a role assignment scoped to one. Each is rare and administratively deliberate in most tenants. For the standing question -- what privilege exists that a tenant-level review would miss -- enumerate scoped role assignments through the directory API rather than reading the portal, because the portal reflects the concealment the feature provides.

value: Add member to role outside of PIM (permanent)

markers.expr: container_visibility set to HiddenMembership or management set to Restricted

caveat: This is documented, supported behaviour and not a flaw, so it will fire on legitimate hardening -- protecting break-glass and executive accounts is exactly what the feature is for. The alert is worth keeping because the rate is low and the consequence of missing it is an eviction that silently fails. A Global Administrator can reverse all of it, so the response is knowable; finding it is the hard part.

name: Mining spread thin across services nobody watches
description: Rather than raising instances in the obvious compute service, the operator runs workloads across several second-tier services -- build, deployment, container and notebook platforms that each accept arbitrary code. Two things follow: the request never trips the quota approval that a burst of ordinary instances would, and eradication requires finding and killing a workload in every service separately rather than terminating a fleet.
logic: Two signals, and the second is the one that survives. First, workload creation in a service the account has no history of using, by a principal or role created in the same session. Second, and the reliable one: cost or compute consumption rising in a service whose resource count has not, or across several services at once with no matching change record. Pair either with egress to mining infrastructure where network telemetry reaches these services.

markers.expr: service_spend_rate_increase without matching resource_count_increase; the bound is unresolved and must be measured against the account's own baseline

caveat: Data science and platform teams legitimately start using a new service for the first time, and a first-use alert alone is noisy in an account under active development. The multi-service simultaneity and the spend-without-resources shape are what separate this from adoption. The spend bound is not supplied here because it has to be measured against the account's own baseline; a fabricated threshold would be trusted and would be wrong.

name: The state file the pipeline needs is also a credential store
description: Infrastructure-as-code tools keep a state file recording what they manage, and that file holds every attribute of every resource in clear text, including generated passwords, access keys and connection strings. It has to be reachable by whatever runs the pipeline, so it commonly sits in shared object storage. Read access to that bucket is therefore read access to the credentials for everything the pipeline built, frequently including accounts other than the one being read from.
logic: Alert on a read of a known state-file object by a principal outside the pipeline identity that maintains it -- the set of legitimate readers is small, stable and knowable, which is what makes this worth alerting rather than hunting. The inventory question that precedes it: locate every state file in object storage, confirm object-level audit logging is enabled on those buckets, and confirm the credentials inside them are not still valid.
caveat: Object-level reads in cloud storage are not logged by default on any major provider, so this detection frequently cannot fire on the estate that most needs it -- the marker asserting object-level logging is enabled is there to make that dependency explicit rather than to be tested at query time. Where it is off, the honest answer is the inventory half: find the state files and rotate what is in them.

name: Five permission systems, no single answer to who can touch this
description: A major cloud platform grants authority through several systems that do not share identifiers, data models or logs -- directory roles, resource-manager role assignments, API permissions held by applications, resource-local access policies, and delegated administration. An intruder who acquires authority in one and pivots to another is not concealed by any single evasion; they are concealed because a reviewer almost never looks at more than one at a time, and no product joins them.
logic: Not a query so much as a standing requirement on the answer. After any identity compromise in a multi-plane cloud platform, the question 'what can this principal still reach' has to be asked once per permission plane and the answers combined by hand. Enumerate directory role assignments, resource-manager assignments at every scope from root to resource, application permissions and consent grants, resource-local access policies, and any delegated administration relationship. A containment that clears one plane and reports success is incomplete.

markers.expr: post_incident_permission_review covers all of: directory_roles, resource_manager_assignments, application_api_permissions, resource_local_access_policies, delegated_administration
principal_identifiers_reconciled_across_planes rather than compared by display name

caveat: The planes use different identifiers for the same principal, so a review that joins on display name will silently miss assignments. This is an analytical constraint rather than a detection, and it is recorded because the alternative -- assuming eviction from the directory plane is eviction -- was observed to leave root-level resource access and a hold on the telemetry pipeline intact.

name: A throwaway hostname the provider gave the attacker for free
description: Several cloud providers issue a working, publicly resolvable, TLS-terminated hostname under their own domain to anyone who runs a client, with no account, no payment and no registration record. The operator gets a host with the provider's reputation, a valid certificate and no WHOIS to age, and it disappears when the process stops. Domain-age heuristics, registrar analysis and newly-registered-domain feeds all return nothing on these, because the parent domain is years old and reputable.
logic: Resolution of, or a request to, a hostname under a provider's ephemeral-hostname domain. These namespaces are enumerable and small in number, so the workable control is an allow list per namespace: decide whether your estate has any legitimate use of each, and alert on everything if it does not. Where there is legitimate use, the discriminator is the request context -- a hostname of this shape arriving as a link in mail, or serving a file rather than an application, is not what the sanctioned use looks like.

markers.note: the provider generates a random multi-word label, so the hostname is unguessable and unrepeatable

markers.expr: hostname first seen and last seen within a short window, with no prior resolution history

caveat: Developers use exactly these namespaces to share work in progress and to receive webhooks during testing, so on an engineering estate this alerts on real work. It is still worth the noise on the mail path, where a link into one of these namespaces has no legitimate business explanation. Do not attempt to age these hostnames or look them up in a registrar: the parent domain is old and reputable, and the label carries no registration record at all.

name: A role that trusts every account there is
description: Cloud roles are assumable by whoever the role's trust policy names. Where that policy uses a wildcard in place of a specific account, any principal in any account of that provider can assume the role, and the only thing standing between an outsider and those privileges is knowing the account identifier and the role name. Neither is a secret: account identifiers appear in ordinary integration documentation and role names are guessable from a wordlist of common ones.
logic: This is answered against configuration rather than against events. Enumerate every role in every account and read its trust policy, flagging any that names a wildcard principal, or that names an external account no longer in a business relationship with you. The provider warns about the wildcard form and still permits it, so it exists in real estates. On the event side, a role assumption whose calling account is outside your organisation is worth an alert wherever it is not an expected third-party integration.

markers.expr: role trust policy Principal contains a wildcard rather than an enumerated account or principal
assuming account identifier not in organisation accounts and not in approved third-party integrations
burst of failed role assumption attempts against non-existent role names, indicating name enumeration

caveat: Cross-account trust is ordinary and widely used, particularly by organisations running many accounts and by third-party tooling, so the finding is the wildcard and the unknown counterparty rather than the cross-account grant itself. Note that unsuccessful assumption attempts against role names that do not exist are the enumeration phase and are visible before any successful access; whether they reach your logs at all depends on where the attempt was made.

name: The sync server is a door between two directories
description: Hybrid identity requires a server holding privileged credentials in both the on-premises directory and the cloud tenant so it can synchronise authentication material between them. That server is therefore a single host whose compromise converts a domain compromise into a tenant compromise, and the reverse. Where the deployment also enables seamless single sign-on, a shared account exists in the on-premises directory whose key can be used to mint tickets for cloud authentication.
logic: Treat the synchronisation host as tier-zero and alert on interactive logon to it, on credential-access tooling running on it, and on its service accounts authenticating from anywhere other than itself. In the cloud tenant, the synchronisation service account performing operations outside directory synchronisation -- role assignment, application consent, credential addition -- is the crossing event and is worth alerting on its own.

markers.expr: interactive or remote interactive logon to the directory synchronisation host by an account outside its administration set

markers.note: conventional prefixes for directory synchronisation service accounts

markers.expr: synchronisation service account authenticating from a host other than the synchronisation server
synchronisation service principal performs an operation other than directory synchronisation in the cloud tenant
seamless single sign-on computer account present in the on-premises directory and its password not rotated within policy

caveat: The synchronisation account authenticates constantly and at volume by design, so a naive rule on its activity is unusable; the discriminators are the source host and the operation type, both of which are narrow and stable. This is a configuration risk rather than a defect -- the privilege is what makes synchronisation work -- so the durable control is treating the host as tier-zero rather than detecting its abuse.

name: A name still pointing at an address you gave back
description: Cloud addresses are allocated from a shared pool and returned to it when an instance is destroyed or re-addressed. A DNS record left behind still resolves, and whoever next receives that address from the pool receives the name's traffic with it -- including anything the name is trusted for, such as certificate issuance, cookie scope or an allow-listed origin. Reclaiming a specific address is a matter of repeatedly requesting addresses until the wanted one appears.
logic: Reconcile two lists rather than watch a stream: every address currently allocated to accounts you own, and every address your DNS records resolve to. Any record resolving to a provider address absent from the first list is a dangling record. The reconciliation is only sound with complete coverage of your own accounts -- partial account coverage produces false findings on addresses you do in fact hold, which is the single most common way this check is got wrong.

markers.expr: dns A record resolves to an address in a cloud provider range that is not allocated to any account under your control
account enumeration for the reconciliation is complete, so an unmatched address is genuinely unowned
certificate issued for a hostname whose address changed ownership within the preceding window

caveat: The check is worthless without complete coverage of your own cloud accounts, and it degrades silently rather than failing: an unenumerated account makes its own addresses look hostile. Run it against a definitive account list and treat gaps in that list as gaps in the finding. Records for hostnames that were never used still matter, because the trust attached to a name outlives the service behind it.

name: Your build runs where the provider keeps its own keys
description: A managed build or static-hosting service exists to execute code its customers supply. Where the execution environment also holds the provider's own operational credentials -- source-control tokens, platform API keys, credentials for the cloud the build platform itself runs on -- a customer who obtains command execution in the build step reaches material belonging to the provider and to every other tenant, not merely their own. The container is routinely treated as the security boundary and routinely is not one.
logic: For a provider, the question is what an arbitrary build step can reach: enumerate the environment variables, mounted files, metadata endpoints and network destinations available from inside a build, and confirm none of them is provider-owned. For a consumer of such a service, the question is different and mostly a supply-chain one: what could the build platform's compromise do to you, given the repository access you granted it and the deployment rights it holds over your site.

markers.expr: build execution context can read credentials scoped beyond the tenant whose build is running
build container can reach the platform's instance metadata endpoint or node agent API
build user can read the orchestration scripts that define the build
granted source-control authorisation is repository-scoped rather than organisation-wide

caveat: This is a design question rather than an alert, and for most readers it is somebody else's design. The consumer-side action is real though: the authorisation granted to a build platform is usually broader than the single repository being built, and narrowing it bounds what a compromise of the platform can take. Sandbox hardening reduces the blast radius without closing the class -- a re-architected platform in the case behind this pattern still exposed source-control secrets through an orchestrator node API.

name: A service-to-service RPC framework carrying the command channel
description: Operators have begun building command channels on general-purpose remote procedure call frameworks -- gRPC over HTTP/2, or WebSockets -- rather than on the HTTP request-response shapes that command-and-control detection was written for. These frameworks normally carry internal service-to-service traffic inside a datacentre, so the same protocol leaving a user workstation for an external host is out of place in a way the protocol itself never looks.
logic: The discriminator is placement rather than protocol. A long-lived HTTP/2 stream or WebSocket upgrade from an endpoint in the user population to an external host is worth hunting, because these frameworks belong between services and not between a laptop and the internet. Where the process is visible, a binary that is not a browser or a known client speaking HTTP/2 with the framework's content type narrows it further.

markers.expr: websocket upgrade or long-lived HTTP/2 stream from a user-population endpoint to an external host
initiating process is a browser or an approved RPC client
session duration far exceeds the estate's normal HTTP session distribution

caveat: Estates that run modern application platforms carry a lot of legitimate traffic of this shape, so this is a hunt on the user population rather than a rule on the whole estate. The framework can also be told to obfuscate its own protocol definition, which removes the method names and leaves only the transport shape -- so anchor on placement and duration and not on readable method names.

name: The user let them in with the tool that shipped with the operating system
description: The remote-access step of a social engineering intrusion increasingly uses the remote assistance utility built into the operating system rather than a tool the operator has to install. Nothing is dropped, nothing is unsigned, no allow list is violated, and the session is authorised by the victim typing a code they were read over a call. Detection built on unapproved remote-access software does not see it, because the software is approved and already present.
logic: Alert on the built-in assistance client running at all where your service desk does not use it, which is the cheap and decisive case. Where it is used, the shape that matters is what follows: a remote assistance session, then within minutes a scripting engine gathering host and domain information, then a binary written to a user-writable path. The session by itself is support; the sequence is not.

markers.expr: remote assistance process started within minutes of an external chat or voice call to the same user
scripting engine performing host or domain discovery within 15 minutes of the assistance session starting
built-in remote assistance is a sanctioned support channel on this estate

caveat: Where the service desk genuinely uses the built-in tool the process marker alone is unusable and the sequence carries the detection. The durable control is not a detection at all: decide which remote support tool is sanctioned, block the rest at policy, and tell users that support will never call them first -- the whole technique depends on the victim believing an unsolicited approach.

name: Your second factor is only as private as the company that posts it
description: A one-time passcode delivered by message passes through a third-party communications provider, and it is legible in that provider's own console. An operator who holds a stolen password and access to the delivery provider can trigger the challenge and then read the code, without touching the identity provider or the victim's device at all. The factor is defeated at a company the account holder has no relationship with.
logic: Two things, and the first is an inventory question rather than a query: know which third parties can read your authentication material, and hold them to the same access standard as your identity provider. For detection, the shape at your own edge is a successful authentication whose password and second factor were satisfied from sources that do not agree -- a passcode consumed without any corresponding delivery to the user's device, or a run of challenges triggered for accounts whose passwords are already known to be exposed.

markers.expr: message-delivered passcode challenge triggered for an account whose credential appears in a known exposure set
passcode consumed successfully with no corresponding user interaction on the enrolled device
third parties able to read authentication material are enumerated and access-reviewed

caveat: Neither marker is available at the identity provider alone, which is the difficulty: the interception happens somewhere you do not log. The honest answer is mostly architectural -- a passcode delivered by message is a shared secret in transit through somebody else's system, and moving to an authenticator bound to the origin removes the intermediary rather than monitoring it.

name: The phishing page checks whether you are worth serving
description: Mature phishing operations no longer serve their page to whoever asks. A chain of gates runs first -- a challenge that proves an interactive browser, redirect hops through link shorteners, and a small serverless function that decides which lure to load for which target -- so that automated crawlers, sandboxes and scanners receive something harmless and only the intended victim sees the phishing page. Every layer is a legitimate, widely used service, which is what makes the chain cheap and hard to block.
logic: The gating defeats the check rather than the user, so a scanner reporting a link as clean is not evidence. Detect on the chain instead of the destination: a link in mail that redirects more than a couple of times before resolving, a landing domain on a low-cost disposable top-level domain, and a serverless-namespace hostname loaded from that page. Any one is weak and the combination is not.

markers.note: low-cost disposable namespaces observed in this class of operation
the serverless gatekeeper the page loads

markers.expr: mail-borne link traverses more than two redirects before its final host
interactive challenge served before any content, on a first visit from a mail-borne link
final host reached through a shared reverse proxy so its address is not the operator's

caveat: Disposable top-level domains carry legitimate traffic too and the serverless namespaces carry a great deal of it, so no single marker here is actionable and this must be correlated. The most useful consequence is not a detection at all: because the gates defeat automated analysis by design, a clean verdict from a link scanner on this shape of URL should be treated as no verdict.

name: The log line is the shell command
description: A component builds a log message by concatenating attacker-supplied input into a string, and then hands that string to a system-execution call rather than to a writer. Writing the log is what runs the command. Because the path runs on the failure branch, the attacker never needs valid credentials -- a rejected authentication attempt is enough, and the parameter that carries the payload is the one the reader thinks of as merely a username.
logic: Look in the authentication parameter rather than in the request body: a username field carrying shell metacharacters, command substitution or a pipe, submitted to a management or RPC endpoint on a device. On the device side, where any process telemetry exists at all, a shell child of the web or configuration service around the time of a failed login is the confirmation. On the network side, a burst of failed authentications from one source where the usernames are not plausible usernames is the shape.

markers.expr: authentication failure whose submitted username contains shell metacharacters
shell process parented by the device web or configuration service within seconds of a failed authentication

caveat: Most embedded devices ship no process telemetry at all, so the device-side confirmation is usually unavailable and the whole detection rests on seeing the request. That means it fails silently for anything reached over an encrypted management interface the estate does not terminate. Where the device cannot be observed, the honest control is patching and network segmentation rather than detection.

name: Exploited after the patch and before anyone said why
description: A vendor ships a fix, the advisory says little, and the technical detail follows weeks or months later. Operators read the difference between the two firmware builds and have a working exploit inside that window, so exploitation begins against a population that has been told a patch exists but not that it is urgent. Detection content and public indicators arrive with the disclosure, which is to say after the exploitation.
logic: This changes what a patch date means rather than adding a query. Treat the release of firmware for an internet-reachable device as the start of an exposure window, not the end of one, and prioritise on reachability and patch latency rather than on whether an advisory has been published or a proof of concept has appeared.
