The corresponding hunt is retrospective: when detail is eventually published, re-run the indicators back to the patch date rather than to the disclosure date.

markers.expr: internet-reachable device running firmware older than the most recent vendor release
retrospective hunt window for a new indicator starts at the vendor patch date, not the disclosure date
device population has no telemetry route that would show exploitation if it happened

caveat: The window is invisible from the outside: there is no advisory to alert on, no identifier to scan for and no public indicator to match, which is what makes patch latency the only lever. It also inverts a common prioritisation rule -- an identifier with no public proof of concept is not therefore lower risk on this class of device, because the patch is the proof of concept.

name: Nearly all of it is scanning, and the scanning is not the story
description: An internet-facing device population receives so much automated traffic that unfiltered counting describes the internet rather than the estate. In a measured 90-day window across eleven exposed devices, 97% of all flagged interactions were management-protocol requests and 95% went to a single device, almost all of them fingerprinting probes at the root of the object tree. Removing that one category cut sixty million events to three and a half million and changed which devices looked most attacked.
logic: Classify and set aside the automated floor before drawing any conclusion about what is being targeted. Fingerprinting probes at the root of the management object tree are identifiable and separable; so are credential-stuffing bursts on remote-shell protocols. What is left is the small residue worth reading, and on this measurement two thirds of it went to the perimeter devices rather than to the exposed control devices everyone worries about.

markers.expr: management protocol requests to object identifier tree roots classified and excluded before ranking targets
remote shell and terminal authentication attempts separated from application layer requests before ranking
residual event count after removing the automated floor is what the target ranking is computed on

caveat: Deleting the floor rather than classifying it loses the ability to notice when its composition changes, which is itself an early signal that a new botnet has added an exploit. Keep the counts and drop them from the ranking, not from the record. The specific proportions here are one publisher's honeypot estate over one window and should not be transplanted as thresholds.

name: The agent is the parent, so the ancestry looks fine
description: A signed, sanctioned coding agent is trusted on a developer workstation to open shells, edit files, call interfaces and install helpers. Anything it is induced to run inherits that trust: the process ancestry terminates in an approved application, the immediate child is usually an ordinary shell rather than the agent executing a binary itself, and every individual step is a normal developer action. Detection built on parent-process reputation or on unapproved-binary lists resolves to approved and stops.
logic: Stop asking whether the parent is approved and start asking what the subtree did. Under a coding-agent ancestry, alert on the combination rather than the components: an outbound tunnel or ephemeral-broker hostname, credentialed HTTP to that hostname, and a persistence mechanism written in the same session. Individually each is ordinary developer work. Arriving together under one agent session within a short window is not, and the sequence is what an analyst can act on.

markers.note: the agent is the ancestor, not usually the immediate parent

markers.expr: process ancestry includes a coding agent and the immediate parent is a shell
same agent session contains an ephemeral tunnel hostname, credentialed HTTP to it, and a persistence write

markers.note: user-scope persistence written in-session

markers.expr: agent durable memory or project configuration file written by a process that is not the agent's own writer

caveat: This fires on legitimate work, and honestly so: developers do publish a local service through a tunnel to demonstrate it, and agents do install helpers. The publisher's own framing is the right one -- treat it as high severity even when it looks like informal operations rather than confirmed malware, because the outcome is a local administrative application exposed to the internet either way. Validation is the hard part, not detection: trusted parents, dual-use destinations and a serious outcome all arrive in the same alert.

name: Opening the repository is executing the repository
description: Editors and coding agents read per-project configuration from files inside the repository, and some of those keys run a command on an event the user does not think of as running anything -- opening the folder, or starting an agent session. A commit that adds such a key turns cloning or opening the project into code execution, with no build step, no install and no dependency resolution involved. Where the operator holds a token with write access, the same keys can be committed across many branches and many repositories at once.
logic: Two places to look and both are cheap. In the repository, treat the editor and agent configuration paths as executable content: any commit touching them deserves review the way a build script does, and an inventory sweep across your own repositories will find planted ones. On the endpoint, a runtime process spawned as a child of an editor or agent immediately after a project is opened, running a script from inside the project's own configuration directory, is the execution moment.

markers.expr: commit adds or modifies an editor or agent configuration key that executes a command on an open or session-start event
script interpreter spawned by an editor or coding agent running a file from the project's own configuration directory
the same configuration file appears across many branches or repositories with a common author

caveat: These keys exist for legitimate project setup and teams use them, so the file's presence is not the finding -- its arrival is. The inventory half matters more than the detection half here, because a planted hook sits dormant until somebody opens the project, which may be weeks later and on a machine with different telemetry.

name: The address is not in the malware, it is in a contract anybody can read
description: Rather than carrying a command-and-control domain, the payload queries a public distributed ledger for the current endpoint at run time, reaching it through several independent gateway providers. The operator rotates infrastructure by updating a ledger entry, without touching the payload and without any of the deployed copies needing to change. Domain blocklists and hash-based hunting both age immediately, and the lookup traffic goes to reputable gateway services rather than to anything suspicious.
logic: The resolvable artefact is the lookup rather than the destination. A development workstation or build agent making requests to distributed-ledger gateway providers, when nothing in its stated purpose involves that technology, is worth an alert on its own, because the population that legitimately does this is small and enumerable. The endpoint it retrieves changes; the fact that it asked does not.

markers.note: common ledger gateway providers used as the lookup path

markers.expr: host outside the approved set makes requests to distributed ledger gateway providers
ledger gateway request followed within minutes by a first-seen outbound destination
process performing the lookup is a package manager, runtime or build tool rather than a wallet application

caveat: Estates doing genuine distributed-ledger work will match on the gateway markers and need an allow list; for everyone else the population is near zero, which is what makes this cheap. Note the fallback path matters as much as the primary one -- where the ledger lookup fails, the same payload searched a public code-hosting service's commit history for the endpoint instead, so blocking the gateways alone does not close it.

name: The trigger that runs a stranger's code as you
description: A continuous integration trigger that executes pull request code in the base repository's security context, giving code from an untrusted fork a writable token and access to secrets.
logic: Nothing is exploited here and no version is vulnerable; the trigger behaves as documented. The mistake is pairing it with a checkout of the pull request head, which turns a documented convenience into arbitrary code execution with the repository's own credentials. Because the exposure lives in the workflow definition, the cheapest detection is an inventory question asked of source control -- which workflows carry the privileged trigger, and of those, which check out the untrusted head -- and it is answerable without collecting a single log. At run time the discriminator is a build job reaching for credential material it was never handed: other processes' environment blocks, the instance metadata endpoint, the repository secrets API. A run whose head commit exists on no branch of the repository is the third leg, and it is what separates a fork's pull request from ordinary internal work.
caveat: Requiring approval before a workflow runs for an outside contributor removes this outright and is worth more than every marker below it. Where the trigger is genuinely needed -- labelling, greeting, triage -- it does not need a checkout of the contributor's code, and splitting those two apart is the fix. Watch for the payload being placed in files the build executes anyway rather than in the workflow file: review attention goes to the workflow, and a test configuration or a build manifest is the quieter place to put it.
derived_from: Wiz Research and Datadog Security Labs public reporting, cited per record

name: Exfiltration that never leaves the building
description: Credential material compressed, encoded and printed into pipeline output, using the build log as the exfiltration channel instead of an outbound connection.
logic: This is the shape that defeats egress monitoring. Where a repository is public its build log is public too, so an operator who can get secrets printed has published them without ever connecting to infrastructure anyone can block or attribute. The material has to survive printing, so it arrives base64-encoded and usually compressed first, and because a build log is long it is typically framed by a fixed marker string so the operator can find it again. Long encoded runs bracketed by a repeated marker are therefore the observable, and the absence of any outbound connection is not evidence of a clean run.
caveat: A hunt input, not an alert: build logs carry base64 legitimately for certificates, encoded fixtures and image digests, and a rule on encoding alone will not survive contact with a real estate. Treat a hit on a public repository as disclosure that has already happened -- rotate first, investigate second.
derived_from: Wiz Research public reporting, cited per record

name: The pull request title was part of the command
description: An attacker-controllable field from the triggering event expanded into a pipeline shell command by template substitution, before the shell parses the line.
logic: The ordering is what makes this work: template expansion happens first, so the event text is not an argument the shell receives but source the shell parses. A pull request title, a branch name and a comment body are all writable by anyone who can open a pull request, which on a public repository is everyone. Because the flaw lives in the workflow file, the whole class is enumerable with a search across the workflow directory for an expansion of an untrusted field inside a script block -- far cheaper and far more complete than any runtime rule. Keep the runtime markers for the estate you cannot fix this week: a build step whose process tree suddenly differs from its own history, carrying metacharacters that came in as event text.
caveat: Binding the value to an environment variable and referencing the variable in the script removes this outright, so the honest answer to 'how do we detect it' is usually 'fix it instead'. Detection earns its place only where the workflow estate is too large or too federated to change at once. Do not read a clean scanner run as absence: published measurement shows scanners differ sharply on this class.
derived_from: Datadog Security Labs public reporting, cited per record

name: The issue body told the agent what to do
description: Untrusted event context reaching a language agent's prompt or its inputs inside a pipeline, where the agent holds tools that write, execute or call an API.
logic: This is the pipeline script-injection class with the shell replaced by an agent, and it is worse in one specific way: the agent's output can reach a later step, so the place the untrusted text enters and the place it executes need not be the same step, and reviewing either one in isolation shows nothing wrong. Ask the flow question in source control -- can an outside party's text reach the prompt, and can the agent's output reach anything that executes or writes. Where both hold, guard wording in the prompt does not save it. At run time, watch for tool calls whose effect is out of family for the workflow during runs triggered from outside.
caveat: Do not credit prompt-level guard text as a control. The measurable fix is the tool grant: an agent summarising an issue does not need a shell, and an agent that has one will eventually be asked to use it. Treat the runtime markers as reasoned rather than observed -- the source is static analysis with coordinated disclosure, not intrusion reporting -- and weight the flow markers accordingly.
derived_from: Peer-reviewed and preprint academic measurement, cited per record

name: A clean scan for something the scanner never looked at
description: Treating a workflow security scanner's silence as assurance for a weakness class that scanner does not test, when published measurement shows coverage varies sharply between tools.
logic: Not a detection and not an attack: an assurance check that belongs beside every workflow-hardening recommendation. Independent evaluation of nine scanners over 2,722 workflows found them differing in both what they look for and how much they report, so 'the scanner is clean' resolves to a statement about one tool's scope. Build the matrix explicitly -- weakness class down one axis, deployed tool across the other -- and mark every empty row unmeasured. The classes most worth putting on that axis are the ones this corpus carries records for, because those are the ones being used.
caveat: Resist turning this into a scanner league table; the measurements are of scope, not quality, and a narrow tool that is honest about its scope is more useful than a broad one that is not. The output of this check is a list of unmeasured classes, and that list is the input to deciding what to detect at run time.
derived_from: Peer-reviewed and preprint academic measurement, cited per record

name: The filter said contains where it meant equals
description: An authorisation decision made with an unanchored expression, so any identifier containing an approved value is accepted, combined with sequentially assigned identifiers that make a qualifying value obtainable on demand.
logic: Two ordinary decisions combine into a bypass. An expression written without start and end anchors is a containment test, and where it gates an authorisation decision it accepts every superstring of an approved value. Sequential identifier assignment then guarantees such superstrings exist and makes their arrival predictable, so the attacker does not need to guess -- they sample the current range, wait, and register in bulk. This generalises well beyond one build service: any place an allowlist is expressed as a pattern rather than a set membership test deserves the same read. The check is static and complete, which is rare enough to be worth doing before any detection is written.
caveat: The anchoring check is the control; the behavioural markers are for estates that cannot audit every integration filter at once. Do not lose the second lesson in the first: the bypass only became repository control because a long-lived, broadly scoped token was sitting in the build environment where a dependency could read it. Fixing the expression and leaving the token is half a remediation.
derived_from: Wiz Research public reporting, cited per record

name: One job, three credential stores
description: A compromised pipeline action collecting credentials from runner process memory, the cloud instance metadata service and the checked-out workspace within a single job, then posting an encrypted archive outbound.
logic: Build hosts are noisy and most single indicators here have honest explanations, so the rule has to be built on co-occurrence inside one job. Reading another process's memory has no legitimate pipeline use at all and is the strongest leg. The metadata call is ordinary alone and damning beside it. Searching the workspace for chat webhook URLs is the third and the most specific to this operator's tradecraft, because a webhook is a durable credential that survives token rotation. The exfiltration leg should be written on shape -- an encrypted archive leaving a build host for a domain the estate has not seen -- and never on the specific domain, which in the reported case was a misspelling of the vendor's own and will differ next time.
caveat: The fallback exfiltration path is the detail worth carrying forward: when upload failed the malware wrote the archive into a new repository in the victim's own account. That is trivial to look for, it is durable evidence rather than transient network state, and almost nobody watches for it. Treat the instance metadata service as a credential store that needs the same controls as any other -- restricting role credentials available to build roles limits what this collects regardless of whether the rule fires.
derived_from: StepSecurity and Sysdig public reporting, cited per record

name: The tag points somewhere the history does not go
description: A pipeline action's published tag resolving to a commit that is not reachable from any branch of its source repository, the durable trace left by tag rewriting.
logic: Every reported instance of this class -- across several distinct actions and at least two separate operators -- left the same trace, because rewriting a tag to point at a fork or an orphan commit necessarily produces a reference that the source repository's branch graph does not contain. Resolving each external action reference to a commit and testing branch membership therefore catches the compromise without needing to understand the payload, without endpoint telemetry, and after the fact: where the actor force-pushed the original commit back to hide the change, the consumer's own run record still names the commit it actually executed. This is the cheapest high-value check in the area.
caveat: Pinning to a commit digest defeats substitution and is the right control, but it does not defend against the pinned artefact itself being malicious, and it shifts the burden to keeping pins current. The repointing marker needs a stored baseline to compare against, so the inventory has to be taken before it is useful -- which is an argument for taking it now rather than after an advisory names an action you use. A 2026 result on signed-commit malleability sharpens this rather than overturning it: an actor without the signing key can mint a second verified commit with an identical tree and a different hash, so a hash is not a canonical name for content and hash denylisting is evadable. Pinning still stops substitution of different content, and the branch membership check here still fires, because a malleated commit is reachable from no branch either. See obs-generic-signed-commit-hash-is-malleable-without-the-signing-key.
derived_from: StepSecurity, Sysdig and Wiz Research public reporting, cited per record

name: Correctly signed, and not what the source says
description: A malicious package version published with a valid build provenance attestation, because the pipeline that signed it was instructed by a commit that never passed review.
logic: Provenance and signing establish that a named pipeline produced an artefact. They establish nothing about whether that pipeline was given honest instructions, and an actor who can push to a branch the pipeline builds from inherits the signing identity along with it. So the question to ask is not 'is this signed' but 'does the signed thing match the source at the commit it names, and did that commit arrive legitimately'. Orphan commits and oddly named branches are the delivery shape reported here, and a workflow diff that newly asks for identity-token write permission is the single highest-signal small change in this whole area. Where payloads are uniquely encrypted per infection, hash indicators are dead on arrival and the manifest diff is what remains.
caveat: The failure mode this pattern exists to prevent is a defender crediting provenance verification as coverage. It verified correctly throughout the reported campaign. Branch protection that actually applies to maintainers, and review on workflow permission changes, are the controls that would have bitten; detection here is the fallback. Note the attacker did not need to defeat signing, only to be upstream of it.
derived_from: Wiz Research public reporting, cited per record

name: The check was rewritten to say yes
description: Authentication processing files on a portal or appliance modified so that one attacker-chosen value always authenticates, producing successes and no failures.
logic: Most multi-factor bypasses in this corpus steal something, replay something or exploit an enrolment path, and all of them leave a trail in authentication events. This one leaves none, because the authenticator was edited to accept a constant: every login is a clean success from a valid account with a valid second factor. Volume-based, velocity-based and impossible-travel logic will never fire. The detection therefore has to move off the event stream and onto the filesystem -- integrity monitoring of the authentication handlers themselves, which is where the durable change has to live. The behavioural corroboration worth pairing with it is a second factor succeeding for an account whose enrolled factor has no history of use, and a portal whose success rate climbs without any matching change in failures.
caveat: The common failure is an integrity baseline that covers vendor binaries but not the script and configuration files that actually implement authentication, which is exactly where this change lands. Check the scope of the baseline before recording this as covered. Note also that a password reset, a credential rotation and a forced re-enrolment all leave the backdoor working, so incident response that stops at credentials has not evicted it.
derived_from: Joint government advisory, cited per record

name: The gateway kept a copy
description: A remote-access appliance's traffic-handling configuration altered so it collects credentials and session material for an internal portal passing through it.
logic: An appliance that terminates or inspects traffic is, by construction, in a position to keep what passes through it, and an actor with administrative access can turn that capability on without deploying any malware. Because no binary changes and no process is spawned, endpoint detection sees nothing and the appliance keeps working normally. The evidence is a configuration diff against a known-good baseline, which means the baseline has to exist before the incident. The downstream tell is session material being presented from an address that never performed the authentication that created it.
caveat: The reporting gives the effect, not the vendor-specific setting, so this is a question to put to your own appliance rather than a rule to deploy as written: which configuration here could capture traffic, is a change to it logged, and does anyone read that log. An estate that cannot answer the third part does not have this covered regardless of the first two.
derived_from: Joint government advisory, cited per record

name: The bill is the breach report
description: Stolen model API credentials monetised by third parties, detected either as consumption departing from a tenant baseline or, earlier, as the removal of the limits that would have capped it.
logic: A model API key is an unusual credential in one specific way: abusing it costs the victim money continuously rather than granting a discrete access, so the exposure is metered and the discovery is usually an invoice. That makes consumption analytics genuinely useful here in a way they are not for most credentials -- but only against a per-tenant baseline, since absolute thresholds are meaningless across tenants of different sizes. Reach for the control plane first regardless. Removing a billing limit, disabling a usage alert, minting a key outside the provisioning process and turning off logging are rare, deliberate and logged, and every one of them precedes the spend that would eventually raise the alarm.
caveat: Published proxy addresses and user-agent strings age out fast and should not carry this rule. Note the ordering argument in full: a spending ceiling is cheaper than any detection here, bounds the loss whether or not anyone is watching, and converts the attacker's next necessary step into a high-signal administrative event. Detection that ignores the availability of a hard limit is doing the expensive half of the job.
derived_from: Unit 42 public reporting, cited per record

name: The warning was deleted before it was read
description: Platform-generated password reset, factor change or security notices removed from the account holder's mailbox shortly after the identity change that produced them.
logic: A factor-change notification is an unusual control: it reaches the one person who can immediately tell that the change was not theirs, and it works at three in the morning with nobody watching a console. That makes deleting it a necessary step for an operator who has taken over an account, and a deliberate one. The detection is a correlation rather than an event -- an identity change in the provider, and a delete of the resulting notice from the affected mailbox within minutes -- and both halves are ordinarily recorded. Watch also for inbox rules that file or delete such notices in advance, which is the same intent expressed as configuration rather than as an action.
caveat: The remediation is more interesting than the detection: if factor-change alerts also go somewhere the account holder's session cannot reach -- a security mailbox, a ticket, a push to a separate channel -- then deleting the copy in the inbox accomplishes nothing and the attacker's step becomes pure signal. Where mailbox auditing records the delete but not the subject, fall back to correlating any delete with the identity change; less precise, still worth running.
derived_from: Google Threat Intelligence Group public reporting, cited per record

name: Nobody reads that fast
description: Bulk collection from a cloud productivity suite performed by a scripting runtime rather than a browser or sanctioned sync client, at a rate no human reader produces.
logic: Once a session is stolen the collection is automated, because manual collection does not scale and the operator is working against the clock before the session is revoked. Cloud audit logs record both the client software and the access rate, and the two together separate scripted collection from a person opening documents. The rate is the durable half: client strings are set by the caller and cost nothing to change, whereas reading tens of thousands of files in an hour is inherent to what the operator is trying to do.
caveat: Enumerate the automation that legitimately reads at volume before deploying this -- backup, retention, compliance search and data-loss tooling all look exactly like this -- or the rule fires nightly and gets turned off. The third marker exists to carry that: a principal that has always read at volume is not the interesting one.
derived_from: Google Threat Intelligence Group public reporting, cited per record

name: Trusting the repository ran the repository
description: Project-scoped coding-agent configuration -- tool-server definitions, environment settings -- executing repository-supplied code at agent initialisation, before the developer issues any instruction.
logic: This is the install-hook problem moved from the package manager to the editor, and it has the same shape: a documented convenience feature executes attacker-supplied code at a moment the user does not think of as execution. Nothing is exploited and no version is vulnerable. The ordering is the whole signal -- a child process of the agent that appears before the agent's first model request cannot have been asked for by the user. The second leg is path resolution: where the search path has been prepended with a directory inside the working tree, the agent's own routine tooling calls resolve to whatever the repository shipped, so the malicious binary is invoked by the agent's normal behaviour rather than by anything unusual. Both legs are collectable anywhere endpoint process telemetry already runs.
caveat: The remediation beats the detection and should be said first: treat opening an untrusted repository in an agent as equivalent to running it, and review project-scoped agent configuration the way a build script is reviewed. Detection earns its place on estates where developers routinely open outside code -- consultancies, security teams, anyone triaging submissions. Note the delivery route reported alongside this is social rather than technical: recruitment pretexts and contribution requests, aimed at getting a developer to open the repository at all.
derived_from: Datadog Security Labs public reporting, cited per record

name: A valid token clones more source than a person could read
description: A legitimate forge credential driving automated cloning of private repositories at a volume, parallelism and source-address spread that no human workflow produces, which is what repository theft looks like when the token itself is not in doubt.
logic: Nothing about the authentication is anomalous -- the token is valid, belongs to a real employee, and carries the access it is using -- so every marker has to come from the shape of the use rather than from the identity. Three things separate it from a developer working: the count of distinct private repositories cloned by one credential in one window, the parallelism, and the spread of source addresses. Reported instances cloned up to thousands of repositories per organisation inside a six-hour window from over a hundred addresses in a single cloud region, and a preceding validation burst began within seconds of itself across several unrelated victims. Threshold the clone count per credential against that credential's own history rather than against a fleet average, because the baseline for a build service and for a person differ by orders of magnitude and a fleet average hides both.
caveat: Do not anchor this on the addresses or the client version string. The reported campaign used a hundred-odd addresses in one cloud region and two different git client versions across its stages, and both are free for the actor to change; the volume and the parallelism are not. The harder constraint is retention: in GitHub Enterprise Cloud the git.clone, git.fetch and git.push events this rule reads are kept for seven days, so an estate that does not stream them off-platform cannot run this rule over any window long enough to catch a staged campaign, and cannot answer the scope question afterwards either. Mirrors, CI checkouts and onboarding automation all clone in bulk legitimately, which is why the threshold is per credential against itself.
derived_from: Wiz CIRT public incident reporting, cited per record

name: The quiet stage the audit log does not keep
description: Enumeration of repository metadata through the forge's REST API, and a small rehearsal clone days later, both performed with the same stolen credential that is used for mass exfiltration afterwards and both largely invisible to the logging most organisations have switched on.
logic: The exfiltration is the loud stage and the cheapest to detect too late. Two earlier stages carry the same credential and are separable: metadata enumeration against the API -- in the reported case the per-repository readme endpoint, queried from one cloud address behind an ordinary desktop browser user agent -- and a low-volume clone of a small subset of repositories a fortnight later from a different provider, which reads as a rehearsal rather than as theft. The transition is the strongest single signal available: one credential presenting as a browser while calling the API, then as a git client days later, is a shape a developer's own token does not take. Where the estate is subject to a wider campaign, the rehearsal bursts begin within the same minutes across unrelated organisations, which no single victim can see and a sector-level responder can.
caveat: Most organisations cannot run the first half of this at all, and should find that out before relying on it. The api.request events the enumeration produces are delivered by enterprise-level log streaming and are absent from the standard audit log, so an estate without streaming sees the mass clone and nothing before it -- and a clean result from this rule in that estate means the telemetry is missing, not that the stage did not happen. Verify the events are present before treating a negative as evidence. The cross-organisation simultaneity is real and is not available to a single victim.
derived_from: Wiz CIRT public incident reporting, cited per record

name: The repository was the credential store nobody inventoried
description: Secrets carried inside exfiltrated repositories -- cloud keys, SaaS tokens, private keys, database and pipeline credentials -- treated as compromised from the moment of the clone, validated for whether they still work, and hunted forward for use from networks they have no history of.
logic: Source theft is rarely about the source. The repositories carry credentials, and the interval between the clone and the actor using them is the defender's whole opportunity. Drive this from the inventory rather than from the intrusion: enumerate what the credential cloned, extract the secrets those repositories contain, establish which are still valid, and hunt each survivor forward for use from an address, user agent or principal that its own history does not contain. The reported response spent most of its effort here rather than on the cloning itself, and the same shape applies to any bulk theft of a repository, backup or configuration store.
caveat: Rotation and detection compete for the same hours and rotation should win, but every rotation has to be recorded as it happens or the hunt afterwards cannot tell the actor's use of a key from the estate's own re-issue of it. Scanning that reports a secret's presence without validating it produces a backlog rather than a finding, because the operative question is which of them still authenticates. A secret absent from the current HEAD may still be live in history, and the actor has the history.
derived_from: Wiz CIRT public incident reporting, cited per record

name: The venue's Wi-Fi decided what your sign-in page was
description: A captive portal network -- or the shared platform behind many of them -- manipulating DNS and HTTP so that the first page a joining device sees is attacker-controlled, placing an adversary in the middle outside every perimeter the victim's employer controls.
logic: The compromise is of the venue, not of the traveller, and the traveller's employer sees only the consequences. Two shapes are visible to a defender who never touches the hotel's equipment. First, resolution: a managed device joining an untrusted network resolves a corporate or provider name to an address that is not the answer its own resolver would give, which is checkable wherever the endpoint agent records both the query and the answer. Second, sequence: authentication activity for a tenant identity beginning within minutes of a device joining an unfamiliar network, from a network the identity has no history of. Compromising the shared platform rather than each venue is what makes this worth a rule rather than an anecdote -- one supplier compromise puts the same adversary in the middle at every venue it serves, which is why the observable is a class of network and not a list of hotels.
caveat: Captive portals legitimately intercept DNS and HTTP -- that is how they work -- so interception alone is not the finding and a rule written on it will fire in every airport. What separates this is the destination: a sign-in surface for the corporate identity provider, or a software update prompt, served from the intercepting network rather than from the provider. Full-tunnel VPN with local proxy disabled removes the exposure and is the actual control; where it cannot be enforced, the detection has to live on the endpoint, because no corporate network sees any of this traffic.
derived_from: Zscaler ThreatLabz and Microsoft Threat Intelligence public reporting, cited per record

name: Every request looks like a browser and the crowd does not
description: A denial-of-service flood whose individual requests carry complete, plausible browser fingerprints, so that the discriminator moves from the shape of the request to the composition of the population making them.
logic: Volumetric filtering assumes attack traffic is malformed, uniform or protocol-abusing. A flood that constructs full browser fingerprints over HTTP/2 satisfies every one of those checks, and the requests remain individually unremarkable however closely they are inspected. What does not survive is the crowd: genuine audiences cluster heavily on a handful of browser and version combinations and arrive from address space with a history, while a generator that randomises fingerprints produces a distribution flatter than any real population, from consumer device space at a concurrency the service has never seen. Compare the population against the service's own baseline rather than the request against a signature.
caveat: No threshold here transfers between services, so this is a hunt until someone fits it to a specific baseline. It fires on legitimate demand spikes -- launches, news cycles, marketing sends -- and the fingerprint distribution rather than the volume is what separates those. Where a scrubbing provider already sits in front, establish what it passes through before writing this, because the population reaching the origin is not the population that was sent.
derived_from: Unit 42 public reporting, cited per record

name: The agent acted as the developer and the log agrees
description: An AI agent with shell access running under a person's account, inside processes that person launched, so that endpoint telemetry attributes every command, file read and network call to the human and no record separates the two.
logic: Endpoint tooling records the process tree and the account, and both are honest: the agent really did run as that user, from that editor. Nothing in the standard record carries the one fact an investigation needs, which is whether a human or a model decided on the action. The gap is answerable as an inventory before any detection is written -- list the hosts running an agent with shell access, list those emitting agent-attributed tool calls, and the difference is the set of machines on which an incident involving an agent cannot be reconstructed. Only once that record exists do the useful detections become writable, because they are all statements about what the agent did rather than about what the process was.
caveat: The hook interface belongs to the agent vendor and differs per product, so this is per-agent work and an estate running several has several differently shaped blind spots. Collecting tool calls means collecting command text and file paths from developer machines, which is a privacy and retention decision to take before the rollout. And the absence of these events must never be read as absence of agent activity, which is the failure this pattern exists to name.
derived_from: Elastic Security Labs public reporting, cited per record

name: Two verified commits, same content, different hash
description: A signed commit re-encoded so that it keeps its tree, its metadata and a signature that still verifies, while carrying a different commit hash -- which breaks any control that treats the hash as a one-to-one name for the content, most directly hash-based blocking.
logic: The assumption under a great deal of supply-chain tooling is that a commit hash names exactly one piece of signed content. Three encoding routes break it without the signing key and without attacking SHA-2: inverting an ECDSA signature to its equivalent form, inserting an unhashed subpacket into an OpenPGP signature, and re-encoding a DER length non-canonically inside an S/MIME envelope. Two of the three still satisfy local verification, and all three earn a persistent verified marking from the forge. What this does and does not permit needs stating precisely, because the natural reading is wrong: the content is identical, so nobody can substitute different code under a pinned hash by this route. What breaks is naming. A denylist of known-bad commit hashes can be evaded by minting an equivalent commit that verifies as happily as the original; a system treating the hash as a content-addressable primary key can hold two keys for one content; and a reviewer comparing hashes can conclude two identical trees are different artefacts. Detect it by comparing trees rather than hashes, and by treating a signature whose encoding is non-canonical as suspect in its own right.
caveat: Do not read this as a reason to stop pinning. Pinning to a commit digest still prevents an actor substituting different content, which is the attack it was adopted against, and this does not touch that. It removes a weaker guarantee that was never separately stated -- that the hash is a canonical name -- and the practical casualty is hash-based blocking, which is the one control here that silently stops working. The signature-encoding markers need a verifier that reports how a signature was encoded rather than only whether it verified, and most tooling reports only the second, so in most estates the tree comparison is the only one of these that can actually be run today.
derived_from: Ginesin, arXiv 2607.02820, cited per record

name: The page is not collecting your details, someone is
description: A credential-harvesting page that keeps an encrypted real-time channel open to an operator, streaming input as it is typed and taking instructions back, so the session is steered live rather than logged and read later.
logic: A static phishing kit collects a form and posts it once, which gives the defender a window between theft and use and gives the victim a chance to notice. An operator-driven kit removes both: the operator watches the typing, and can ask for whatever the real site asks for at the moment it is needed. The observable that separates the two is the channel. A page presenting as a payment or login surface holding a persistent socket to a host that is not the brand it imitates has no legitimate reading, and it is visible at the proxy without decrypting anything, because the upgrade and the long-lived flow are metadata. The second observable is the ask: no genuine checkout requests a passport image, a national identity number and a one-time code in the same flow, and a page that does is describing the operator's shopping list rather than a purchase.
caveat: Do not describe what this does to a one-time code as a bypass. The code is requested while it is still valid and the victim supplies it correctly; the factor works exactly as designed and is simply answered on the attacker's behalf, which is the same shape as device code phishing and has the same consequence -- strengthening the factor does not help, and only a phishing-resistant credential bound to the origin does. Real-time channels are also entirely ordinary on legitimate sites, so the socket marker carries nothing without the brand mismatch beside it, and most of this is only visible for traffic that traverses a corporate path at all, which consumer-targeted lures deliberately avoid.
derived_from: Cisco Talos public reporting, cited per record

name: The attacker's tool is built on your own engineering library
description: Tooling assembled from the same open-source industrial protocol library that legitimate monitoring and engineering software uses. Because the library implements the protocol correctly, the traffic it produces is indistinguishable on the wire from an approved tool, and the resulting program can be presented as a monitoring product. The library artefact on the host is the only stage that is distinctive.
logic: Presence, load or import of an industrial protocol library on a host outside the approved engineering set -- snap7 and python-snap7 for S7comm, and the equivalent commodity libraries for other controller families. The detection is the host rather than the library, so it requires a maintained list of approved engineering workstations and yields nothing without one.
xql_sketch: dataset = <edr_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.filename in ("snap7.dll", "snap7.so") or xdm.target.process.command_line contains "snap7" | filter xdm.source.host.hostname not in (<approved_engineering_workstations>)
caveat: The library is legitimate software and may be exactly what an integrator's own tooling is built on, so a hit is a question about the host rather than a verdict. Endpoint agents are frequently not permitted on engineering workstations for vendor support reasons; where that is the case this pattern cannot be implemented and only the network-side patterns remain. It is also the inverse of the purpose-built framework case: there is no custom binary to find and no vendor attribution to lean on, because the attacker wrote nothing that a defender could recognise as theirs.

name: Assume a working exploit exists the day the advisory does
description: Agencies reporting that AI assistance is being used to turn public vulnerability information into working exploitation scripts for control equipment. The effect is on timing rather than on mechanism: the interval between a disclosure becoming public and a usable exploit existing collapses, against equipment whose patch cycle is measured in outages rather than in weeks.
logic: Prioritise control-equipment patching from the disclosure date of the vendor advisory rather than from the date exploitation is first reported publicly. Where an outage window cannot be brought forward, compensate at the network layer -- the exposure begins when the information becomes public, not when a proof of concept is seen.
xql_sketch: -- no detection query; the output is a revised patch-priority list joining the controller inventory to vendor advisory dates
caveat: This changes planning, not alerting, and nothing in it is observable in defender telemetry. The agencies assert the capability and describe its effect without publishing evidence of the generation step, so it must not be passed on as a detectable event. Its practical force is against the common OT argument that a known vulnerability can wait for the next scheduled outage because no exploit has been seen yet.

name: The error message tells the attacker the key is right
description: On an ASP.NET ViewState endpoint two different HTTP 500 responses mean opposite things. A MAC validation failure means the MachineKey used was wrong. An InvalidCastException means it was right and the payload deserialised. Attackers read the difference to confirm stolen key material before running anything, and defenders who alert on status code alone cannot see either.
logic: Parse the exception type from the application error log rather than the status code from the access log. An InvalidCastException on a ViewState endpoint is a successful deserialisation and should be treated as compromise until disproved. Repeated MAC validation failures from one source are key trial, not application noise, and are the only stage of this that looks like an attack in the conventional sense.
xql_sketch: dataset = <app_error_log> | filter xdm.target.url contains "__VIEWSTATE" and xdm.network.http.response_code = 500 | alter kind = if(xdm.alert.description contains "InvalidCastException", "key_valid_deserialised", if(xdm.alert.description contains "MAC", "key_trial", "other")) | comp count() by kind, xdm.source.ipv4
caveat: This is the counter-example to pat-deserialisation-failure-in-application-log, whose caveat says a successful attack may raise no exception at all. Here success raises one, and the exception type is the whole signal. The practical obstacle is that the ViewState parameter lives in the POST body and the exception lives in the application error log, so an estate forwarding only web access logs holds neither half. The durable control is not detection at all: the attack is gated entirely on MachineKey confidentiality, so rotating keys and keeping them out of published configuration removes the capability rather than observing it.

name: Something excluded the server's own module directory from scanning
description: An antivirus exclusion path added for a directory a server loads native modules or extensions from, written shortly before something is dropped there. The exclusion has to come first, which makes it the earliest catchable point in the chain and the one the operator cannot skip.
logic: Alert on an exclusion being written whose path names a server module or extension directory, by either route -- the management cmdlet or a direct write to the exclusions key. Correlate forward: a file appearing in that directory within a short window of the exclusion is the completed sequence.
xql_sketch: dataset = <edr_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.command_line contains "Add-MpPreference" or xdm.target.registry.key contains "Windows Defender\\Exclusions\\Paths" | filter xdm.target.registry.value_name contains "inetsrv" or xdm.target.process.command_line contains "inetsrv"
caveat: Installers and backup agents do legitimately write exclusions, so the act is common and the path is what carries the fidelity: a server's own module directory has no legitimate reason to be excluded from scanning. Where an operations team maintains such an exclusion deliberately, this fires on every policy reapplication, and the correct response is to remove the exclusion rather than tune the rule. The inverse case is worth stating too -- an estate that does not collect exclusion changes at all will see none of this, and the first evidence will be the module itself.

name: A ten-year-old package just took its first dependency
description: A dependency added to a package whose dependency set has been stable for years. The anomaly is in the package's own history rather than in the new name, which makes it checkable without a candidate list, a threshold, or any knowledge of what the added package is.
logic: Diff each dependency upgrade's manifest against the version it replaces and gate on the delta, not the version number. A package that has added no dependency since publication and suddenly adds one is anomalous against itself. This is strictly stronger than typosquat name-matching, which requires a list of names worth protecting and a string-distance threshold that legitimate forks trip, and it catches the case where the added dependency has a name nobody would flag.
xql_sketch: -- pipeline check, not a SIEM query: for each upgraded dependency, compare the manifest of the new version against the manifest of the version being replaced, and fail the build where the dependency count rises on a package whose prior versions declared none
caveat: Belongs in the build pipeline rather than in detection tooling, and needs the previous manifest to compare against -- an estate that resolves fresh on every build keeps no baseline and cannot run this. It does fire on legitimate releases, because mature packages do occasionally take a first dependency; what makes that acceptable is that the population is small enough to read by hand, which is not true of any rule keyed on version numbers or publication dates. It says nothing about a malicious change made inside a dependency the package already had.

name: A trusted root authority the estate never issued
description: Malware that wants to read or rewrite HTTPS on a host does not attack TLS. It generates its own certificate authority, adds it to the host trust store using the platform's own certificate utility, and serves the traffic from a proxy it runs locally. Every certificate it mints afterwards validates, and nothing warns the user.
logic: Two surfaces, answering different questions, and they need different query shapes. The install is a process event: the platform certificate utility invoked with store-add arguments naming the root store, weighed against the small set of products that legitimately do this. The state is an inventory question that outlives the process record: enumerate the trust store on every host, at machine and at user scope, and compare it against the authorities the estate actually trusts. Only the process half belongs in a filter; the state half needs rule_shape inventory or it emits as a nonsense clause on a process dataset. Expect the certificate file itself to be short-lived, written to a temporary path immediately before the store-add and deleted immediately after.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name ~= "^certutil" and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i)-addstore\b.*\broot\b"    // and separately: dataset = <asset_dataset> | filter root_store_authority not in (<approved_authorities>)
caveat: Inspection proxies, endpoint management and some development tooling install root authorities for good reasons, so the approved list has to exist before this is a rule rather than a queue. The utility is not the only route in: anything able to call the platform certificate API can add a store entry with no distinctive command line, which is why the inventory half of this pattern carries more weight than the process half. The parent test is a local baseline question, not something any single source establishes, so treat a parent-image condition as tuning rather than as evidence.

markers.expr: store_add_process_ancestry includes an approved endpoint management, deployment or inspection product

name: The security product's own repair driver, staged by something that is not the product
description: Security and maintenance products ship signed helper drivers that the product itself stages on demand to do privileged file and registry work its user-mode agent cannot do. The driver is legitimate, carries the vendor's signature, sits on no vulnerable-driver blocklist, and takes its instructions from a configuration the caller supplies rather than from a fixed interface. Anyone with administrative privilege who understands that configuration format gets kernel-mode file and registry operations with no exploit and without carrying a driver in, so nothing about the driver itself is the finding. The finding is that it was staged and loaded by something outside the product it belongs to.
logic: Two halves, either of which stands alone. Registry: a kernel driver service key is created whose image is one of the vendor's helper drivers and whose configuration value points at a caller-supplied blob, with a load order group that starts the driver earlier than the security drivers loading in the same phase. Lineage: the driver load event for that image where the process that wrote the driver file or created its service key is not one of the product's own processes. Neither half depends on the driver being unsigned, unusual or blocklisted, because it is none of those things.

markers.note: on Windows the driver service key lives here; the equivalent on another platform is the driver load unit

markers.expr: driver service key created whose image is a vendor helper driver and whose staging process is outside that vendor's own enumerated process set
the service load order group starts the driver earlier than the security drivers that load in the same start phase
a service installation record exists in the platform log for the same service name

caveat: The product stages the same driver, the same keys and the same group in the course of its ordinary work, so the event is not rare and the fidelity sits entirely in the lineage test. That test needs the vendor's own process set enumerated for the estate first, and it is defeated by staging the driver from a process inside that set. Vulnerable-driver blocklists and signature checks do not help, because the driver is being used for exactly what it was built to do.

name: The deletion has no user-mode author
description: Where a signed kernel driver carries out the file operation, endpoint telemetry attributes it to the kernel itself rather than to whatever asked for it, so every rule keyed on a process image, a command line or a parent-child pair has nothing to match. What is left is the driver load that must precede the operation, the lineage of whatever staged that driver, and the target of the operation itself. This is also how such a driver crosses tamper protection, which is enforced against user-mode callers.
logic: Join the operation to the driver load that preceded it. Alert where a file deletion or a registry key deletion targets a security product's binary, service key or policy key and a driver load occurred on the same host inside a window measured locally, and treat an operation recorded with the kernel as its actor rather than a user-mode process as the strongest form of it. The window and the target list are the two things the consumer has to set.

markers.note: on Windows the kernel is recorded as System, process id 4

markers.expr: file deletion attributed to the kernel rather than to a user-mode process
driver load on the same host inside a locally measured window before the operation
target is a security product binary, service key or policy key

caveat: Legitimate remediation, patching and the operating system's own maintenance also work from kernel mode, so the target list carries most of the fidelity and has to be written for the estate. The harder limit is timing: where the driver is staged to run early in boot it acts before user-mode security services start, and an agent that begins recording when its own service starts holds no record of the operation at all. No window is supplied here because it has to be measured against the estate's own boot timeline. Kernel attribution is documented for file deletion; do not assume the actor field on a registry event names the kernel the same way without checking it on the platform in front of you.

name: The sentence is describing the sentence
description: Text heading into a model context carrying a phrase that states something quantitative about the whole text containing it. Published as the discriminator for a payload embedded in plain prose, where there is no emoji, no encoded block and no invisible formatting for a filter to key on and the structural instruments therefore see nothing.
logic: Test the shape of the assertion rather than its meaning: does a phrase in the input quantify the body of text it is itself part of. Scope strictly to content entering a model context, since a self-describing sentence is unremarkable anywhere else. Apply it at the policy check rather than after it, because the whole class of payload is defined by being invisible to the check that follows.
caveat: Hunt-grade. Writing about word counts, style guides, puzzle text and documentation about prompts all describe themselves quantitatively and will match. The false positive cost is acknowledged by the source and not measured by it. This is the complement of matching on instruction structure, not a replacement for it: a payload carried this way contains no role marker, no turn delimiter and no control character, so the structural test and this one look at disjoint populations and both are needed. The absence of emoji, encoded blocks and invisible formatting is why this pattern exists and not a condition to test alongside the phrase: ANDing it in would drop a wrapper padded with a single unrelated emoji, which is the case most worth catching. Keep it as scoping context, never as a filter clause.
derived_from: Check Point Research public research, cited per record

name: It wrote code to read a poem
description: A model turn in which a prose-only prompt with no attachment and no stated computational task drives sustained reasoning and repeated code-interpreter executions. The work is the signature: the source states that recovering a payload embedded this way is not semantic in nature and is gated behind reasoning effort and interpreter access, so the cost lands on the target side of a guardrail that saw nothing.
logic: Attribute reasoning duration and interpreter invocations to the turn and to the prompt that opened it, then baseline both against the same population: prompts that ask for no computation. The signal is the gap between what the visible request would cost to answer and what the turn actually cost. Where a preceding policy check exists, join its verdict in: a turn passed as safe and then answered with minutes of reasoning and several scripts is the shape worth pulling, and neither half is interesting alone.
caveat: Depends entirely on the pipeline recording reasoning duration and interpreter invocations per turn and attributing them to the input, which is not universal and is the first thing to establish. Every bound here is left unresolved on purpose: the published figures are a floor observed on one target configuration and a bound has to be measured against the estate's own prompt mix. Both bounds baseline against one population, prompts requesting no computation, so a consumer builds one baseline rather than two. Analytical prose prompts legitimately produce long reasoning, so the discriminator is that the visible request asks for no computation at all, and a caller who cannot separate those two populations should not build this.
derived_from: Check Point Research public research, cited per record

name: Nothing in the prompt asked for that
description: A model or agent turn in which a tool call or file operation has an effect with no antecedent anywhere in the prompt as a person reading it would understand it, on input a preceding policy check passed as safe. The scenario is a direct-prompt runtime rather than a pipeline step: the untrusted text is the submitted prompt itself, and the control that failed is a separate screening model rather than a review of a workflow triggered by an outside contributor.
logic: Watch the output side rather than the input side. Attribute each tool call and file operation to the turn and to the prompt that opened it, then ask whether the visible prompt asked for anything of that family. Where a screening model sits in front, join its verdict in, because the screening verdict is the thing the action contradicts: an effect with no antecedent, on a turn screened and passed as safe, is the shape worth pulling. This is the instrument of last resort for an input screen that saw nothing, which is exactly the population this scenario produces.
caveat: Hunt-grade and honestly so: deciding that an action has no antecedent in the prompt is a semantic reconciliation an analyst performs, and nobody should promote this to alert without first implementing that judgement and measuring it. Depends on the runtime attributing tool calls and file operations to the turn and to the prompt, and on a record of what the prompt displayed, neither of which is universal. Endpoint evidence types apply only where the interpreter or tool runtime sits on infrastructure the consumer instruments; a provider-hosted interpreter leaves only the provider's audit trail. Distinct from the pipeline case where untrusted event text reaches an agent inside a workflow: there the flow question is answerable in source control before any rule is written, and here there is no workflow to inspect because the prompt came straight from the requester.
derived_from: Check Point Research public research, cited per record

name: The only validation was the opening element
description: An endpoint that exists so a device can post to it, rather than a person, checks the opening element of the submitted document and nothing else, then lifts a named field out of the parsed body and concatenates it into a query or a command. Because the payload rides in the body, a web log that keeps request lines records the attack as an ordinary POST.
logic: Two tests, and which one is available is decided by what the web tier retains. With bodies: the named field carries syntax rather than the value type it is supposed to hold -- quotes, separators, comment sequences or keywords in a field declared to be an address, an identifier or a name. Without bodies: the caller set of a machine-facing endpoint can usually be baselined, and a request from outside that baseline is worth reading on the path and source address alone. Baseline it before relying on it, because product documentation rarely states who the legitimate callers are. Enumerate the machine-facing endpoints per product first; they are routinely missing from an access control review because they predate any login.

markers.expr: named field in the parsed request body contains syntax characters rather than the value type the field is declared to hold
request to a device-facing endpoint whose source address is outside the baselined caller set

caveat: The two markers are alternative tests, not a conjunction: a consumer that ANDs them demands body retention and a caller baseline at the same time, and will build a rule that matches nothing. Take whichever the telemetry supports. The opening element, magic string or content type that the handler checks is present on a legitimate submission too, so matching it identifies the endpoint and never the attack, and it is not a marker for that reason. Retaining request bodies is the precondition for the stronger half and most estates do not retain them; establish that before building on it. On an internet-exposed device the source-address half will carry ordinary scanning with it.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public research, cited per record

name: The database wrote down the statement that attacked it
description: Where an application or its database engine logs the SQL it executes, a successful injection is recorded in full, the attacker's half included. The evidence is already held and needs no signature, which makes it answerable retrospectively as well as prospectively.
logic: Search the query log for two shapes. First, a predicate that should hold one value carrying a statement separator or a trailing comment sequence, which is the concatenated string being closed early and the remainder of the original query discarded. Second, any clause by which the engine reads or writes outside the database or hands a string to the operating system, which is the injection reaching for execution rather than for data. The second shape is short, literal and effectively never legitimate on an appliance.

markers.expr: logged SQL statement carries a statement separator or trailing comment sequence inside a predicate that holds a single value
logged SQL statement contains the engine's own file or program execution clause

caveat: The two markers are separate searches, not a conjunction: ANDing them finds only an injection that both closed a predicate early and reached the engine's execution clause, and misses every injection that did one without the other. Whether the two can even land on one event depends on whether the log writes a submitted string as one line or one line per statement, which is a per-product question. The query log normally sits on the appliance or the database host and is frequently forwarded nowhere, so establish that it is collected before relying on this; where it is collected the check costs nothing. An engine configured to log only slow or failing statements holds the injection only where the injection was slow or failed. Applications that build SQL by concatenation produce odd-looking statements legitimately, so the separator test needs the legitimate set characterised once.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public research, cited per record

name: The database ran the command, so the web server's ancestry looks clean
description: Injection that reaches the database engine's own program execution facility rather than stopping at data. The operating system process is then a child of the database backend and not of the web or application tier, so a detection keyed to the web server as the parent does not see it at all.
logic: Any operating system process whose parent is the database backend. On most estates the engine spawns nothing at all, which makes the parentage the entire signal and keeps the rule to one clause. Do not narrow it with a process name list without first establishing what the engine's program execution facility spawns on the product in hand, because the immediate child is not necessarily the command named in the statement. Pair it with the engine's query log, where the clause that caused the execution is recorded.

markers.expr: operating system process whose parent is the database engine backend

caveat: A process name list was removed from this pattern's markers. It conjoined with the parentage and narrowed a one-clause rule down to the handful of payloads someone happened to observe, and it named the payload rather than whatever the engine actually spawns first. Appliances that embed a database frequently ship no process telemetry, and on those the parentage cannot be observed however good the rule is; the query log is then the only evidence and this pattern is unanswerable. A few products do shell out from the database for reporting or backup, so characterise that set once -- it is normally very small, which is what makes the rule cheap.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public research, cited per record

name: The answer came back in the URL
description: Command output encoded and placed in the path of an outbound HTTP request, so the exfiltration is a single GET with nothing in any body and no second channel to find. The path is typically prefixed with an identifier so the operator can match an answer to the target that produced it, which means the encoded output is a run inside the path rather than the whole of it.
logic: An outbound HTTP request from a device that does not normally originate web traffic, addressed to an address literal rather than a hostname, whose path carries a long base64 run. Because the output is in the request line, a control that inspects bodies sees nothing, and because the destination is an address there is no domain to block or sinkhole.

markers.expr: outbound HTTP request path carries a base64 run longer than a length bound measured on the estate
HTTP request host is an address literal rather than a hostname
originating host is an appliance whose baseline includes no outbound web requests

caveat: The length bound must be measured locally and is deliberately left unresolved: applications legitimately carry base64 in paths, cache keys and tracking parameters, and a bound imported from another estate either fires constantly or never fires. Test for a base64 run inside the path rather than for a path that decodes in full, because an identifier prefix is normal and breaks a whole-path test. The host test is written as an address literal rather than as an absent DNS lookup, so that a proxy log answers it without a DNS feed to join against. Where no proxy terminates the appliance's egress the request survives only as a flow record, which keeps the destination and the port and loses the path, reducing this to a destination check.
derived_from: Horizon3.ai public research, cited per record

name: A read-only spreadsheet query API used as the command and control channel
description: A document service exposes an unauthenticated, read-only query API over any spreadsheet published to the web. The actor publishes a sheet, hides the payload in cells, and has the victim's own browser fetch it with an ordinary HTTPS request to the service's genuine domain. Appending back to a sheet through an attached form response endpoint makes the same channel two-way.
logic: Destination reputation, certificate validity and domain age all return reassuring answers, because the destination genuinely is the document service. The discriminator that survives is the query API path rather than the interactive document paths. An absence test over other document service activity from the same host is the obvious second discriminator and is the one to be careful with, because it fails wherever the actor hosts the lure or the loader on that same service.
xql_sketch: dataset = <proxy_dataset> | filter xdm.target.domain = "docs.google.com" and xdm.network.http.url contains "/gviz/tq" | comp count() as hits by xdm.source.host.hostname, xdm.network.http.url | sort desc hits
caveat: The API is a long-standing documented feature with legitimate users, so it cannot be blocked or alerted on by destination without breaking real work. It also requires full URI logging: a sensor that records only the SNI or the domain cannot tell this from somebody opening a spreadsheet, which is why nothing but proxy evidence is declared. Do not add an anti-join against other document service activity from the same host without checking whether the actor also hosts the lure there; where they do, that test is false for every true positive and the rule returns nothing. The sketch is a triage aggregation, not a finished rule: the dataset is the author's to choose and any bound is theirs to set. The published document identifier is disposable, since an actor who loses one publishes another, so anchoring on it buys days rather than months.

name: The user pasted the script into the browser, not into a shell
description: A ClickFix variant with no operating system stage. The target is talked into running attacker JavaScript inside their own browser session, either through the address bar behind the javascript: scheme or by pasting it into a userscript manager extension, so the code executes with the page's own origin and privileges and never becomes a process.
logic: Every artefact the operating-system form of this attack leaves is absent: no interpreter process, no encoded command line, no parent chain, nothing on disk. Detection moves to the web tier. The durable shape is a browser fetching a raw script body from a text-sharing or document service and then fetching from the service holding the next stage, by the same host, within a window the consumer sets. The absence of any process artefact is what tells you which kind of ClickFix this is, but it is a property of the technique rather than a test a rule can run, because interpreters start continuously on a managed host and a host-wide no-interpreter condition is never true.
caveat: The absence of process telemetry is the point, so an endpoint-only programme does not see this and reports clean. It is also unusually hard to alert on, because every leg is a browser making an ordinary HTTPS request to a reputable service, and where the actor moves both legs onto one service the two-destination shape disappears entirely. The window is a local decision and is not supplied here. The standing exposure, which hosts can run pasted script at all, is a browser management question and is carried by pat-userscript-manager-hosts-pasted-script rather than here, because an inventory test cannot be evaluated inside a sequence. The controls that work are browser management, meaning extension allow-listing and restricting developer-level functionality by role, and telling users that pasting code into a browser is the same act as pasting it into a terminal.

name: A legitimate userscript manager hosting script the user pasted in
description: The extension is legitimate, user-installed from the official store and not malicious in itself. What makes it matter is that it re-runs whatever userscript the user pastes into it every time they visit a matching site, so an attacker who talks a user into pasting once has persistence without publishing anything to the store and without writing anything an endpoint agent inspects.
logic: Inventory which browsers have a userscript manager installed and which host roles have no reason to run one. Separately, whether browser policy restricts extension installation and developer-level functionality by role is the standing exposure. Both are configuration state rather than events, and together they say which hosts could run a pasted script; neither says which are running one.
caveat: This is not the same scenario as a malicious extension published to a store, and the tests for that one do not reach it: nothing was force-installed, nothing unapproved was necessarily installed, and the extension is one a lot of people have a good reason to run. An extension inventory holds the extension, not the userscripts inside it, so reading which sites a script is registered against means reading the script bodies the extension stores, which standard inventory collection does not carry. Where browsers are unmanaged there is no inventory to query at all, and the answer is a browser management control rather than a detection.

name: Injected page script rewriting the payment destination
description: A web skimmer that alters rather than steals. Script running inside the page hooks the browser fetch API, rewrites wallet or account destinations in responses and in the rendered page as it updates, substitutes the value the user copies to the clipboard, and adds counterfeit interface elements to explain the changed figures.
logic: There is nothing to detect on the network or the endpoint: the substitution happens inside the browser, after TLS termination, with no process, no file write and no unusual destination. The detection surface is the application's own served JavaScript. Look for code that reassigns the fetch API, registers a mutation observer over elements holding payment destinations, names payment form element identifiers without being part of a declared dependency, registers a copy or clipboard handler that rewrites the copied value, or decodes itself at runtime from arrays of encoded values.
caveat: These markers are alternatives, any one of which is worth a look, not a conjunction. A consumer that ANDs all four is describing a complete specimen rather than hunting for one, and a skimmer that only rewrites the clipboard will not be found that way. Only the site operator can run this check; the organisation whose user was defrauded has no telemetry that shows it.
