The artefact is the application's own deployed bundle read as source, which no evidence type in the vocabulary names, so file_artefact stands in and request logs are not declared, because they record requests rather than response bodies. Signatures written against a decoded sample do not survive, because the obfuscation is regenerated per revision with fresh keys and fresh random identifiers while the underlying script is unchanged. The control that actually limits loss is verifying the destination through a second channel before sending value, since the displayed address, the copied address and the address in the API response can all be the attacker's at once.

name: The process joined a container it does not belong to
description: Anything that decides what a process is by reading its control group membership out of the proc filesystem can be made to decide wrongly by an attacker with root, who moves the process into another container's control group. The identity decision is then correct with respect to the evidence and wrong with respect to reality.
logic: The mapping from a process to a container is reported by the cgroup and mountinfo entries under the proc filesystem, and is decided by control-group membership, which root can change by writing to the cgroup filesystem. Detect the write rather than its consequence: a process identifier appearing in the cgroup.procs file of a container scope where the writer is not the container runtime, the kubelet or the init system, and the identifier written belongs to a process outside that container. Enumeration of running containers through the runtime command line interface, and the read of the victim's control group path out of the proc filesystem, are precursor events rather than conditions of this one, because the attacker needs the victim's cgroup path before it can be copied; a rule joining them is a sequence and not this filter.

markers.note: the layout between the cgroup mount point and the leaf file depends on how the host is configured, so this is deliberately left wide and narrowed per estate

caveat: Everything that manages containers writes to these files legitimately and constantly, so the exclusion list for the runtime, the kubelet and the init system carries the entire fidelity of this pattern and has to be built for the estate before the rule is worth running. Debugging and profiling tools that enter a container's control group on purpose produce the identical event and no exclusion here covers them, which is what keeps this a hunt. Sensors that do not record writes to cgroup pseudo-files cannot see any of it, and establishing whether yours does is the first task rather than a detail. Note also that the attacker does not need a new directory: writing into the victim's existing control group works, so a rule that keys on an odd-looking cgroup path only catches the tidy version of the technique.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: Something outside the workload asked the local issuer for credentials
description: Workload identity systems issue short-lived credentials over a local socket to whatever connects and passes attestation. Where attestation can be satisfied by attributes the host controls, the caller itself becomes the thing worth watching, independently of the verdict.
logic: The socket is meant to be reached by the workloads on the host and by nothing else. The condition is one thing: the local issuing socket opened by a process that is not running inside a workload container. Where the issuer records its own decisions, a refusal followed shortly by a success for the same caller is the sharper variant, because that pair is what a successful attestation forgery looks like from the issuer's side; it is a separate detection on the issuer's logs rather than a second condition on this one, and requiring it here would exclude the base case this pattern exists to catch.
caveat: Operators troubleshoot workload identity from a node shell using the same socket, so separate by account rather than by binary and expect a standing allow list of administrators. The client is interchangeable, so a process name is never the anchor; what the process is not inside is. No evidence type in this vocabulary describes a Unix socket connection, so whether the sensor records one is the first thing to establish.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: The identity client was run from the host, not from a workload
description: A workload identity client belongs inside the workload it fetches for. The same binary run from a host shell is either an operator troubleshooting or someone collecting credentials, and the two are told apart by the account rather than by the command.
logic: One process execution. A client of the local identity issuer, run by a process that is not inside a workload container, with a command line that asks the issuer for a token or a certificate. The literals belong to whichever client the source showed; the condition is the execution context, because any program speaking the local API does the same job.
caveat: Operators run these clients legitimately when troubleshooting, so this is a hunt for tooling rather than a rule. It catches the demonstration and not the technique: a different client, or a few lines of code against the same API, leaves nothing to match. Pair it with the socket condition, which does not depend on which client was used.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: One caller, every identity on the host
description: Once a single workload identity can be obtained by forging the attribute the issuer attests, the same step repeats for every workload on the host. The tooling that automates it is distinguishable by repetition rather than by any one action.
logic: A genuine workload adopts its own attested attribute and no other. Harvesting tooling enumerates the workloads on the host and adopts each one's attribute in turn, so the signal is a count of distinct container control groups joined by one process inside a window. Neither the bound nor the window can be supplied here; both depend on how many workloads the node normally runs. Counting what the issuer handed back is the same thesis on a different source and is a separate pattern, because an estate may collect one and not the other.
caveat: More than one is the arithmetic minimum of repetition rather than a measured threshold, and it is offered only because one is the correct answer for a legitimate workload. Node agents that inspect containers read many control group paths legitimately, so the condition has to be joining a control group and not reading one.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: The issuer handed one caller more than one identity
description: Where a local credential issuer keeps a record of what it hands out, harvesting is visible from the issuer's side rather than from the host's: one caller, many identities, in a short window.
logic: A legitimate consumer of a local credential issuer asks for its own identity and no other, so the count of distinct identities returned to one caller inside a window is the signal. The window and the bound are local measurements. This detection exists only where the issuer logs its own decisions and those logs are collected.
caveat: Many local issuers do not record what they issue, or the record is not collected, and an empty result then means nothing at all. Establish that the log line exists and carries both the caller and the identity before building on this. The bound of more than one is the arithmetic minimum of repetition rather than a measured threshold.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: What one compromised node is worth in identities
description: Where a host attests the workloads running on it, root on that host yields every identity scoped to it. The exposure is a property of scheduling and of how the issuing policy was written, and can be enumerated before anything happens.
logic: Two lists and a join. For each node, the workloads scheduled on it; and for each issuing policy entry, the selector set it requires. Every entry whose selector set is satisfied by any workload on that node is obtainable by anyone with root there, because the attributes the check relies on are supplied by the host. Rank nodes by the number of distinct identities co-located on them and treat the top of that list as the blast radius of one host compromise. Entries that select only on coarse attributes such as a namespace and a service account are satisfied by many workloads at once, which raises a node up the ranking rather than deciding whether it belongs in the answer.

markers.expr: count_distinct(identity whose issuing policy selector set is satisfied by a workload scheduled on the node) by node

caveat: The answer is never zero for a node running more than one workload, and it is not evidence of anything wrong; it is the number that decides how much a node compromise costs. The two lists come from different systems, and only the scheduling half is asset state: the issuing policy entries are the issuer's own configuration and are read from it. It is an argument for node hardening, for restricting root, for refusing privileged containers and host access, and for selectors that are not trivially satisfied, none of which a detection replaces. The pattern does not say which selectors are strong enough, only that any attribute the host itself supplies is decided by the host.
derived_from: Unit 42 public threat research, cited per record

name: Somebody tried the account nobody is supposed to sign in as
description: The cloud account root user, and its equivalents elsewhere, is an identity the platform owner tells you to monitor in full. An authentication attempt against it is worth reading on its own, because attempts against it do not arrive in the volumes a brute force rule is built for: one reported campaign ran at a median of two attempts per organisation and at most eight across a month, with the requests tunnelled through proxies whose source addresses spanned a wide range of countries and autonomous systems.
logic: Alert on every authentication event for the emergency or root identity, on both outcomes and without a count, then reconcile each one against a change record or a named on-call operator. No outcome clause belongs in the rule, since a failure and a success are both worth reading. The identity is the detection; the volume is not. Where the platform requires a distinct piece of knowledge to reach that identity at all, such as an account email address, a failed attempt also tells you that piece of knowledge is held externally.

markers.note: which field carries this is platform specific, so it is left computed rather than bound to a field path that would be wrong on most of the classes this pattern applies to

caveat: An organisation's own break-glass use produces exactly this event, so the rule is usable only where root sign-ins are genuinely rare and something exists to reconcile them against. Where the root identity is still used for routine work the first step is removing that dependency rather than writing the rule, and until that is done the rule reports the estate's own habits. Distinct from a brute force threshold: adding a count to this makes it miss the low-volume case it exists for.

name: The browser started the download, because something got inside it
description: The last stage of an in-browser exploit chain injects into the browser's own parent process and creates a process from there, so the fetch and execution of the next stage inherit the browser as their parent. Ancestry checks pass, signature and publisher checks pass, and the only thing that is anomalous is the command line.
logic: A command interpreter or script host whose parent is the browser, with a transfer utility and an output path in its arguments, and an execution of that same path in the same command line. This is the counterpart of the pattern where the user is persuaded to run the command themselves: there the browser is deliberately absent from the ancestry, here it is the whole point.

markers.note: both the dash and slash flag forms are reachable, so the utilities this list names that use a slash verb are covered rather than named and then excluded

caveat: Browsers spawn children constantly and a user opening a downloaded file produces a genuine browser-parented execution, so the image-name pairing is a filter and not a finding. The argument form is what carries it. Note also that a chain which injects into the browser process rather than the renderer has already escaped the sandbox, so anything found this way is post-escape and the host should be treated as fully compromised rather than as a blocked exploit attempt.

name: The exploit page does not know what it delivers
description: The exploit and the payload are separated: the delivery page receives the payload location as a query parameter from the loader that opened it, and an arming parameter decides whether it runs at all. The operator changes payloads without touching the exploit, the page can be tested safely against itself, and the page as retrieved contains no reference to the malware it installs, which is what defeats retrospective analysis of a captured copy.
logic: A request whose query string carries an absolute URL to an executable as a parameter value, fetched into a subframe with no corresponding top-level navigation, shortly after the same client fetched a small script from the same host. The gating stage before it filters on the user agent, so the population that fetches the loader and never fetches the next stage is large and the population that proceeds is the targeted one.
caveat: Advertising, analytics and single sign-on flows all pass URLs as query parameters and all load subframes, so the executable extension in the parameter value is doing most of the work and legitimate software distribution pages will occasionally match. Nothing here is visible where traffic is not decrypted. A captured copy of such a page is not evidence of what was delivered, because the page never contained it; the delivered artefact has to be recovered from the request that carried the parameter.

name: It asked for a file named after itself
description: The implant builds its download or check-in URL from the host's own name, so the operator provisions a payload per victim and returns nothing to anyone else. Sandboxes and researchers get a 404 and conclude the infrastructure is dead; the intended victim gets a payload chosen for it. The scheme also tells the operator which hosts are alive without any separate beacon.
logic: An outbound request whose URL path or query contains the requesting device's own hostname, to a destination with no other client in the estate. Compare the request against the asset inventory rather than against a list of known-bad paths, because the path is generated and never repeats between victims.
caveat: Inventory, management and telemetry agents put the hostname in a URL as a matter of course, so an allow list of destinations is a prerequisite rather than a refinement. The consequence for analysis matters as much as the detection: a not-found response from this infrastructure is not evidence that it is inactive, and an analyst who concludes the campaign is over on that basis has been told exactly what the scheme was built to tell them.

name: Persistence that does not wait for the next logon
description: A scheduled task named to resemble a platform component, whose repetition interval is measured in minutes rather than hours or days, so that the chain it launches is reinstated almost immediately after any removal. The short interval is the tell: it exists to win a race against an analyst or a cleanup, not to survive a reboot.
logic: Enumerate scheduled tasks by repetition interval rather than by name, and look at the short tail. For each, resolve what the action runs and when that file was written. A task repeating every few minutes whose action launches a binary written into a user, temporary or application-data directory is the finding.
caveat: Updaters, monitoring agents and endpoint tooling register short-interval tasks legitimately and in numbers, so the interval alone is a sorting key and not a detection; the action and the age of what it launches are what decide. No fixed bound is given here on purpose. The interval that is anomalous is a property of the estate's own task inventory and has to be measured there. There is also an operational consequence: removing the payload without removing the task means the payload comes back within minutes, so the task is the thing to take first.

name: Strip the new signature so the old one is trusted again
description: An application protects a sensitive state file with a newer, stronger authenticator while still accepting an older, forgeable one for compatibility. Rather than attacking the strong scheme, the attacker deletes the strong authenticators, forges the weak ones it can compute, and lets the application's own migration path re-authenticate the tampered state under the strong scheme on next start. The integrity control ends up vouching for the modification it was added to prevent.
logic: Two observables, and the second is the one that survives a rebuild of the tooling. First, the protected state file written by a process that is not the application that owns it. Second, a state file in which the strong authenticators are absent while the legacy ones are present and valid, which is the fingerprint of the downgrade rather than of the tool that performed it. Compare across the estate rather than reading one file, because the same absence is what an unmigrated profile looks like.
caveat: The legacy fallback is normally enabled by default and cannot be turned off through configuration, so there is no hardening step to recommend and the detection is the whole answer. Backup, profile-migration and endpoint management tooling writes these files legitimately, so allow-list by signer. Beware the reverse reading: a newly built or long-dormant profile that has not yet migrated shows the same absence, which is why the population comparison rather than the single file is the control.

name: A library run straight off a remote share, selected by number rather than by name
description: The payload is never written to the local disk. A command mounts a remote WebDAV path and hands it to the library host, which is asked for export number one instead of a named function, so there is no function name in the command line to read and no file on disk to scan. Two loaders using different code and protection methods shared this launch shape, which is what makes it the part of the chain worth detecting.
logic: The library host process started with a remote UNC path as its argument and an ordinal selector rather than a named export, in the same short window as the operating system's web-sharing client service starting. Either half is uncommon on a workstation; the pair is close to unique. The remote file name deliberately does not end in the library extension, so any rule keyed on the extension misses it.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.process.name = "rundll32.exe" and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "(?i),\s*#[0-9]{1,4}" and xdm.target.process.command_line ~= "\\\\\\\\"
caveat: Some enterprise software genuinely loads libraries by ordinal, and the web-sharing client is used legitimately by document collaboration suites. Neither half alone is worth an alert. Disabling the web-sharing client service by policy, or blocking outbound WebDAV at the proxy, closes the whole branch and is cheaper than detecting it.

markers.note: ordinal selector rather than a named export
remote UNC path in the same command line; the host class admits the @port and @SSL@port forms a WebDAV UNC takes on a non-default port
the WebDAV client service starts on first use, so its start is the mount

name: The handshake names a service the address has nothing to do with
description: An implant dials a hard-coded address directly and presents a well-known service name in the TLS server name extension and in the request host header. There is no name lookup, because there is no name to look up. Allow lists keyed on the presented name pass it, reputation keyed on the name passes it, and the address is the only field that tells the truth.
logic: Join outbound TLS sessions to that host's own name-resolution history. Alert where the presented server name, or the request host header, names a service whose addresses this host has never been told about, and the destination address was never returned to it by any lookup. Compare against what the host itself resolved, not against a published address list, so the rule survives the actor changing which brand it borrows.
xql_sketch: dataset = <network_dataset> | filter xdm.network.tls.server_name != null | join type = left (dataset = <dns_dataset> | filter _time > <lookback_start>) as d d.answer = xdm.target.ipv4 and d.client_host = xdm.source.host.hostname | filter d.answer = null or d.query_name != xdm.network.tls.server_name
caveat: Content delivery networks and cloud front ends legitimately serve many names from shared addresses, and hosts with long-lived connections may outlive the resolution record, so the lookback window has to be generous and has to be stated: without one the left join finds nothing and the rule matches every session. The join key is the resolving host, not the queried name. Where TLS metadata is not recorded, the server name field does not exist and this cannot be built at all; the fallback is the weaker signal of an outbound session to an address with no preceding lookup. Where the borrowed name is carried only in a request header it is inside the TLS session, so that half needs interception.

name: A signed driver whose kill interface asks nobody who is calling
description: A legitimately signed third-party driver is carried in and loaded so that a user-mode component can pass it the process identifier of a security agent and have the kernel terminate it. The driver is not malware and its signature validates. The defect is that its device interface takes a process identifier from any caller and acts on it. Because the termination happens in the kernel, the agent being killed does not get to report its own death.
logic: Two halves that should be built together. First, a kernel driver written to disk or registered as a service by a process that is not a security, storage, backup or virtualisation product, with its image path under a user-writable directory. Second, the absence that follows: an endpoint agent stops reporting while the same host keeps producing network, authentication or proxy telemetry. The second half is what catches the next driver, since the driver itself will be a different one.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.extension = "sys" and xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)\\\\(?:Users|AppData|Temp|ProgramData)\\\\" and xdm.source.process.name not in (<security_storage_backup_virtualisation_executables>) | join type = inner (dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type = "driver_load") as l l.image_path = xdm.target.file.path | filter l._time - _time < <window>
caveat: The driver is signed, so signature and reputation checks pass it, and hash hunting ages the moment the operator picks a different one. A vulnerable-driver blocklist enforced by the platform is the control; detection is what covers the gap before the blocklist has the entry. The absence half needs a reliable agent-heartbeat feed and will fire on ordinary agent upgrades and reboots, so pair it with the driver-arrival half rather than alerting on silence alone.

name: The remote access client under an assumed name, found by the files it cannot rename
description: Commercial remote access products are deployed under a changed executable name so that detections keyed on the process name find nothing. The runtime library the stub loads, the configuration file it reads and the licence recorded in that configuration cannot be renamed without breaking the product, so those are what identify it. The licence serial in particular recurs across unrelated intrusion sets, which makes it a marker of shared deployment lineage rather than of one operator.
logic: Identify the product by its invariants, not by its executable name. Alert where the vendor's runtime library is loaded by a process whose image name is not the vendor's own, where the product's configuration file appears under a per-user application data directory, or where a configuration is written that suppresses the tray icon and the user-visible controls. Then correlate to the gateway the configuration names, which will be neither the vendor's cloud nor an internal address.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "image_load" and loaded_module_name in (<remote_access_runtime_libraries>) and xdm.target.process.name not in (<vendor_executable_names>)
caveat: An estate that genuinely licenses the product will match the library marker constantly, so the discriminator is the mismatch between the loading process name and the vendor's own, plus the install path. Suppressed tray icon and disabled user-visible controls are a supported configuration used legitimately for unattended kiosks and servers, so treat that marker as weight rather than as proof. The licence serial is worth retaining as an indicator but identifies a shared build, not an actor.

name: A burst of developer traffic wrapped around the one request that matters
description: Before fetching its payload, a script starts background threads that request a spread of well-known package registries, code-hosting APIs and container registries. The intent is to make the single malicious retrieval unremarkable inside a burst of plausible developer activity, and to give an analyst reviewing the proxy log a reason to stop reading. The decoys are the tell, because the host making them has no developer role.
logic: Count distinct package-registry, code-hosting and container-registry destinations reached by one host in a short window, then keep only hosts with no developer or build role and no history of reaching any of them. Within the same window, take the destinations that are not in that well-known set: the payload is one of them. Ranking by the decoys rather than by the payload works because the decoy set is fixed and reputable while the payload destination is new every time.
xql_sketch: dataset = <proxy_dataset> | filter xdm.target.domain in (<developer_service_domains>) | comp count_distinct(xdm.target.domain) as known_dev by xdm.source.host.hostname, bin(_time, 5m) | filter known_dev > <bound> | join type = left (dataset = <asset_dataset>) as a a.hostname = xdm.source.host.hostname | filter a.role not in ("developer", "build") // then re-query the same host and window for destinations absent from <developer_service_domains>: the payload is one of them
caveat: Developer workstations and build agents match constantly and must be excluded by role before this reads as anything; where role data does not exist, this cannot be built. The count has to be taken over a known list of developer services rather than over every destination, or it counts ordinary browsing, and the bound has to be measured against the estate rather than assumed. The requests go to reputable services over valid certificates, so neither reputation nor certificate inspection helps. A script that drops the decoys loses nothing operationally, so treat this as a hunting lead with a short shelf life rather than a durable control.

markers.note: the observed set spanned a code-hosting API, a JavaScript registry, a container registry, a Python registry, a dotnet registry and a script gallery; the bound is anchored on that set of six and must be measured against the estate before use

name: The address you copied is not the address you pasted
description: A payload polls the clipboard, recognises several cryptocurrency address formats and rewrites a matching value with an address it carries. The substitution takes nothing from the host and sends nothing, so collection-based and exfiltration-based detections see nothing of it, whatever else the payload carrying it does. The loss happens when the victim confirms a transfer they believe they addressed themselves.
logic: A process that both reads and writes the clipboard on a short repeating interval, is not a clipboard manager, a password manager, a remote access client or an office application, and has no window the user is interacting with. Where clipboard content is recorded, the direct test is a clipboard value replaced by a different value matching the same address format within one user session.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.operation_sub_type in ("clipboard_read", "clipboard_write") | comp count() as ops by xdm.source.process.name, xdm.target.host.hostname, bin(_time, 10m) | filter ops > <bound>
caveat: Very few endpoint sensors record clipboard operations at all, and fewer record content, so establish what the sensor collects before designing around this. No polling rate is given by the sources behind this pattern, so the count bound is left unresolved and has to be measured on the estate: a guessed one will either flood or never fire, depending on the sensor. Clipboard managers, password managers and remote access clients poll the clipboard legitimately and will need an allow list. The durable control is not detection: the substituted addresses are embedded in the payload, so verifying the pasted address against a saved address book before confirming a transfer defeats it outright.

name: The browser is the parent of a download-and-execute pair
description: A browser exploit chain that finishes by running an ordinary command line rather than by staying in memory. The final stage injects a small process-creation stub into the browser's own broker process, so the command it runs appears as a child of the browser rather than of the renderer, and the browser's sandbox is behind it by the time anything is written to disk. Cheap for the operator and loud for the defender, which is why a chain that does this was assessed as rushed.
logic: Browser process as the ancestor of a command interpreter or a transfer utility, where the child writes an executable into a user-writable directory and that executable then runs. The ancestry is the detection; the individual images are all ordinary and several of them ship with the operating system.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "process" and xdm.source.process.name in (<browser_images>) and xdm.target.process.name in (<command_interpreters_and_transfer_utilities>)

markers.expr: child command line writes a file into a user-writable directory and that file is executed within the same process tree

caveat: Browsers legitimately launch helper processes, and some enterprise software drives a browser from a script, so an estate baseline of which browser-parented children are normal is a prerequisite. A chain that stays in memory produces none of this, so absence of the signal says nothing about whether a browser was exploited.

name: The browser's own extension integrity check is recomputed rather than bypassed
description: Chromium protects sensitive profile settings, including which extensions are installed, with a keyed checksum over each protected value and a master checksum over all of them. The inputs are a seed compiled into the browser binary, the logged-in user's account identifier and the value itself, all of which a local process running as that user can obtain. An installer that computes the checksums correctly gets an extension the browser accepts as legitimate, with no externally-installed warning and nothing to revert.
logic: A write to the browser's protected preferences file by a process that is not the browser and is not the managed deployment agent. The browser must be closed for the write to hold, so the durable shape is browser termination, a preferences write, and a relaunch, all within a short window and all driven by one non-browser process. Because the checksums end up valid, the browser reports nothing and an inventory of extensions taken from the browser's own view of itself will show the extension as legitimately installed.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.target.file.path ~= "(?i)\\\\User Data\\\\[^\\\\]+\\\\(Secure Preferences|Preferences)$" and xdm.source.process.name not in (<browser_images>)

markers.expr: writing process is the owning browser executable or an approved extension deployment agent
browser process terminated and relaunched by the same non-browser process within minutes of the preferences write
extension id listed in the browser profile is present in the approved extension list

caveat: This is the case where an inventory taken from inside the browser actively misleads: the extension verifies, so asking the browser what is installed returns a clean answer. The evidence has to come from outside the browser, which means file-write telemetry on the profile directory and the process that produced it. Managed extension deployment writes the same files, so the deployment agent has to be known and excluded first. The technique is publicly documented, so a match indicates the technique rather than any particular actor.

name: The command address arrives in a TXT record your resolver never sees
description: The payload carries a lookup hostname rather than a command-and-control address, and fetches the current address from that hostname's TXT record over DNS-over-HTTPS against a public resolver, decrypting the answer before use. The operator rotates infrastructure by editing a DNS record. Two defensive assumptions fail at once: the estate's DNS logs never see the query because it travelled inside HTTPS to somebody else's resolver, and blocklisting the retrieved address achieves nothing because the next answer differs.
logic: The observable is the process, not the query. A process that is neither a browser nor the configured system resolver making HTTPS requests to a public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint is the signal, corroborated by a first-seen outbound destination appearing on the same host minutes later. Where the estate forces DNS through its own resolvers, the same design shows up instead as the absence of any DNS query preceding a new outbound connection.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "network" and xdm.target.domain in (<public_doh_endpoints>) and xdm.source.process.name not in (<browser_and_resolver_processes>)

markers.expr: process issuing requests to a public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint is not a browser and not the configured system resolver
a first-seen outbound destination appears on the same host within minutes of that request

caveat: Browsers enable DNS-over-HTTPS by default in many configurations and some endpoint agents use it deliberately, so the requesting process is the whole discriminator and the protocol on its own is noise. The record type and the answer itself are not markers here, because over DNS-over-HTTPS neither is visible to the estate; where the estate forces DNS through its own resolvers the same design shows up instead as the absence of any DNS query preceding a new outbound connection, which is a different query shape. Blocking public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoints is a real control here but breaks legitimate software, so enumerate what in the estate uses it before enforcing. The lookup hostnames are disposable; the shape is not.

name: The fix is public upstream weeks before it is installable downstream
description: Software built on an open-source upstream inherits its fixes on a delay. The upstream commit is public the moment it lands, with a readable diff naming the flaw, while the downstream stable build that users can actually install follows weeks later. For anyone willing to read the commit, that interval is a window in which the vulnerability is fully described and nobody can patch it. Distinct from reverse engineering a shipped binary patch: here there is no reverse engineering to do, because the source change is published.
logic: A scheduling and hunt-scoping constraint rather than a query. For every product in the estate that is built on an open-source upstream, the exposure window opens at the upstream commit and not at the downstream advisory, so measure the interval from a downstream stable release being published to it being deployed, and compare it against the upstream-to-downstream lag the product habitually runs. When an indicator for such a product is later published, start the retrospective hunt at the upstream commit date.
xql_sketch: -- no detection query; the output is an inventory of downstream products joined to their upstream release lag and the estate's own deployment latency

markers.note: no bound is supplied; it is measured per product against the estate's own deployment records

markers.expr: product built on an open-source upstream whose published fix interval exceeds the estate's own deployment interval

caveat: Nothing here is observable in telemetry, and the window is invisible from outside: there is no advisory to alert on and no public proof of concept, because the commit is the proof of concept. It inverts the common prioritisation rule that an identifier with no published exploit can wait. It does not apply to closed-source products, where a binary diff is still required, and the lag differs sharply between downstream consumers of the same upstream, so it has to be measured per product rather than assumed.

name: An executable and the library it loads, written into the same directory together
description: Not a search-order hijack of a system library name. The operator drops a genuine, often signed, application executable and a malicious library of the name that executable loads into one user-writable directory, and runs the executable there. The load path is ordinary for that application, the library name is the application's own, and neither the image name nor the load location is anomalous on its own. What is anomalous is that both files arrived together, minutes earlier, into a directory an installer would not have used.
logic: An executable and a library it goes on to load were written into the same user-writable directory within a short window of each other, and the executable then runs from there. Where an encrypted data file is written into the same directory in the same window and is read by the library rather than by the executable, that is the payload and it is decrypted in memory, so nothing runnable is ever on disk to scan.
xql_sketch: dataset = <endpoint_dataset> | filter xdm.event.type = "file" and xdm.target.file.path ~= <user_writable_path_regex> | comp count() as written by <directory>, bin(_time, <window>) | filter written > 1   // an executable and the library it loads arriving together; join to the process start from that directory

markers.expr: an executable and a library it loads were written into the same user-writable directory within minutes of each other, and the executable ran from that directory
a file with no executable extension written into that same directory in the same window is read by the loaded library rather than by the executable
markers.note: the encrypted payload; present in some chains and absent in others, so corroborating rather than required
the user-writable trees where this shape is worth looking for; legitimate installers and updaters write here too, which is what the caveat is about

caveat: Portable and per-user applications legitimately ship their libraries beside their executables, and software updaters legitimately write an executable and its libraries together, so the write-together shape alone is noisy and needs the estate's own software distribution paths excluded first. Where the dropped executable is a genuine signed application binary its signature validates, so the signature is not a discriminator. Where the pair is fetched and run entirely in memory, none of this appears.

name: A forgotten platform utility used as the download channel
description: The platform ships a client for an obsolete directory protocol. It speaks to an arbitrary host on a fixed port, returns whatever that host sends, and is present on every installation. Used as a retrieval tool it needs no download, no script engine and no signature exception, and both the utility and its port are absent from almost every estate's legitimate traffic.
logic: Two independent controls, both cheap because the legitimate population is near zero: the utility executing at all, and outbound sessions to the protocol's port. Either is worth an alert on its own in an estate that has established it does not use the protocol, and establishing that takes one query over historical flow data. The marker set below is the endpoint control only, because markers in one set are conjunctive; the flow control is a second single-event filter on the protocol's port and belongs in its own block.

markers.expr: obsolete protocol utility executing on a host that has no history of executing it
utility output consumed directly by the shell rather than written to a file

caveat: The value of this one is that it is a denial decision as much as a detection: an estate that confirms it does not use the protocol can block the port and the binary and be done, which is rarely true of a living-off-the-land technique. Where a niche application does use it, the allow list is short and stable. The flow-side half is deliberately not in the marker set above: a process event and a flow record cannot both satisfy one conjunctive set, and combining them produces a filter that matches nothing.

name: It brought its own interpreter
description: Rather than using the platform's script engines, which are watched, the chain downloads a portable language runtime from the project's own release infrastructure, unpacks it into a user-writable directory and runs its scripts through that. The interpreter is legitimate, signed by its project, and absent from every rule keyed on the platform's own script hosts.
logic: The durable shape is an interpreter that arrived rather than one that was installed: a language runtime executing from a user profile or application data directory with no installation record, usually renamed, usually invoked with an inline script argument carrying a decode or decompress call. Retrieval from the project's official release page is what makes the download itself unremarkable, so the download is not the place to look.

markers.expr: language runtime executing from a user-writable directory with no corresponding installation record
interpreter image name differs from the original filename recorded in the binary

caveat: Developer and data science estates run portable interpreters legitimately and will match the first marker constantly, so this belongs on populations where a language runtime has no business appearing rather than everywhere. Application control that allow-lists by publisher will pass the interpreter, because it really is signed by its project. The retrieve-and-execute-in-memory half of the scenario is a network and memory test on a different event and belongs in its own block rather than in this conjunctive set.

name: Every infected host presents the same key
description: The implant authenticates to its command server with a credential compiled into the build and sent in a header of the author's own choosing, then carries a per-session token afterwards. The compiled-in half is the weakness: it is identical on every host that build reaches, so it is a fingerprint for the whole campaign rather than for one session.
logic: Count distinct hosts per value of any non-standard authentication header. A value shared by more than one host is either a deployed integration, which is enumerable, or a build credential, which is not supposed to exist. The header name and the paths are attacker choices and rotate; the one-value-many-hosts property is a consequence of compiling the key in and does not.

markers.expr: count_distinct(host) by non-standard authorisation header value
markers.note: more than one is the definitional minimum for a shared build credential, not a tuned bound

markers.expr: small fixed set of url paths polled by one host against one external destination
request body is base64 of non-printable content rather than json field values

caveat: This needs header visibility, which means either the traffic is not inside TLS or the estate decrypts it, and an implant that pins its server certificate removes that option entirely. Where that is the case, this whole scenario is unavailable and the destination and session shape are all an estate has; say so in the record rather than shipping a rule that cannot evaluate. Integrations legitimately share an API key across hosts, so the enumeration of those is the prerequisite; it is usually short.

name: The malware checks your proxy's certificate and hangs up
description: The client holds the expected server certificate hash in its own configuration and compares it during the handshake, dropping the connection when an inspecting proxy substitutes its own. The estate's decryption capability is not bypassed so much as declined, and the only thing left in the logs is a session that ended before any request was made.
logic: Inspection failures are usually treated as noise and excluded. Invert that: build the inventory of applications that legitimately pin, then treat a pin or decrypt failure to a destination outside that inventory as a lead, counted per client process and destination so that a one-off handshake problem does not surface. The absence of a request is the evidence, which is why it needs looking for deliberately rather than arriving as an alert.

markers.expr: tls session terminated by the client immediately after the server certificate is presented, with no request sent
decrypt or pin failure recorded for a destination absent from the pinned-application inventory
count of inspection failures by client process and destination
markers.note: more than one is the definitional minimum for a repeat; the bound that separates an implant from an ordinary pinned client has to be measured in the estate and is left unresolved here

caveat: Legitimate pinned clients behave identically and are numerous enough that the inventory is the whole cost of this. The wider consequence is worth stating to whoever owns the decision: interception coverage is not detection coverage, because the traffic that most wants hiding is the traffic most likely to refuse interception.

name: The commands look like a shell, but no shell ever runs
description: The operator types what look like ordinary administrative commands, and the implant services them inside its own process through direct API and management-instrumentation calls instead of launching an interpreter. Command names in the operator's console have no relationship to anything the host records, because nothing is executed as a command.
logic: A detection library built on process creation and command-line content has no coverage of this, and that is the finding. Where a sensor records native API and management instrumentation activity, the shape is one process performing broad host and account discovery with no child processes at all, which is the opposite of what discovery normally looks like, joined against process-creation telemetry that carries nothing to account for it. Where the sensor does not record it, the coverage question has to be answered before any rule is written.

markers.expr: one process performing account, group, process, service and security product discovery with no child process created
management instrumentation queries issued by a process outside the inventory and management agent set
discovery output leaving the host with no process-creation events to account for it

caveat: Confirm what the sensor records before designing around this. Many endpoint products record process creation richly and native API calls barely at all, in which case the honest answer is that this activity is invisible and the network side is the only place left to look. Treating a quiet host as a clean host is the specific error this exists to prevent. A command set of this kind usually still contains one or two commands that do create a process, so check the set before concluding that a process-creation rule sees nothing at all.

name: The setting changed, and the cmdlet never ran
description: A security product's configuration is exposed both as an administrative cmdlet and as a management-instrumentation class. Detections are almost always written against the cmdlet name, because that is how administrators do it, and a caller that goes to the class directly changes the same setting without any of them firing.
logic: Watch the setting, not the command. The product's own configuration-change record is the authoritative event and is produced whichever route made the change. Pair it with management-instrumentation activity against the product's namespace from a process with no management role, and treat a change with no matching administrative action as the finding.

markers.expr: security product configuration change recorded with no corresponding administrative command on the host
management instrumentation connection to the security product's namespace by a process outside the management agent inventory
protection or real-time scanning setting moved to a weaker value outside a change window

caveat: Management agents change these settings legitimately through the same route, so the agent inventory has to come first. Do not add an exclusion for the administrative shell being absent from the host: it runs routinely on managed estates and such a clause removes the population the rule exists to find. The general lesson is worth carrying past any one product: where a control has two administrative surfaces, a rule on one of them is coverage of neither.

name: A startup entry that could never have worked
description: Persistence written incorrectly is still written. A startup value whose command cannot resolve to anything, or a component registration pointing at a class nothing references, are artefacts no installer produces, which makes a broken attempt a cleaner signal than a working one.
logic: Two tests, both about validity rather than location, which is what the existing startup-entry rules key on. A startup value whose data names a binary with no arguments it requires, or names a path that does not exist. And a newly created component registration under a class identifier that no installed product claims, which is the shape of a component hijack attempt that generated its own identifier instead of replacing one. The key marker below is written as one alternation so that either location matches; a set carrying both locations as separate conjunctive markers can never match an event.

markers.expr: startup value data references a path that does not exist, or a loader binary with no module argument
component registration created under a class identifier claimed by no installed product

caveat: Uninstalled software leaves startup values pointing at paths that no longer exist, so resolve against the removal history before treating a dangling entry as malicious. The component-registration half is the stronger of the two and needs a view of which class identifiers installed products actually claim. The two computed markers describe the two branches and are alternatives in practice, so a consumer building one rule per branch will get better results than one rule carrying both.

name: The script engine ran, its executable did not
description: The platform's scripting engine is a library before it is a program. A process that loads the runtime and the automation assembly can execute scripts with none of the process creation, command line or window that every detection assumes, and with the engine's own logging dependent on a host that did not have to honour it.
logic: The module-load pair is the detection: the managed runtime and the scripting automation assembly loaded into a process that is not the scripting engine's own executable and is not a known managed host. It requires image-load telemetry, which is the first thing to check, and the population of legitimate hosts is small enough to enumerate.

markers.expr: process loads the managed runtime and the scripting automation assembly and is not the scripting engine's own executable
process loading the automation assembly is absent from the managed-host inventory
scripting engine activity present with no corresponding script engine process creation

caveat: Management agents and administrative tooling host the runtime this way by design, so the inventory is the cost. Where image loads are not recorded, this cannot be written at all and the compensating question is whether the scripting engine's own logging is even produced by a hosted engine, which should be tested rather than assumed. A cached output file left by the hosted engine is residue, not a detection, unless its content is tested as well as its path.
